matches.segment_text: 1 Global Security Environment Current trends in the security environment have several features. First, states that do not share universal values or political and economic systems based on such values are expanding their influence. Unilateral changes to the status quo by force and such attempts represent significant challenges to the free and open international order underpinned by the rule of law. Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has revealed this in a most blatant way. The international community is facing its greatest post-war trial yet and has entered a new era of crisis. In addition, the global power balance has significantly changed, and interstate competition across the political, economic and military spheres is emerging. The interstate competition between China and the United States in particular is expected to further intensify in various fields. Second, rapid advances in science and technology are fundamentally changing the paradigm of security. Countries are striving to develop cutting-edge technologies that could dramatically alter the character of warfare and thus prove to become “game changers.” The organization of military and the methods and means of warfare are changing. Third, there exists a range of global security challenges such as increasingly serious risks in cyber and other domains, information warfare, including the spread of disinformation, and climate change. In addition, gray zone situations over territories are constantly occurring. It is highly likely that hybrid warfare, combining military and non-military means to achieve military objectives, such as information warfare that utilizes the spread of disinformation prior to an armed attack, will be conducted in an even more sophisticated form in the time ahead. In cyber, maritime, space, and electromagnetic domains and other areas, the risks that impede free access and utilization of these areas are becoming increasingly serious.

In particular, the threat of cyberattacks, in which the risk of exposure is relatively low and where attackers have an advantage, is growing rapidly. Cyberattacks have been used constantly to disable or destroy critical infrastructures, interfere in foreign elections, demand ransoms, and steal sensitive information, even in the form of state-sponsored cyberattacks. Furthermore, addressing those issues not necessarily deemed as security targets in the past, such as supply chain vulnerabilities, increasing threats to critical infrastructures, and leadership struggles over advanced technologies, has also become a major security challenge. As a result, the scope of security has expanded to include the economic sector, making economic measures even more necessary to ensure security. Overview Gray Zone Situations So-called “gray zone” situations simply represent a wide range of situations that are neither peacetime nor wartime. In a gray zone situation, for example, a country that confronts another over territory, sovereignty or maritime and other economic interests uses some forceful organization to demonstrate its presence in the relevant disputed region in a bid to alter the status quo or force other countries to accept its assertions or demands.

KEY WORD Hybrid Warfare The so-called “hybrid warfare” represents methods intentionally blurring the boundaries between the military and non-military realms, forcing affected actors to take complex measures that are not limited to military actions. The means of hybrid warfare include operations using military units of unidentified nationality, cyberattacks to affect communications and other critical infrastructure, the spread of disinformation through the internet and the media, and other influential operations. The combination of these measures is considered to amount to hybrid warfare. In hybrid warfare, a country takes measures that are difficult to identify definitively as an “armed attack” based on its outward appearance. It is said that such an approach is taken with the intent to make it difficult for the target country to address the situation, such as delaying the military’s initial response, while denying the attacker country’s own involvement.

2 Security Environment in the Indo-Pacific Region The global security environment and challenges articulated above are particularly prominent in the Indo-Pacific region, where Japan is situated, and may get severer in the future. The Indo-Pacific region is the core of global vitality, home to more than half of the world’s population. The dynamism of the intersection of the Pacific and the Indian Oceans is a growth engine for the global economy. Japan, situated in this region, is well positioned to benefit from this. At the same time, the Indo-Pacific region faces a host of security challenges. For example, several nations and regions that possess large military forces, including nuclear weapons, do not share universal values, nor political and economic systems based on such universal values. Furthermore, there exists a complex intertwining of diplomatic and other relations based on historical backgrounds. In the case of Japan, the territorial issues of the Northern Territories and Takeshima, which are inherent territories of Japan, remain unresolved. In addition, Japan faces threats and challenges of various types and intensities, such as attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion in the East and South China Seas and other areas, piracy, terrorism, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and natural disasters. Japan is facing the most severe and complex security environment since the end of World War II. Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has easily breached the very foundation of the rules that shape the international order. The possibility cannot be precluded that a similar serious situation may arise in the future in the Indo-Pacific region, especially in East Asia. Across the globe, historical changes in power balances, particularly in the Indo-Pacific region, are occurring. The Indo-Pacific is a region in which a complex mix of continents, peninsulas, and islands are located within a vast geographical area. Japan is not in an environment in which it is connected to other countries primarily by land borders as are China, Russia, the Korean Peninsula, and Europe, but taking into account cases such as Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, we cannot deny the possibility that even regions far away across the ocean could have an impact on Japan’s security. Generally speaking, as cross-border economic activities and flows of people grow, events occurring in geographically distant regions begin to have an impact on other regions through the transactions and flows of people among regions. In the military sphere, these kinds of links are being seen in the form of the transfer of military equipment and military technologies among regions, the stationing of units in other countries, and the dispatch of personnel and military assets to other countries, among other developments. There is a possibility that these activities could have an impact on the military balance and the military activities in the region. It is believed that the aggression against Ukraine shows the military links between Europe and the Indo-Pacific. One notable example of this is the progress in Russia-North Korea military cooperation. It has become clear that Russia-North Korea military cooperation is progressing in the form of the procurement of weapons and ammunition made in North Korea, including ballistic missiles, in the aggression against Ukraine and their use against Ukraine, as well as the dispatch of North Korean soldiers to Russia. In addition, there is a risk that nuclear and missile-related technologies could be transferred to North Korea by Russia, and the possibility that this could have an impact on the military balance in the Indo-Pacific region in the medium to long term has not been denied. In this way, events in one region can have a multilayered impact on the security environments of other regions. Commentary The Impact on Japan of the Links among the Security Environments of Each Region There are several countries and regions surrounding Japan that have large-scale military forces, including nuclear weapons, and missile forces that can serve as a means of delivering nuclear weapons have increased significantly in both quality and quantity, so missile attacks on Japan are a real threat. It has been noted that countries and regions in the vicinity of Japan possess missiles capable of attacking other nations in quantities already numbering in the thousands, and that they are further increasing these quantities. For example, it has been reported that for weapons with a range of 300 km or above, China currently possesses over 3,000 ground-launched missiles alone, along with a current cache of 1,000 land attack cruise missiles, a number that is expected to rise to 5,000 by 2035. In addition, it is estimated that North Korea currently possesses 700 to 1,000 ballistic missiles in total. Russia also possesses a variety of different missiles, including about 350 intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), and it is believed to have launched over 13,000 missile attacks during its aggression against Ukraine. Moreover, the increase in missile forces is also being seen in the form of development of hypersonic weapons, enhancement of precision strike capability, and increase and diversification of launch platforms, among other developments. In particular, hypersonic weapons fly at lower altitudes than normal ballistic missiles, thus delaying detection. It is considered that their great maneuvering capabilities make it difficult to predict their trajectories and impact points, making their interception more difficult.

For example, it has been pointed out that in 2020 China began operating DF-17s, which are said to be medium-range ballistic missiles, as ballistic missiles capable of carrying Hypersonic Glide Vehicles (HGVs), and it has been pointed out that China may have deployed DF-27s, which are said to be long-range ballistic missiles, as well. North Korea has been repeatedly launching missiles it calls “hypersonic missiles.” Russia is also proceeding with the deployment of the HGV “Avangard” and the Hypersonic Cruise Missile (HCM) “Zircon” and is using the “Zircon” against Ukraine. The Ministry of Defense (MOD) is working to ceaselessly strengthen the quality and quantity of Japan’s missile defense capabilities. However, it is believed that it will become increasingly difficult to fully respond to this threat with the existing missile defense network alone, particularly if Japan continues to rely solely on the means of missile defense. Therefore, in the event of a missile attack by an adversary, Japan will use its missile defense network to intercept incoming missiles while preventing further armed attacks from the adversary through counterstrike capabilities as an absolute minimum self-defense measure that is unavoidably necessary in cases where it is recognized that no other means are available. Through these initiatives, the MOD hopes to deter the occurrence itself of armed attacks by enhancing Japan’s deterrence and response capabilities. 1 General Situation Russia’s aggression against Ukraine undermines the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. It is a serious violation of international law, including the United Nations Charter, which prohibits the use of force. Such unilateral changes to the status quo by force have shaken the very foundation of the international order, including in Asia. In addition, brutal and inhumane acts committed by Russia have been revealed throughout Ukraine. The murder of numerous innocent civilians is a grave violation of international humanitarian law (IHL) and a war crime, and utterly unforgivable. After the end of World War II, denial of unilateral changes to the status quo by force became one of the foundations of international order. But, Russia, a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), which is supposed to take primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, is now openly taking military actions challenging international law and the international order, claiming innocent lives, and repeatedly issuing statements implying the use of nuclear weapons. This is an unprecedented situation. If such Russian aggression is tolerated, it could send a message with the wrong implication that unilateral changes to the status quo by force are acceptable in other regions as well, including Asia. Therefore, the international community, including Japan, should not tolerate Russia’s action. The international community works together in solidarity against Russia’s aggression by imposing sanctions against Russia and continuing to provide Ukraine with equipment such as tanks, artillery, and ammunition in order to support Ukraine’s efforts to defend itself and eject the Russian military from Ukraine. The future developments surrounding Russia’s aggression against Ukraine remain unpredictable. Japan needs to monitor the related situation closely with grave concern.

2 Russia’s Aggression against Ukraine and the Future Outlook

1 The Failure of Russia’s Blitzkrieg and Ukraine’s Successful Defense On February 24, 2022, Russia started full-scale aggression against Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed the clear intention to remain in Kyiv from the early stage of the aggression, and the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) and other military and para-military units obstructed the advance of the main units of the Armed Forces of Russian Federation (AFRF) in the suburbs of the capital, which caused heavy losses for AFRF, which intended to take control of the city within a short time period. It is pointed out that Russia’s goal to eliminate the Zelenskyy administration failed after the AFU fought off the AFRF in the Kyiv direction in the end of March through the early April. The AFU successfully defended Kharkiv in northeastern Ukraine, the country’s second-largest city and a major transportation hub. Meanwhile, the Russian forces made territorial gains in southern Ukraine more quickly than in other areas. The AFRF occupied Kherson, the capital city of Kherson oblast on the west bank of the Dnipro River, in early March 2022, and temporarily advanced further west in the direction of Mykolayiv, the capital city of Mykolayiv oblast. It is probable that the AFU strived to conceal its plan for the counteroffensive in the northeast, unlike in the south where the counteroffensive was conspicuous. (2) Russia’s Response Russia responded in various ways to Ukraine’s full-fledged counteroffensive, such as with troop buildups and making its occupation of Ukrainian territory a fait accompli. With respect to the buildup of forces, President Vladimir Putin signed executive orders related to partial mobilization in September 2022. Regarding the mobilization, then Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said that he was planning to mobilize some 300,000 reservists. Regarding Russia’s fait accompli of the occupied areas in Ukraine, Russia illegally “annexed” four regions of the occupied areas in the oblasts of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson based on the results of a “referendum” conducted in the area in September to ask the people whether their territory was to be “annexed” to Russia or not. In addition, the AFRF has built multi-layered defenses, including trenches, anti-tank ditches, concrete anti-tank obstacles known as “Dragon’s Teeth” and minefields along the entire contact line in anticipation of counterattacks by the AFU. At the same time, the AFRF has intensified bombardments with missiles and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) loitering munitions all over Ukraine. This was apparently aimed at depleting Ukraine’s air defense missile reserves and weakening Ukraine’s sustained operational capability (SOC) and will to fight by damaging power grids critical for civilian life in winter and increasing civilian casualties. While the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) estimates the number of noncombatant victims caused by the Russian attack in Ukraine amount to be over 15,000 as of January 2026, the actual number is possibly much higher as accurate numbers cannot be determined due to the ongoing fighting, and the number is still increasing now. In January 2023, the Russian military and the private military company (PMC) “Wagner” intensified their offensive in the eastern Donetsk oblast. In May 2023, they seemed to have taken control of Bakhmut, a key transportation hub in the oblast.

4 Stagnation of Ukrainian Counteroffensive on the Zaporizhzhia Front in 2023 and Russian Eastern Offensive (1) Provision of Western Weapons to Ukraine and Stagnation of the Ukrainian Counteroffensive While thrown on the defensive in the face of the offensive on the Bakhmut front by the Russian military and other forces, the Ukrainian military received various equipment from Western countries, including main battle tanks such as the “Leopard 2A6” and “Challenger 2” and air-launched long-

4 Stagnation of Ukrainian Counteroffensive on the Zaporizhzhia Front in 2023 and Russian Eastern Offensive (1) Provision of Western Weapons to Ukraine and Stagnation of the Ukrainian Counteroffensive While thrown on the defensive in the face of the offensive on the Bakhmut front by the Russian military and other forces, the Ukrainian military received various equipment from Western countries, including main battle tanks such as the “Leopard 2A6” and “Challenger 2” and air-launched long-

range cruise missiles such as the “Storm Shadow.” It seems to have been preparing a counteroffensive by reorganizing its new units and training its soldiers in Europe. The Ukrainian military is believed to have launched a counteroffensive in early June 2023 and sequentially recaptured multiple villages, centering on the front of southern Zaporizhzhia oblast. However, the Ukrainian military is also said to have suffered significant losses in personnel and equipment as its advance was blocked by numerous antipersonnel mines and anti-tank mines laid by Russian forces and anti-tank missiles from attack helicopters. The Ukrainian military’s counteroffensive seemed to be aimed at breaking through the Russian military’s defensive line in the southern Zaporizhzhia oblast to advance southward down to the Sea of Azov, thereby cutting off the Russian military’s land logistics route connecting mainland Russia and the Crimean Peninsula. However, it appears that the original goals were not achieved. Ukraine seemed to be lacking in firepower, short-range air defense system to cover advancing units, mine-clearing equipment and trained manpower. These shortages likely brought the counteroffensive to a halt. In October 2023, the United States provided Ukraine with the Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), a surface-to-surface ballistic missile system. However, no major breakthrough was achieved in ground operations. In November 2023, President Zelenskyy ordered the construction of defensive positions in preparation for a Russian military offensive, and the Ukrainian military was on the defensive. (2) Intensifying Russian Military Offensives and Missile Attacks in Eastern Ukraine Russian forces allegedly intensified their offensive on the Avdiivka and Bakhmut fronts in Donetsk oblast and the Kupiansk front in Kharkiv oblast from October 2023. In February 2024, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that Russia had taken control of Avdiivka. In addition, since late December 2023, the Russian military has intensified its missile attacks across Ukraine. While the missile attacks in the winter of 2022 targeted power grids, some observers have pointed out that the targets of the missile attacks in the winter of 2023 were military industries, with an eye on a protracted war. This trend continued into the spring of 2024, while a shortage of air defense equipment led to exacerbating damage to Ukraine.

5 Ongoing Eastern Offensives and the Kharkiv Offensive by Russia, and Cross-border Attacks into Russia by Ukraine in 2024 (1) Ongoing Eastern Offensives and the Start of the Kharkiv Offensive by the AFRF As the AFU faced a shortage of artillery, shells, air-defense missiles, and other supplies, the AFRF, after taking control of Avdiivka, continued with its offensives to the west toward Pokrovsk, a key transportation hub. From April 2024, the AFRF also strengthened its offensive operations against Chasiv Yar, which is located in the highlands of the Bakhmut front. At the same time, although support from the United States had stagnated since December 2023 due to delays in approving the budget, the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act was enacted at the end of April 2024. The resumption of support seemed to mitigate Ukraine’s shortage of air-defense missiles and reduce the artillery-firepower gap. In May 2024, the AFRF launched an offensive against Kharkiv oblast. Although it was able to seize many villages on that front within about a week, the situation on the Kharkiv front appears to have reached a stalemate. It has been pointed out that the purpose of the offensive was to establish a buffer zone to prevent cross-border attacks into the Russian territory and to divert the Ukrainian forces away from eastern Ukraine, the main fronts of attacks. (2) Cross-border Attacks into Russia by the AFU and Territorial Gains in Eastern Ukraine by the AFRF Around June 2024, in response to Russia’s offensive against Kharkiv, the United States, the United Kingdom and certain European countries gave Ukraine the permission to attack Russian territory near the border using weapons provided by them except long-range missiles. In early August 2024, the AFU launched a cross-border attack on the Russian oblast of Kursk, which is adjacent to the border of northeastern Ukraine, and secured territory around Sudzha in the oblast. In terms of the meaning of this cross-border attack, in February 2025, President Zelenskyy proposed a plan to exchange the occupied Kursk oblast area for territory held by Russia if Russia commences negotiations. Meanwhile, the Russian military continued its offensive against eastern Ukraine beyond August 2024, while responding to cross-border attacks into Kursk oblast. A Ukrainian thermal power plant severely damaged by Russian missile and drone attacks (February 2026) [AFP-Jiji]

Although it was able to seize many villages on that front within about a week, the situation on the Kharkiv front appears to have reached a stalemate. It has been pointed out that the purpose of the offensive was to establish a buffer zone to prevent cross-border attacks into the Russian territory and to divert the Ukrainian forces away from eastern Ukraine, the main fronts of attacks. (2) Cross-border Attacks into Russia by the AFU and Territorial Gains in Eastern Ukraine by the AFRF Around June 2024, in response to Russia’s offensive against Kharkiv, the United States, the United Kingdom and certain European countries gave Ukraine the permission to attack Russian territory near the border using weapons provided by them except long-range missiles. In early August 2024, the AFU launched a cross-border attack on the Russian oblast of Kursk, which is adjacent to the border of northeastern Ukraine, and secured territory around Sudzha in the oblast. In terms of the meaning of this cross-border attack, in February 2025, President Zelenskyy proposed a plan to exchange the occupied Kursk oblast area for territory held by Russia if Russia commences negotiations. Meanwhile, the Russian military continued its offensive against eastern Ukraine beyond August 2024, while responding to cross-border attacks into Kursk oblast. They steadily gained territory, particularly in the direction of Pokrovsk and further south toward the Kurakhove area. In December 2024, the AFRF reached the vicinity of Pokrovsk, and, in January 2025, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that it had taken control of Kurakhove. Since late August 2024, the Ukrainian military is believed to have been striving to hold on to the occupied areas in the Kursk oblast. However, at the end of April 2025, Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov reported to President Putin that the entire oblast had been recaptured. He also stated that North Korean soldiers participated in the recapture of the area. Meanwhile, on the same day, the General Staff of the AFU declared that Ukrainian forces were continuing defensive operations in Kursk.

6 Continuation of Russia’s Eastern Offensive in 2025 and Expansion of Operations to the South Around May 2025, the AFRF continued their offensive toward Pokrovsk in Donetsk oblast while also conducting attacks against Ukraine’s Sumy oblast, which borders Russia’s Kursk oblast. On May 2, the Russian Ministry of Defence also stated that efforts to establish a “security zone” in the border areas of Sumy oblast were ongoing. On the other hand, in June, General Oleksandr Syrskyi, Commander-in-Chief of the AFU, stated that the Russian offensive in the border areas of Sumy oblast had been halted and that the front line had stabilized, suggesting that the fighting there had reached a stalemate. During this period, while there were no major changes along the Pokrovsk front, the AFRF units operating south of Pokrovsk continued to advance gradually toward Dnipropetrovsk oblast, located west of Donetsk oblast, and are believed to have begun attacks into Dnipropetrovsk oblast in July 2025. Beginning around September of the same year, observers began pointing out that Russia noticeably advanced toward the Hulyaipole direction in Zaporizhzhia oblast farther to the south, and in November Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi stated that the situation in that sector had deteriorated significantly. Furthermore, regarding the Pokrovsk front, at the end of October 2025, the General Staff of the AFU stated that the AFRF had concentrated approximately 200 troops inside Pokrovsk City by infiltrating small infantry units through gaps between AFU defensive positions. It has been pointed out that, as the infiltrating Russian soldiers spread out in all directions, Ukrainian defenses began to collapse, and the situation within the city reportedly deteriorated rapidly. As of March 2026, the city is believed to be under Russian occupation.

In addition, regarding the Siversk direction in Donetsk oblast, in December 2025 the commander of the Russian unit responsible for that sector informed President Putin that the AFRF had captured the city of Siversk, thereby creating conditions for an advance toward Sloviansk, a strategic hub located west of Siversk. Russian offensives against Sloviansk are currently ongoing. Meanwhile, in the Kupiansk direction in Kharkiv oblast, the city was subjected to Russian attacks for a period of time, with Andrii Besedin, head of the Kupiansk City Military Administration, stating at the end of September 2025 that Russian forces were present within the city. However, in mid-December, Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi announced that the AFU had succeeded in repelling Russian troops and had regained control of approximately 90% of the city. During the same year, Russian forces also continued missile and UAV attacks across Ukraine. In particular, the number of long-range UAVs flying into Ukraine increased substantially from around May onward, placing a growing burden on Ukraine’s air defense network. In addition, in January 2026, in retaliation for what Russia claimed was a Ukrainian UAV attack on the Russian presidential residence at the end of December 2025, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that it had conducted a large-scale strike against Ukrainian UAV production facilities and energy infrastructure using long-range precision-guided weapons and UAVs, including the new “Oreshnik” intermediate-range ballistic missile. The Russian Ministry of Defence further stated that the attack had rendered an aircraft repair facility in Lviv oblast in western Ukraine inoperable. Furthermore, the AFRF continued attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure during the winter period from 2025 into 2026, and in January 2026 President Zelenskyy stated that power outages had occurred across 60% of Kyiv City. In addition, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that it had also used the Oreshnik missile in an attack on Ukraine in May 2026. At the same time, Ukraine has been conducting attacks against Russian territory, primarily using long-range UAVs, with the aim of degrading Russian offensive capabilities among other objectives. 7 Russia’s Attack on Nuclear Power Stations and Nuclear Facilities and the Situation Surrounding Nuclear, Biological and Chemical (NBC) Weapons Russia repeatedly takes dangerous actions around nuclear facilities in the ongoing aggression against Ukraine. Russia occupied the Chornobyl nuclear power plant near the Belarusian border in February 2022 and also occupied the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine in March 2022. In addition, Russia attacked the Kharkiv Institute of Physics and Technology (KIPT), which has experimental reactors and handles nuclear substances, multiple times in and after March. Regarding nuclear weapons, in September 2022, President Putin stated that Russia would use every possible means to repel threats to the territorial integrity of the nation, including nuclear capabilities. Furthermore, in May 2024, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that it would conduct exercises to test non-strategic nuclear forces for the first time since the collapse of the Soviet Union in response to provocative statements and threats from Western officials. In November 2024, it was reported that Western countries had given their permission to utilize long-range missiles provided by them in attacks against Russian territory, and Ukraine used the ATACMS to launch an attack against Russian territory for the first time. On the day of this attack, Russia announced a revised version of a policy document they had previously indicated, Basic Principles of State Policy of the Russian Federation on Nuclear Deterrence, which is equivalent to its so-called nuclear doctrine. Two days later, as a countermeasure in response to the attack on Russian territory using long-range weapons supplied by Western countries, President Putin announced that Russia had attacked the Ukrainian city of Dnipro by using the new “Oreshnik” type of intermediate-range ballistic missile, an attack he called a test. In this way, with nuclear weapons clearly in mind, Russia has repeated behavior and statements which can be interpreted as nuclear blackmail. Russia has repeatedly claimed that Ukraine may use chemical and biological weapons, while the United States and the United Kingdom assesses that Russia’s claim is a preparation for the so-called “false flag campaign.”1 In May 2024, the U.S. Department of State stated that Russia had used chemical weapons. contributed to the capture of Bakhmut in the eastern Donetsk oblast by deploying numerous troops. However, subsequent discord between the military and Wagner led to Prigozhin instigating an “armed rebellion” in June 2023. In an effort to prevent the recurrence of such an armed uprising, Russia’s Defence Ministry has been encouraging former “Wagner” soldiers to sign contracts with the military. It has also been pointed out that the Ministry is trying to centralize the chain of command by managing other private military companies under the control of the General Staff Office. The AFU continues fighting today undauntedly against the AFRF which has superior quality and larger numbers. Continuation of fighting is made possible by several factors such as a number of reservists with combat experience derived from the eastern front campaign since 2014, significant progress in training non-commissioned officers who assume leading roles in battle realized with the reorganization of the Defense Ministry and the AFU aiming to achieve the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) standard and the introduction of rapid and highly accurate fire coordination systems based on commercial off-the-shelf technologies including the command and control support software “GIS Arta” and situational awareness system “Delta.” In terms of human SOC, it is pointed out that the number of casualties was about 500,000 to 600,000 for the AFU and around 1.2 million for the AFRF as of January 2026.3 As a result of the fighting dragging on, it seems that both Russia and Ukraine are facing an increasingly serious shortage of personnels. In June 2023, President Putin signed a law allowing prisoners and suspects, excluding felons, to sign military service contracts. In October 2023, the military personnel registration regulations were revised to include a new provision for “special military personnel registration,” which has facilitated the enlistment of prisoners without requiring a physical examination. Such measures have created an environment for deploying prisoners more quickly in actual combat operations. In addition, in July 2024, President Putin signed an executive order to approximately double the enlistment bonus paid by the federal government to newly contracted military personnel. In November of the same year, he signed a federal law stipulating partial debt relief for newly contracted military personnel and others. This seems to be part of the government’s efforts to secure manpower by increasing the number of contracted military personnel. Meanwhile, in Ukraine, although President Zelenskyy signed legislation in April 2024 lowering the minimum mobilization age from 27 to 25, Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi stated in January 2025 that such mobilization alone was not enough to satisfy the needs of the front line, and that Ukraine was taking personnel reduction measures within reasonable limits in logistics, support, and servicing components. He also stated that it was necessary to transfer personnel from other divisions to infantry, and mentioned that approximately 70,000 personnel had been reassigned to combat units in February 2025. Ukraine also faces problems that include the desertion of soldiers. In November 2024, President Zelenskyy signed a law that would protect first-time deserters from criminal liability if they voluntarily returned to their units. In January 2026, Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov stated that approximately two million people were wanted on suspicion of evading mobilization and that around 200,000 personnel had deserted. Ukraine is believed to be struggling to secure manpower. Against this backdrop, President Zelenskyy and others announced in February 2025 the launch of the “Drone Line” initiative, which integrates UAVs into frontline operations. The initiative reduces requirements for defensive positions by continuously operating UAVs to create areas in which ground forces cannot move without suffering losses. Furthermore, in the same month, Ukraine announced the introduction of “Contract 18-24,” a volunteer enlistment system targeting young people aged 18 to 24 that provides preferential measures such as lump-sum payments upon enlistment.4 It is pointed out that Russia’s SOC for materiel has been undermined by hindered equipment acquisition caused by economic sanctions against the country. Even in this situation, the Russian military maintains its power by various means, such as the ammunition industry operating around the clock, diverting missiles not used for ground attacks, the acquisition of UAVs made in Iran, taking over tanks from Belarus, and the procurement of ammunition and missiles from North Korea. Furthermore, it is pointed out that Russia is capable of continuing war for a long period of time, even under sanctions, because it has sufficient production capacities for equipment including ammunition belonging to the technical scope of the former Soviet Union.

Meanwhile, the equipment used by the AFU is believed to consist primarily of former Soviet-made systems and equipment provided by Western countries and others. In recent years, however, Ukraine is believed to have been working to expand domestically produced equipment, particularly unmanned assets, while also promoting joint production with European countries. In terms of equipment manufactured in the former Soviet Union, only limited parts and ammunition can be acquired from outside of Russia. In addition, although some equipment can be repaired or acquired domestically, it is difficult to carry out such repair or acquisition because the major ammunition industrial cities, such as Kharkiv and Dnipro, are within the attack range of the Russian ground forces. Therefore, support from foreign countries is important in the acquisition of equipment and ammunition as well as in education and training to change over former Soviet Union equipment to Western equipment to maintain SOC. In addition, in September 2025, President Zelenskyy stated that approximately 60% of the weapons possessed by the AFU were domestically produced. Ukraine is currently developing its domestically produced long-range cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, strengthening its long-range strike capabilities against Russia. Ukraine is also believed to be developing a domestically produced air defense system. Regarding peace negotiations, from January 2026 onward, the United States, Russia, and Ukraine held a series of intermittent trilateral meetings. It has been announced that discussions during these meetings covered documents related to peace as well as reconstruction, the economy, territory, and security guarantees for Ukraine. The progress of the peace negotiations remains unpredictable, and fighting between Russian and Ukrainian forces is expected to continue even as the talks proceed. Ukraine is currently developing its domestically produced long-range cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, strengthening its long-range strike capabilities against Russia. Ukraine is also believed to be developing a domestically produced air defense system. Regarding peace negotiations, from January 2026 onward, the United States, Russia, and Ukraine held a series of intermittent trilateral meetings. It has been announced that discussions during these meetings covered documents related to peace as well as reconstruction, the economy, territory, and security guarantees for Ukraine. The progress of the peace negotiations remains unpredictable, and fighting between Russian and Ukrainian forces is expected to continue even as the talks proceed. • Effects of Russian Aggression against Ukraine on International Affairs and How Various Countries Respond to It

1 General Situation In response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, in addition to Ukraine’s own strong resistance, the international community has implemented strong coordinated sanctions and other measures against Russia. In Europe, the security environment has reached a major turning point in the wake of the aggression against Ukraine, with countries not only increasing their defense spending but also Finland and Sweden, which had previously advocated policies of neutrality, joining NATO. Clearly, the aggression by Russia, which saw NATO’s eastward expansion as a threat to itself, prompted European countries to shift their security policies in this manner. In this view, Japan needs to pay attention to the future developments of the situation in Europe, including its strategic effects and recognize that Euro-Atlantic security and Indo-Pacific security are inseparable. This is because Japan is a close ally of the United States, a NATO member state and is located on the opposite side of Europe across the Eurasian Continent where Russia also sits. In addition, the change in the European situation in response to the Russian aggression against Ukraine can also have an impact on global affairs including developments of the strategic competition between the United States and China and impact on Asia. In any case, it is necessary to monitor the related situations closely with great interest.

2 How NATO Member States and Other Countries Deal with the Situation Russia’s aggression against Ukraine prompted a rapidly growing alarm amid European countries, and Russia’s aggressive actions are being viewed as the most severe and direct threat to European and northern Atlantic security.5 With renewed awareness of the threat of Russia, NATO member states direct their efforts at enhancing defense cooperation under the collective defense system of NATO and pursue the development of defense capabilities in each country. For example, the unit scale in the eastern direction is expanded as needed, and an agreement has been made to put 300,000 and more troops into high readiness conditions in place of NATO Response Forces. Chapter 3, Section 9-2 (Enhancement of Multilateral Security Frameworks) Several nations including NATO member states provide equipment, training support and the like to Ukraine depending on the progress of the war. At the beginning of the war, the donor countries provided portable anti-tank missiles and man-portable surface-to-air missiles that seemed to contribute to preventing front-line expansion by delaying the advancement of Russian military armored units and reducing the strength of airborne troops. After the AFU stopped Russia’s full-scale aggression, the countries moved toward providing large equipment that helps suppress and secure wide areas in ground fighting, such as tanks, armored vehicles and howitzers, for the Ukrainian military’s counteroffensive. In January 2023, each country announced for the first time the provision of tanks and infantry fighting vehicles not made by the former Soviet Union, beginning with the delivery of German tanks to Ukraine by Poland in February of the same year. They also came to provide longer-range artillery to attack enemy bases, following the concentration of AFRF troops in the eastern Ukraine region. Furthermore, the handing over of air defense systems from various countries rapidly progressed as a result of Russian armed forces commencing missile attacks targeting the entirety of Ukraine, including civil facilities, starting in October

5 NATO adopted a new Strategic Concept for the first time since 2010 in the summit meeting held in June 2022. In the previous strategic concept, the Europe-Atlantic region was considered peaceful and the possibility of an attack on the NATO territory was considered small; however, in the current strategic concept, the Europe-Atlantic region is not considered peaceful and the possibility of an attack on the member states’ territories is deemed impossible to rule out. Furthermore, Russia, with which a “genuine strategic partnership” was pursued in the previous strategic concept, has been positioned as “the most serious and direct threat to the security of the member states and the peace and stability of the Europe-Atlantic region.” and the United Kingdom and the Netherlands stated in May that the two countries would establish an “international union” for fighter jets acquisition and flight training. Furthermore, the United States stated in the G7 Hiroshima Summit Meeting that it would support the multilateral initiative for the flight training of fourth-generation fighter jets including F-16 fighters. By early 2024, the Netherlands, Denmark, Belgium, and Norway offered to provide F-16 fighters. In August 2024, President Zelenskyy announced that F-16 fighters had been provided and that Ukraine had commenced related operations. It appears that, by January 2025, fighters had already been provided by the Netherlands, Denmark, and Norway. In addition, in November 2024, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France apparently granted their permission to use long-range missiles on Russian territory.

3 How Other Regions Respond On February 23, 2023, ahead of the first anniversary of the start of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, the United Nations (UN) General Assembly adopted a resolution calling for, among other things, the immediate cessation of the aggression. A total of 141 countries—over 70% of all member states—voted in favor of the resolution. On the other hand, in addition to Russia, some countries and regions do not sympathize with this movement. For example, six countries and regions including Belarus and North Korea were against the draft resolution, and 32 countries including India and China abstained from voting. North Korea is showing its stance of standing by Russia, for example, as it voted against the UN General Assembly’s resolution calling for the immediate withdrawal of Russian troops from Ukraine and claims that the United States and other Western countries are to be blamed for the conflict

Since the United States’ withdrawal from the nuclear agreement in 2018, Iran has intensified its confrontational stance toward the West, while strengthening its ties with Russia, particularly in the economic and military fields. Although Iran advocates a diplomatic resolution to the aggression against Ukraine, it has shown a certain degree of understanding toward Russia’s position and has criticized the sanctions imposed on Russia by the United States and its allies. The United States announced in July 2022 Iran’s plan to provide UAVs to Russia and, in September 2022, pointed out that Russia was using Iran-made UAVs for attacks as well as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR). The Ukrainian military also announced that Russia conducted attacks in various parts of Ukraine using Iranian UAVs. To this, Iran claims that the delivery of Iranian UAVs to Russia was carried out before the aggression against Ukraine and suggests that their purpose was not for use in the aggression against Ukraine. In February 2023, William Burns, then Director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), pointed out that Russia is investigating the possibility of supporting Iran’s missile plan and providing fighter jets in return for Iran’s support. In September 2024, he also indicated that Russia had received ballistic missiles from Iran and that the progress of cooperation between the two countries must be closely observed.

China avoids direct criticism of Russia in respect of the aggression, requesting “self-restraint and dialogue” to both Russia and Ukraine and takes a standpoint from which China will play constructive roles in its own ways toward a solution to the Ukraine issues. However, China insists that Russia’s actions are caused by the “Cold War mentality” of the United States and other NATO countries and that it understands Russia’s reasonable concerns about security issues and criticizes sanctions against Russia and equipment delivery to Ukraine from Western countries. In September 2022, President Xi Jinping, during the first in-person China-Russia summit since the aggression began, expressed strong support for issues related to each other’s core interests. Furthermore, during the China-Russia summit held online in December of the same year, Xi stated that China would continue to uphold an objective and impartial stance on the aggression against Ukraine and would play a constructive role in promoting international unity and cooperation toward a peaceful resolution of the Ukraine crisis. Furthermore, he stated that China will play constructive roles in peace negotiations and reconstruction after the conflict in a document titled “China’s Position on the Political Settlement of the Ukraine Crisis” published in February 2023. During his visit to Russia in March of the same year, Xi held talks with Putin and released a joint statement. In the statement, Xi positively evaluated Russia’s commitment to resuming the early resumption of peace negotiations and expressed opposition to unilateral sanctions not based on UN Security Council resolutions.

During his visit to Russia in March of the same year, Xi held talks with Putin and released a joint statement. In the statement, Xi positively evaluated Russia’s commitment to resuming the early resumption of peace negotiations and expressed opposition to unilateral sanctions not based on UN Security Council resolutions.

1 General Situation In January 2025, Donald Trump was inaugurated as the 47th president of the United States. During his election campaign, President Trump focused mainly on economic policy as well as border control and immigration policy under the slogans “America First” and “Make America Great Again” while claiming with regard to security that he would “end wars.” Specifically, he mentioned an early end to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, deterrence of the activities of pro-Iranian armed groups in the Middle East through strengthened pressure on Iran, and the stabilization of the Taiwan situation through the introduction of tariffs on China and other measures. Of these issues, regarding an early end to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, President Trump expressed his intention to meet with President Putin soon after taking office. In February 2025, he held the first U.S.-Russia Summit Telephone Talk of his second administration, and in the same month held a U.S.-Ukraine Summit Meeting with President Zelenskyy. In August, the first U.S.-Russia Summit Meeting since President Trump’s return to office was held in Alaska. Although both sides assessed the talks as being constructive, no ceasefire agreement was reached. Thereafter, consultations between the United States and Russia and between the United States and Ukraine continued, and in November the United States presented a peace proposal to both Ukraine and Russia. For this peace proposal, the United States engaged not only in discussions with Ukraine and Russia but also in consultations between European leaders and President Trump. January 2026 saw developments such as the first trilateral talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine. On the other hand, as of that month there was still no prospect of a ceasefire, and future developments continue to be closely watched.

2 Defense Policies In January 2026, following the release of the NSS in the previous month, the second Trump administration published the National Defense Strategy (NDS). The NDS states that when President Trump took office in January 2025, the United States was facing one of the most dangerous security environments since the end of the Cold War due to factors such as the overseas outsourcing of industry, including the defense industrial base, and prolonged involvement in overseas wars with unclear objectives such as regime change and nation-building. It further states that this situation was changing following President Trump’s return to office. The document states that the Department of War will focus on restoring “peace through strength” and will adopt an approach based on flexible, practical realism, looking at the world in a clear-eyed way and serving U.S. national interests. Regarding the security environment, the NDS states that from the perspective of “America First,” it is essential to evaluate, sort, and prioritize threats. At the same time, it states that even lower-priority threats will not be neglected and will instead be addressed in a sustainable manner. It also discusses simultaneous challenges involving the U.S. homeland and the Western Hemisphere, China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and multiple theaters. In addition, in line with the NSS, the NDS identifies four major lines of effort for achieving “peace through strength”: (1) defend the U.S. homeland; (2) deter China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, not confrontation; (3) increase burden-sharing with U.S. allies and partners; and (4) supercharge the U.S. defense industrial base.

With particular regard to deterring China in the Indo-Pacific, the NDS states that the United States seeks a stable peace, fair trade, and respectful relations with China, while emphasizing the importance of negotiating from a position of strength. The NDS also states that China is the second most powerful country in the world—behind only the United States—and that the speed, scale, and quality of China’s historic military buildup speak for themselves, including forces for operations in the Western Pacific as well as capabilities of reaching targets much farther away. In addition, the NDS states that given that the Indo-Pacific will soon account for more than half the global economy, the security, freedom, and prosperity of the American people are directly linked to the United States’ “ability to trade and engage from a position of strength” in the region. It warns that, should the region come under the dominance of China or another power, the United States could effectively be denied access to the global economy, potentially resulting in long-term adverse effects on its economic outlook, including the ability to reindustrialize. For this reason, the NDS states that the United States will erect a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain and urge key regional allies and partners to do more for collective defense. It further states that a “decent peace” in the region—on terms favorable to Americans but that China can also accept and live under—is achievable, and that this constitutes the premise of President Trump’s diplomacy, while the efforts of the Department of War are intended to provide the undergirding strength for this approach. The NDS also states that the objective is not confrontation with China, but rather the maintenance of stability through deterrence based on “peace through strength,” with emphasis placed on supporting strategic stability as well as deconfliction and de-escalation.

In addition, the NDS states that given that the Indo-Pacific will soon account for more than half the global economy, the security, freedom, and prosperity of the American people are directly linked to the United States’ “ability to trade and engage from a position of strength” in the region. It warns that, should the region come under the dominance of China or another power, the United States could effectively be denied access to the global economy, potentially resulting in long-term adverse effects on its economic outlook, including the ability to reindustrialize. For this reason, the NDS states that the United States will erect a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain and urge key regional allies and partners to do more for collective defense. It further states that a “decent peace” in the region—on terms favorable to Americans but that China can also accept and live under—is achievable, and that this constitutes the premise of President Trump’s diplomacy, while the efforts of the Department of War are intended to provide the undergirding strength for this approach. The NDS also states that the objective is not confrontation with China, but rather the maintenance of stability through deterrence based on “peace through strength,” with emphasis placed on supporting strategic stability as well as deconfliction and de-escalation.

Regarding Russia, the NDS describes it as a persistent but manageable threat to NATO’s eastern member states and indicates that, through its aggression against Ukraine, Russia has demonstrated deep reservoirs of military and industrial power as well as national resolve to sustain a prolonged war in a neighboring region. The NDS further states that Russia’s modernization and diversification of the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, together with its undersea, space, and cyber capabilities, could also pose a threat to the U.S. homeland, making homeland defense necessary. At the same time, the NDS states that European NATO member states significantly surpass Russia in terms of economic scale, population, and latent military power, and have also committed to defense spending and related expenditures equivalent to 5% of their GDP. It further states that, while the United States will continue its engagement in Europe, it will prioritize homeland defense and deterrence against China, and that ending Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is first and foremost Europe’s own responsibility. Regarding North Korea, the NDS describes it as a direct military threat to the ROK and Japan, stating in particular that its missile forces are capable of striking targets in both countries with conventional weapons, nuclear weapons, and other weapons of mass destruction. The NDS also states that North Korea’s nuclear forces are increasingly capable of threatening the U.S. homeland and that, through their growing scale and sophistication, they constitute a “clear and present danger” of nuclear attack on the U.S. homeland. In addition, regarding the simultaneous emergence of challenges across multiple theaters, the NDS states that it is reasonable to prepare for the possibility that multiple potential adversaries could act in a coordinated or opportunistic fashion. It further states that allies and partners should bear a fair share of the burden for collective defense, emphasizing that this is not only the right thing to do but also strategically vital. The second Trump administration released its National Security Strategy (NSS) in December 2025 and National Defense Strategy (NDS) in January 2026. President Trump has emphasized “America First,” “peace through strength,” and the importance of homeland defense, as well as a focus on the Indo-Pacific region, burden-sharing of defense spending, strengthening of the defense industrial base, and similar matters. As documents clearly reiterating the above approaches of the second Trump administration, the Strategies are expected to serve as an important guide to understanding the U.S. government’s future defense policies. The priority of the NSS and NDS is homeland defense, an approach directly tied to U.S. national interests. Both documents identify illegal immigration and the influx of drugs, in addition to nuclear weapons, various conventional forces, and threats on the space, cyber, and electromagnetic spectrum as major threats to the U.S. homeland, as well as prioritizing homeland defense and deterrence against China. This section gives an overview of the development of the Golden Dome for America (GDA) and the modernization of the country’s nuclear forces, which are both initiatives related to homeland defense that the United States is particularly focused on, and whose developments Japan should also closely monitor. The GDA initiative was announced in an executive order given in January 2025. Along with ballistic missiles, hypersonic missiles and other aerial attacks have been identified as the most catastrophic threats facing the United States. Moreover, the GDA will be integrated with existing systems, including space-based sensors and interceptors, to build a multi-layered, multi-domain system capable of intercepting any type of missile. It was stated that by enabling operation of the system within three years, during President Trump’s term of office, even if hostile forces develop advanced long-range attack capabilities, the U.S. homeland will not be vulnerable to threats.

7 Established in September 2021 and aimed at deepening diplomatic, security and defense cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region. which is a security cooperation framework by the three countries of Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States,7 and other frameworks. Under the second Trump administration as well, similar policies were presented in November 2025 during Secretary Hegseth’s consultations with various countries at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers’ Meeting Plus (ADMM-Plus) held in Malaysia. In particular, at the Japan-Australia-Philippines-U.S. Defense Ministerial Meeting—the fifth such meeting in the past three years—the participants emphasized their continued commitment to promoting their shared vision of FOIP. They also reaffirmed joint efforts among the four countries focused on deterrence and readiness and concurred on strengthening coordinated defense cooperation activities. In addition, the participants expressed serious concern regarding China’s destabilizing activities in the East China Sea and South China Sea and strong opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion. In a meeting with Chinese Minister of National Defense Dong Jun as well, Secretary Hegseth expressed concern at the activities of China in the South China Sea, the vicinity of Taiwan, and the Indo-Pacific region, and communicated the fact that the United States would continue to protect its interests going forward. The two sides concurred on the need to establish channels of communication between their two militaries to avoid conflicts. In addition, during the U.S.-Philippines defense ministers’ meeting, Secretary Hegseth announced the establishment of Task Force-Philippines, aimed at improving operational coordination and interoperability in the South China Sea. During the U.S.-India defense ministers’ meeting, the two countries stated that they would work closely together toward realizing FOIP and signed the Framework for the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership for the next decade, demonstrating active engagement in consultations with various countries. Regarding AUKUS as well, the United States stated at the U.S.-Australia Summit Meeting in October 2025 that it would promote the initiative with full commitment.

United States deployed two Carrier Strike Groups in the South China Sea for the first time in about six years and conducted naval exercises. Since then, the United States has continued Carrier Strike Group operations in the same region to demonstrate continuously its commitment to promote FOIP to allies in the region. In January 2022, the State Department released a study examining China’s claims regarding its maritime rights in the South China Sea in light of international law. The study noted that China’s claims over most of the South China Sea are inconsistent with international law and gravely undermine the rule of law in the ocean. As part of its activities around strengthening its presence in the Indo-Pacific region, the U.S. Navy, which promotes Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO),8 deployed the USS America, an amphibious assault ship with enhanced ability to carry F-35B fighter aircraft and other carrier-based aircraft to Sasebo in December 2019, and deployed for the first time the MQ-4C Triton unmanned maritime reconnaissance aircraft in Guam in January 2020. The U.S. Air Force promotes Agile Combat Employment (ACE)9 and conducts ACE exercises in the Indo-Pacific region using fighter jets and unmanned aircraft. Furthermore, the U.S. Army promotes the multi-domain operation concept, and announced in September 2022 the deployment of a Multi-Domain Task Force10 that conducts operations in all domains including human cognitive behavior parallelly, in Hawaii.

The NSS issued by the second Trump administration states with regard to the importance of technology in the defense field that the United States will equip and field technologically advanced military forces and secure continued prosperity, competitive advantage, and military dominance for future generations through investment in emerging technologies and basic science. In addition, the NDS states that new technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), will be introduced as part of efforts to strengthen the defense industrial base. 5 Nuclear and Missile Defense Policy The NDS released by the second Trump administration refers to threats such as the nuclear forces of Russia and North Korea, and states that the United States will modernize and adapt its nuclear forces for homeland defense. It further states that while placing emphasis on deterrence and escalation management, the United States will never allow itself to be placed in a position vulnerable to nuclear blackmail. As part of its nuclear deterrence strategy, the United States has long deployed a nuclear triad consisting of Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), strategic nuclear submarines equipped with Trident II D5 submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs), and B-52 and B-2 strategic bombers equipped with nuclear cruise missiles and nuclear bombs. At the same time, because many of these systems have exceeded their design service lives, the United States has indicated its intention to proceed with replacement programs for all three legs of the triad. In addition, the Nuclear Posture Review (NPR) released by the former Biden administration outlined plans to shift the role of dual-capable aircraft (DCA) supporting NATO’s nuclear posture from F-15E fighter aircraft to F-35A fighter aircraft. Moreover, the Missile Defense Review (MDR), also released by the former Biden administration, identified missile defense as a top priority for protecting the United States and deterring attacks, stating that it contributes to negating the benefits of enemy attacks and limiting damage even if deterrence fails. Also, the U.S. government declared that it would recognize attacks on any U.S. territory overseas including Guam as attacks directed at the U.S. homeland and stated that Guam is vital as an operation base to maintain FOIP and that defending Guam helps realize integrated deterrence.

1 General Situation The operation of the U.S. Forces is not controlled by the individual branches of the broader armed forces; rather it is operated under the command of the Unified Combatant Commands, composed of forces from multiple branches of the armed forces. In May 2018, the Cyber Force, which had been under the U.S. Strategic Command, was elevated to a unified combatant command and in August 2019, the Space Command was founded to serve as a geographic unified combatant command. The Unified Combatant Commands now consist of four functional combatant commands and seven geographic combatant commands. In December 2019, the Space Force was established as the sixth branch of the military within the Department of the Air Force. The U.S. ground forces14 have about 450,000 Army soldiers and about 170,000 Marines, which are forward-deployed in Germany, the ROK, and Japan, among other countries. The U.S. maritime forces have about 970 vessels (including about 70 submarines) totaling about 6.50 million tons. The 7th Fleet is responsible for the western Pacific and the Indian Ocean; the 3rd Fleet in the eastern Pacific; the 4th Fleet in South America and the Caribbean Sea; the 2nd Fleet in U.S. East Coast, North Atlantic Ocean, and Arctic Ocean; the 6th Fleet in the Eastern Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean Sea, and Africa; and the 5th Fleet in the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and the northwest Indian Ocean. The U.S. air forces have roughly 3,200 combat aircraft across the Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps. In addition to carrier-based aircraft deployed at sea, part of the tactical air force is forward-deployed in Germany, the United Kingdom, Japan and the ROK, among others. In regard to strategic offensive weapons including nuclear force, the United States proceeded with its reduction based on the New START that came into force in February 2011. However, as noted above, the treaty expired in February

2026. The United States announced that its deployed strategic warheads15 stood at 1,419, while its deployed delivery platforms stood at 662 as of May 1, 2023. 1 The Central Military Commission is a leading and commanding organ to China’s armed forces. Formally, there are the Chinese Communist Party CMC and the People’s Republic of China CMC. However, each consists of the same members, indicating both commissions as an organ for the party to control the armed forces. China, the world’s most populous country, has a vast landmass surrounded by a long borderline as well as a long coastline. It also has various races, religions, and languages. China’s pride in its unique history of having shaped a distinct culture and civilization, and semi-colonial experience in and after the 19th century are driving its desire for a strong nation and fueling its nationalism. Xi Jinping, the general secretary of the Central Committee (General Secretary Xi) in the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), has established a power base in the CCP through actions such as purging leaders using an anti-corruption campaign. The concept of “Two Safeguards,” meaning safeguarding the core status of General Secretary Xi in the CCP’s Central Committee and party, and safeguarding the Committee’s authority and centralized, unified leadership,” was incorporated into the party’s constitution at the 20th National Congress of the CCP (20th CCP Congress) held in October 2022. In addition, in the 1st Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee held immediately after the 20th CCP Congress, General Secretary Xi was reaffirmed for a third term.

Xi Jinping, the general secretary of the Central Committee (General Secretary Xi) in the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), has established a power base in the CCP through actions such as purging leaders using an anti-corruption campaign. The concept of “Two Safeguards,” meaning safeguarding the core status of General Secretary Xi in the CCP’s Central Committee and party, and safeguarding the Committee’s authority and centralized, unified leadership,” was incorporated into the party’s constitution at the 20th National Congress of the CCP (20th CCP Congress) held in October 2022. In addition, in the 1st Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee held immediately after the 20th CCP Congress, General Secretary Xi was reaffirmed for a third term.

In 2014, China presented the concept of a holistic approach to national security and established the National Security Commission of the Central Committee of the CCP. This was based on the idea that various areas are related to the country’s security as a whole, including political, military, homeland, economic, cultural, societal, science and technology, cyber, ecological, resource, nuclear, overseas interests, outer space, deep sea, polar, and biological security. In addition to drawing up the National Security Strategy (2021–2025) and issuing a white paper titled “China’s National Security in the New Era” (May 2025), China is advancing various legislation to strengthen the domestic counterintelligence system and bolster management of cyberspace. China is also strongly opposed to any foreign intervention in the unification of China as well as any move toward the independence of Taiwan, and has repeatedly stated that although it will strive with utmost effort to realize a peaceful reunification, it will not promise to renounce the use of force. The Anti-Secession Law, enacted in March 2005, explicitly states non-renunciation of the use of force, specifying that, “In the event that the ‘Taiwan independence’ secessionist forces should act under any name or by any means to cause the fact of Taiwan’s secession from China, or that major incidents entailing Taiwan’s secession from China should occur, or that possibilities for a peaceful reunification should be completely exhausted, the state shall employ non-peaceful means and other necessary measures to protect China’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.” In the revised party constitution adopted at the 20th CCP Congress, the phrase “the CCP resolutely opposes and deters separatists seeking ‘Taiwan Independence’” was added, and blocking the independence of Taiwan was placed as a party duty.

China is facing various domestic problems. Among the problems emerging are the spread of corruption among the leadership of the CCP and disparities between urban and rural areas, coastal and inland regions, and within cities, as well as environmental pollution. The spread of corruption has also been seen in the military, with the removal of then Defense Minister Li Shangfu in October 2023, the expulsion from the party of He Weidong, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC),1 Miao Hua, CMC Member and Director of the CMC Political Work Department, and other top military officials, in October 2025, the announcement in January 2026 that Zhang Youxia, CMC Vice Chairman, and Liu Zhenli, CMC Member and Chief of Staff of the CMC Joint Staff Department would be proved and investigated for serious discipline and law violations. Five out of the seven members who made up the CMC at the inauguration of the third Xi administration (October 2022) were expelled from the party or proved and investigated for suspected serious General Secretary Xi Jinping giving a report at the 20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party [China News Service/Jiji Press Photo]

1 General Situation For more than 30 years, China has sustained high-level growth of its defense budget without transparency, engaging in broad, rapid improvement of its military power in qualitative and quantitative terms with focus on nuclear, missile, naval, and air forces. China has also intensified its unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion and such attempts in the sea and airspace of waters, such as the East China Sea and South China Sea, including its incursions into Japan’s territorial waters and airspace around the Senkaku Islands. China is also expanding and intensifying its military activities in waters such as the Sea of Japan and Pacific Ocean, which impact Japan’s national security. In strengthening its military capabilities, China has so far emphasized improving its ability to carry out practical joint operations by modernizing its military through military reforms and other measures. China has also been placing emphasis on the “informatization” of its military, with the aim of improving the military’s overall operational capability through the acquisition of information superiority and hindering the enemy’s ability to demonstrate its military power. For example, it has been rapidly expanding its capabilities in the cyber domain, enabling it to disrupt enemy communications networks, and in the field of electromagnetic spectrum, which offers the potential to render enemy radar ineffective. In the space domain, China is also focusing on securing supremacy in new areas, including continuing to strengthen its capabilities to limit its enemies’ use of space. Bolstering these capabilities will reinforce China’s “Anti-Access/Area Denial (A2/AD)” capabilities and lead to the establishment of operational capabilities further afield.

2 Defense Policies China is emphasizing the role of its military as a strategic pillar for achieving its goal of creating world-class military forces and the Chinese Dream, which is the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In its defense white paper released in 2019, China stated

the objective of its national defense policies to be protecting the sovereignty, security, and development interests of the state. These goals include protecting state interests overseas and supporting ongoing state development. It also stressed the idea of “active defense” as a military strategic policy, outlining a strategy of defense and advancement in operations and tactics. Additionally, China has spoken of strengthening its military by building up national defense and a powerful military that are proportionate to the state’s international standing and conform to state security and development interests. In combat, it emphasizes the ability to fight and win, discussing the acceleration of intelligentization, the enhancement of joint operational abilities, and the improvement of practical training standards. Such military buildup in China apparently indicates that China has given top priority to dealing with a Taiwan contingency by improving its capabilities to deter or deny Taiwan’s independence and foreign military support for the Taiwanese independence and has recently considered the improvement of operational capabilities in more distant waters to protect its expanding overseas interests. Furthermore, China seems to emphasize not only physical means but also non-physical means in military affairs and warfare. It regards the concept of “Three Warfare”—“Media Warfare,” “Psychological Warfare,” and “Legal Warfare”—as part of the political work of the military. In addition, China has set forth a policy of coordinating military struggle closely with political, diplomatic, economic, cultural, and legal endeavors. As for the timeline for achieving the goals of the development of national defense and military forces, General Secretary Xi’s report to the 19th CCP National Congress in October 2017 and the defense white paper released in 2019 noted that China would try to (1) fundamentally achieve mechanization and make great progress in informatization to dramatically improve strategic capabilities by 2020, (2) fundamentally complete the modernization of national defense and military forces by 2035, and (3) generally transform Chinese forces into world-class forces by the mid-21st century.

3 Transparency Concerning Defense Policies and Military Affairs China has neither set out a clear and specific future vision of its military strengthening, nor ensured adequate transparency of its decision-making process in relation to military and security affairs. Although China had released a defense white paper roughly every two years since 1998, it has not released a defense white paper in recent years since “China’s National Defense in the New Era” released in July 2019 for the first time in four years. Even the white paper did not sufficiently clarify the specific situation of equipment possession, procurement goals and results, the organization and deployment of major units, the military’s major operations and training results, and the breakdown of the national defense expenditures. Incidents in which Chinese authorities provide factually inaccurate explanations or refuse to admit facts regarding Chinese military activities have been confirmed, inciting concerns over China’s military decision-making and actions. For example, the submerged transit of a Chinese Navy submarine through Japan’s contiguous zone around the Senkaku Islands was confirmed in January 2018, but China did not acknowledge this. In the same way, in the cases of submarines in the contiguous zone around Amami Oshima Island presumed to belong to China confirmed in June 2020 and September 2021, China did not acknowledge this fact. On the contrary, there were some Chinese media reports that criticized the Japanese side by claiming it was making exaggerations. China’s influence in the international community has risen politically, economically, and militarily. It has become increasingly important for China to improve its transparency
