The PLA is defined as a people’s force created and led by the CCP, and comprises the Army (PLAA), Navy (PLAN), Air Force (PLAAF), Rocket Force (PLARF), Aerospace Force, Cyberspace Force, Information Support Force, and Joint Logistics Support Force (PLAJLSF), an integrated logistical support force. In September 2025, the military parade for the Commemoration of “the 80th Anniversary of the Victory in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War” was held. The parade showcased a variety of nuclear capabilities, including intercontinental ballistic missiles, to demonstrate China’s strengthened nuclear deterrence. It also displayed several anti-ship missiles, including hypersonic missiles that are considered difficult to counter, to demonstrate long-range anti-ship attack capabilities, thereby showcasing the achievements of the military’s modernization to both domestic and international audiences. The PAP is designed to engage mainly in patrol, emergency response, counterterrorism, maritime rights protection and law enforcement, emergency rescue, defense operations, etc. The militia is planned to engage in economic construction, etc., in peacetime and undertake logistic support missions in an emergency. China has explained that it is committed to “no first use” of nuclear weapons under any circumstances, to “unconditional negative security assurance” that it would not use or threaten to use nuclear weapons against non-nuclear-weapon states or nuclear-weapon-free zones unconditionally, and to keeping its nuclear capabilities at the minimum level required for national security. In recent years, however, doubts have been expressed about the explanation.7 China is aiming to modernize, diversify, and expand its nuclear capabilities. It is increasing production of nuclear warheads and investing in the means to deliver nuclear weapons by land, sea, and air to increase their numbers. The number of operational nuclear warheads in its possession remained in the low 600s through 2024, and it has been pointed out that it may remains on track to have over 1,000 by 2030.8 It is believed that China plans to strengthen deterrence against the United States and will continue to place importance on nuclear and missile capabilities. China possesses ballistic missiles of various types and ranges, including intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs), air-launched ballistic missiles (ALBMs), intermediate-range ballistic missiles (IRBMs), medium-range ballistic missiles (MRBMs), and short-range ballistic missiles (SRBMs). The update of China’s ballistic missile forces from a liquid propellant system to a solid propellant system is improving their survivability and readiness. Moreover, it is believed that China is working to increase their performance by such means as extending ranges, improving targeting accuracy, and employing maneuverable reentry vehicles (MaRVs) and multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs).

China’s main ICBMs, its strategic nuclear asset, had been the fixed-site liquid-propellant DF-5 missiles. deemed that China is ahead of the United States in relation to ground-launched ballistic missiles and cruise missiles.12 As for the IRBMs/MRBMs capable of reaching the Indo-Pacific region including Japan, China possesses the mobile solid propellant DF-21 and DF-26, which can be transported and operated on TELs. These are viewed as capable of carrying both conventional and nuclear warheads. Furthermore, DF- 21D anti-ship ballistic missiles (ASBMs), called “carrier killers,” have been deployed, which carry conventional warheads to attack overwater ships including aircraft carriers. In recent years, the DF-26, which has a range including Guam and is called “Guam killer,” is considered a “second-generation ASBM” developed on the basis of the DF-21D. Its deployment was announced in April 2018. In addition to these ground-launched missiles, development and operation of ASBMs and long-range cruise missiles which can be launched from aircraft and ships is also under way. Specifically, regarding ASBMs, China possesses the YJ-21, an air-launched ballistic missile that can reportedly attack land and sea targets. In addition, at the military parade in September 2025, it showcased for the first time the YJ-20, a ship-launched anti-ship ballistic missile. Furthermore, the long-range cruise missiles it possesses include, for example, the air-launched missile CJ-20, a land-attack cruise missile with a long range over 1,500 km which reportedly can be carried by an H-6 bomber, and ship-launched missiles such as long-range land-attack cruise missiles and YJ-18, an anti-ship cruise missile which can strike targets at supersonic speed. It is deemed that these missiles can complement ballistic missile forces, covering the Indo-Pacific region including Japan. The deployment of these ASBMs and cruise missiles is expected to strengthen China’s A2/AD capabilities.

In recent years, efforts have been made to increase the size and armament of its vessels. At the end of December 2025, the CCG possessed 175 ships with full load displacement of 1,000 tons or more,21 including two 10,000-ton-class patrol ships that are among the world’s largest. Operations of vessels equipped with artillery have also been observed. perspectives. It has been noted that retired naval destroyers and frigates were delivered to the CCG, suggesting that the military has been supporting the CCG in terms of equipment as well. It has also been noted that the PLA and CCG are conducting joint navigation and training. The enhanced cooperation between the PLA and PAP, including the CCG, is believed to be intended to strengthen operational capabilities in gray-zone situations. Amid such a situation, in June 2020, Law of the People’s Republic of China on the People’s Armed Police (PAP Law) was revised, and “protection of maritime interests and law enforcement” were added to the duties of the PAP. The revised version also stipulates that the PAP shall be centrally and uniformly guided by the Central Committee and the CMC of the People’s Republic of China. The Coast Guard Law of the People’s Republic of China (CCG Law), which stipulates the CCG’s responsibilities and authority including the use of weapons, was newly enacted in January 2021 and entered into force in February 2021. In June 2024, procedural regulations also came into effect for the execution of the CCG Headquarters’ administrative laws, which prescribe details of law enforcement by the CCG. The CCG Law includes problematic provisions—such as vague definitions of applicable maritime areas and the authority to use weapons—that are seen as inconsistent with international law. The CCG Law must not be allowed to infringe on the legitimate interests of the relevant countries including Japan. Furthermore, it is completely unacceptable that the law would increase tensions in maritime areas such as the East China Sea.

As China is continuing the modernization of its bombers as well, the Air Force has increased the number of H-6 bombers, which are capable of carrying long-range land-attack cruise missiles. In an attempt to improve bombers’ long-range operation capabilities, the Air Force has reportedly begun to operate H-6N bombers that can take advantage of aerial refueling to fly longer. It is believed to be developing a new long-range stealth bomber called H-20. It is also pointed out that China is developing an ALBM with nuclear capability to be carried by such bombers, and the JL-1, an ALBM said to be capable of carrying nuclear warheads, was showcased for the first time at the military parade in September 2025. China is also making continuous efforts to improve capabilities which are essential for operations of modern air power by introducing H-6U and IL-78M aerial refueling tankers and KJ-500 and KJ-2000 early warning and control aircraft. Furthermore, it has been pointed out that the KJ-600 early warning aircraft has been deployed aboard the aircraft carrier Fujian, and it is said to have contributed to the improvement of the operational capabilities of the carrier-based aircraft. Moreover, since July 2016, China has promoted the deployment of the indigenously developed Y-20 large transport aircraft. The Y-20U, an aerial refueling tanker based on this transport aircraft, has also been deployed since June 2021. China is rapidly developing a variety of domestic unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), including high-altitude, long-endurance (HALE) UAVs for reconnaissance and other purposes as well as those capable of carrying weapons such as missiles.

0 (6) Space, Cyber, and Electromagnetic Spectrum Capabilities In recent years, information gathering, and command and communication in the military sector have increasingly relied on satellites and computer networks. As such, China stated that “outer space and cyberspace have become new commanding heights (capture point) in strategic competition among all parties,” indicating that it has recognized the importance of taking on information mastery in wartime when it must protect its own information systems and networks while neutralizing those of its adversaries. Regarding the space domain, it is believed that China is also planning to improve its ability to conduct military operations in space, given the fact that China’s administrative organizations and state-owned enterprises involved in space utilization are said to have close cooperative ties with the military.24 Specifically, in recent years China has rapidly increased the number of artificial satellites it has which can be used for military purposes, and it is now operating more than 260 such satellites, approximately three times as many compared to ten years ago.25 For example, the BeiDou global satellite positioning system, which is called a Chinese-version GPS and pointed out as available for ballistic missiles and other guided weapons systems, started its global operation service in late 2018, and it is deemed that the launch of all satellites constituting the BeiDou system was completed in June 2020. Furthermore, it has been pointed out that the Yaogan reconnaissance satellite collects image and radio wave intelligence and obtains location information of naval vessels and others. These capabilities could strengthen the surveillance capabilities of China’s naval vessels and others in the Pacific, potentially leading to the building of so-called A2/ AD capabilities and operational capabilities at longer ranges.

(2) Military Activities in Japan’s Surrounding Waters and Airspace The Chinese Navy and Air Force have in recent years expanded and intensified their activities in Japan’s surrounding waters and airspace, such as in the area surrounding the Senkaku Islands, including activities viewed to be based on China’s claim to the Senkaku Islands. Incidents involving the one-sided escalation of activities have also been seen, creating a situation of great concern to Japan. In this context, in 2025, a series of incidents occurred, including: the activity of an aircraft carrier in the waters east of Iwo-To and the activity of two aircraft carriers in the Pacific Ocean in June; the unusual close approach by a Chinese fighter aircraft to a JSDF aircraft in June; the unusual close approach by a Chinese fighter-bomber to a JSDF aircraft in July; the activity of an aircraft carrier in the Pacific Ocean from the east of the main island of Okinawa to east of Amami Oshima Island in December; and intermittent radar illumination against a JSDF aircraft by a Chinese fighter for approximately 30 minutes in December. Part III, Chapter 1, Section 1-2-1 (Continuous, Persistent Information Gathering and Warning and Surveillance Surrounding Japan), 2 (Warnings and Scrambles in Preparation against Airspace Violation) a. Activities in the East China Sea (including the Areas around the Senkaku Islands) Chinese naval vessels have been conducting operations in the East China Sea continuously and actively. Declaring its own position regarding Japan’s Senkaku Islands, China claims that patrols by Chinese naval vessels in the sea areas under its jurisdiction are completely justifiable and lawful. Chinese naval vessels have been continuously operating in the areas near Japan’s Senkaku Islands. In June 2016, a Jiangkai I-class frigate became the first ever Chinese Navy combatant vessel to enter Japan’s contiguous zone around the Senkaku Islands. In July 2022, a Jiangwei II-class frigate passed into the contiguous zone southwest of the Uotsurishima Island. Submarine activities have also been confirmed. In January 2018, a submerged Shang-class submarine and a Jiangkai II-class frigate each entered the contiguous zone around the Senkaku Islands on the same day. This was the first time a Chinese submarine was identified and announced as conducting submerged transit through the contiguous waters around the Senkaku Islands. In June 2020 and September 2021, submerged transit of a submarine presumed to belong to China was confirmed in the contiguous zone surrounding Amami Oshima Island.

In recent years, activities by Chinese Navy intelligence gathering vessels (AGIs) and survey vessels have also been found. In November 2015, a Dongdiao-class AGI sailed back and forth in waters outside the contiguous zone south of the Senkaku Islands. In June 2016, a Dongdiao-class AGI sailed through Japan’s territorial waters near Kuchinoerabujima Island and Yakushima Island in Kagoshima Prefecture, then passed through Japan’s contiguous zone north of Kitadaitojima Island (Okinawa Prefecture). Subsequently, the vessel repeatedly conducted east-west passages outside the contiguous zone south of the Senkaku Islands. Furthermore, a Shupang-class survey vessel sailed through Japan’s territorial waters near Kuchinoerabujima Island, Kuchinoshima Island, and Yakushima Island in November 2021; April, July, September, November, and December 2022; February, June, and September 2023; and August 2024. In recent years, Chinese military aircraft have also been active in the airspace closer to the Nansei Islands, including the Senkaku Islands and the main island of Okinawa. Such activities are thought to include warning and surveillance, combat air patrols (CAPs), and training, or may be intended to operate the East China Sea Air Defense Identification Zone. Further, in August 2024, a Chinese military intelligence-gathering aircraft intruded into Japan’s territorial airspace over the waters off the Danjo-gunto Islands in Nagasaki Prefecture. That was the first confirmed and publicized intrusion into Japan’s territorial airspace by a Chinese military aircraft since Japan began measures against intrusions into its territorial airspace. The intrusion into Japan’s territorial airspace by a PLA aircraft is not only a grave violation of Japan’s sovereignty but also a threat to its safety, and it is absolutely unacceptable. Given that China has acknowledged the facts of the incident and indicated it will strive to prevent the recurrence of such an incident, Japan will keep a close eye on China’s actions going forward.

Since the activities of CCG vessels based on China’s own assertion conducted in Japan’s territorial waters around the Senkaku Islands are violating international law, Japan has been strongly protesting against these activities and requested them to leave many times. However, despite Japan’s strong protests, CCG vessels continued to repeatedly intrude into Japan’s territorial waters in FY2025, with violations occurring every month. Additionally, incidents occurred in which CCG ships attempted to approach Japanese fishing boats navigating in Japanese territorial waters near the Senkaku Islands. China Marine Surveillance vessels previously intruded into Japan’s territorial waters for the first time in December 2008. Since then, vessels belonging to the Chinese government have gradually amplified their activities in Japanese territorial waters. Such activities have intensified greatly since September 2012, when the Japanese Government acquired three of the Senkaku Islands (Uotsurishima Island, Kitakojima Island, and Minamikojima Island).

China is seen to be steadily strengthening an operational posture intended to use CCG vessels to intrude into Japan’s territorial waters. For example, the number of vessels involved in each territorial sea intrusion was about two to three until around 2016, whereas in recent years, the number of four-vessel intrusions has increased. In addition, since December 2015 vessels equipped with guns have repeatedly intruded into Japan’s territorial waters. In June 2024, four vessels equipped with guns intruded into the territorial waters. Thereafter, CCG vessels active within the contiguous zone have all carried guns (as of the end of March 2026). In 2025, the number of days on which CCG vessel activities were confirmed in the contiguous zone around the Senkaku Islands reached 357, the highest on record. Cases indicating the improvement of CCG vessels’ operational capabilities have been also confirmed. From November 2024 to October 2025, CCG vessels were seen in the contiguous zone of the Senkaku Islands for a record 335 consecutive days. In December 2012, a fixed-wing aircraft of the State Oceanic Administration was identified as the first Chinese aircraft to intrude into Japan’s airspace around the Senkaku Islands. In May 2017, an object that appeared to be a small drone was flying above a CCG vessel intruding into the Japanese territorial waters around the Senkaku Islands and the object intruded into Japan’s territorial airspace. In May 2025, a CCG helicopter, which took off from a CCG vessel intruding into Japanese territorial waters around the Senkaku Islands, violated Japan’s territorial airspace. China has thus relentlessly continued attempts at unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion in the sea area around the Senkaku Islands, leading to a grave matter of concern. Japan cannot accept China’s actions to escalate the situation.

In addition, in the East China Sea, China continues to engage in unilateral resource development activities even though the boundaries between Japan’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and continental shelf and those of China have not yet been demarcated. Since June 2013, it has been confirmed that construction work is progressing on a new offshore platform. This is in addition to the four offshore platforms installed on the Chinese side of the Japan-China median line in the East China Sea prior to the 2008 agreement on resource development in the East China Sea. Japan has repeatedly protested against this ongoing unilateral development by China, while simultaneously requesting that the work be halted. 24 (The number of intrusion into Japanese territorial waters) (Year) (4) Trends of Activities around Taiwan China has intensified military activities around Taiwan. According to announcements from the Ministry of National Defense of Taiwan, entry into airspace around Taiwan by Chinese military aircraft has been on the rise since September

2020. The total number of aircraft that entered its airspace was over 970 in 2021, over 1,700 in 2022 and 2023, over 3,000 in 2024, and over 3,700 in 2025. Furthermore, according to an announcement by Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense, Chinese military aircraft have repeatedly entered the airspace east of the “median line”30 of the Taiwan Strait since Nancy Pelosi, then Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives visited Taiwan in August 2022. In addition to conventional fighter aircraft and bombers, other aircraft such as attack helicopters, air refueling tankers, and UAVs have reportedly been observed entering the airspace since

2021. The number of Chinese naval vessels confirmed in the waters around Taiwan has also been increasing. There were approximately 1,900 in 2023, approximately 2,500 in 2024, and approximately 2,600 in 2025. Furthermore, since August 2022, China has frequently conducted military exercises in the sea and airspace surrounding Taiwan. On August 2, 2022, China announced that it set six training areas surrounding Taiwan, and that it would conduct “a series of integrated military operations” around Taiwan, in conjunction with the visit of Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Pelosi to Taiwan. China launched nine ballistic missiles on August 4, 2022, five of which landed within Japan’s EEZ, and another landed at the closest point to Japanese territory, which was about 80 km from Yonagunijima Island. This is a serious issue relating to Japan’s security and the safety of its people and was perceived as a threat to local residents. In addition, some of the missiles passed over Taiwan. After that, the PLA continued the large-scale military exercise covering subjects such as integrated blockage, surface/ground attack, air superiority combat, aerial reconnaissance, and anti-submarine warfare in air space and sea space around Taiwan for about one week. Since that exercise, China has also conducted military exercises in the sea and airspace around Taiwan in April and August 2023, May and October 2024, and April and December 2025. Although China has not announced its activities, on December 9, 2024 Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense stated that China’s military fleets of the Eastern, Northern, and Southern Theater Commands as well as CCG vessels are entering the waters around the Taiwan Strait and western Pacific Ocean waters, and conducting activities such as long-distance navigation on the far seas. Taiwan’s President Lai took a week-long tour from November 30 to the Marshall Islands, Tuvalu, and Palau, which diplomatically recognize Taiwan, by way of Hawaii and Guam. The exercises conducted in the vicinity of Taiwan by the PLA may have rehearsed some parts of military operations directed at unification with Taiwan, including invading Taiwan.

During the exercise held in May 2024, activities by CCG vessels conducted in areas including the waters to the east of Taiwan were announced for the first time. During the exercise held in October of the same year, CCG vessels expanded their activities, including navigating around the entirety of Taiwan. It has been noted that China may be placing more emphasis on the role of its CCG in causing a gray-zone situation. Moreover, compared to past exercises, the exercise conducted in April 2025 stepped up specific blockade related actions, such as warning, expulsion, interception and detention by the military. In an exercise in December of the same year, it was announced that long-range live-fire drills directed at the sea areas surrounding Taiwan (northern and southern Taiwan) would be conducted, which is believed to be the first such exercise since August 2022. It is believed that through the series of activities around Taiwan, China seeks to create a fait accompli that the PLA is continuously operating there and improve its actual combat capabilities. These intensified military activities indicate a situation, where the possibility could not be excluded that tension between China and Taiwan rises in the military sense. Stabilizing the situation surrounding Taiwan is important for the stability of the international community. Therefore, it is necessary that we pay close attention to the situation with a sense of crisis more than ever before. (5) Trends of Activities in the South China Sea China has also been intensifying its activities based on assertions of unlawful maritime claims in the South China Sea, such as in waters around the Spratly Islands and Paracel Islands, over which territorial disputes exist with neighbors, including Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries. Since 2014, China has pressed ahead with large-scale and rapid land reclamation at seven features31 of the Spratly Islands. The Philippines-China arbitration award issued in July 2016 denied the “historic rights” as the basis of the “nine-dash line” claimed by China, and determined the illegality of China’s activities such as land reclamation. However, China has made clear it would not comply with this decision and is currently carrying out militarization, including continuing military activities while promoting the development of various kinds of infrastructure that can be used for military purposes. It has been pointed out that if China were to consider bastion operations (fortification) to enhance the survivability of new types of long-range SLBMs capable of hitting the continental United States, the South China Sea would be the suitable choice.32 If these features in the South China Sea are used for full-scale military purposes, it could significantly change the security environment in the Indo-Pacific region. Attention must continue to be paid to the situation in the South China Sea going forward. On Fiery Cross Reef, Subi Reef, and Mischief Reefs, called the Big Three of the seven features of the Spratly Islands, China has developed batteries for anti-aircraft guns, missile shelters, underground storage facilities pointed out to be ammunition storage, large ports capable of accommodating combatant ships, and runways available for takeoff and landing of fighter aircraft and bombers.

(6) Trends in the Indian Ocean and Other More Distant Waters The Chinese Navy is considered to be shifting toward “protection missions on the far seas” and has been steadily increasing its capabilities to conduct operations in more distant waters, such as the Indian Ocean, in recent years. Progress has been seen in the Navy’s development of such equipment as large combatant ships and replenishment ships and in its operational initiatives, such as deployment to distant sea areas and securing bases for this purpose. Since December 2008, Chinese naval vessels have been deployed off the coast of Somalia and in the Gulf of Aden to take part in international counter-piracy efforts. The dispatched ships are also conducting joint trainings34 with the militaries of other countries in the Indian Ocean and elsewhere, and in 2025 they conducted joint trainings with Russia and Iran at Iran’s Chabahar Port in March. China has also deployed a space observation support ship in the southern Pacific Ocean and dispatched a military hospital ship under the operation, Mission Harmony, to offer medical services. In 2025, it was dispatched to the South Pacific Ocean, the South America region, and other places.

In September 2022 and August 2023, Russia announced that Chinese vessels participating in joint navigation with Russia sailed through the Bering Sea. KEY WORD (7) Objectives of Activities in Waters and Airspace The development and activities of Chinese naval and air forces, descriptions in defense white papers, China’s geographical conditions and globalizing economy, and other factors indicate that the recent water and airspace activities of the Navy, Air Force and other Chinese organizations have

KEY WORD (7) Objectives of Activities in Waters and Airspace The development and activities of Chinese naval and air forces, descriptions in defense white papers, China’s geographical conditions and globalizing economy, and other factors indicate that the recent water and airspace activities of the Navy, Air Force and other Chinese organizations have

the following objectives. The first is to intercept operations by adversaries in waters and airspace as far as possible from China in order to defend its territorial land, waters and airspace. Behind this objective is an increase in the effectiveness of long-range attacks due to recent progress in science and technology. The second is to develop capabilities to deter and prevent Taiwan’s independence. China maintains that it will not allow any foreign intervention in solving the Taiwan issue and realizing the unification of China. To ensure the prevention of foreign intervention in the Taiwan issue, China needs to enhance its operational capabilities at sea and airspace as Taiwan is surrounded by the sea in all directions. The third is to weaken the control of other countries over islands and the surrounding waters and airspace on which China’s one-sided claims to sovereignty and marine interests exist, by means of various surveillance activities and the use of force, thereby strengthening such one-sided claims. Such activities of China are considered to also have the purpose of creating a fait accompli as part of the reasons for unilaterally changing the status quo and justifying China’s claims based on its own concept of “legal warfare.” The fourth is to acquire, maintain, and protect its maritime rights and interests. China is engaged in oil and gas drilling as well as fishing and navigating in the East and South China Seas. In order to continue these activities safely and stably, the Chinese military is believed to be playing a role as a backstop, deterring the activities of maritime law enforcement organizations of other countries through its military presence. The fifth is to defend its sea lines of communication. In the background is the fact that its sea lines of communication, including its oil transportation routes from the Middle East, are essential for the Chinese economy. Given the recent strengthening of the Chinese Navy and Air Force, it is believed that they have been expanding military capabilities to cover distant waters beyond China’s near seas. Given these objectives of China’s recent sea and airspace activities and trends, it is believed that China plans to further expand the sphere of its activities and further intensify its operations in waters surrounding Japan, including the East China Sea, the South China Sea, and the Pacific Ocean, as well as the Indian Ocean.

7 International Military Activities In recent years, the PLA has been indicating its positive attitude on nontraditional security missions such as peacekeeping, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief, and counterpiracy, dispatching numerous units for such overseas missions. China has vowed to consistently support and actively participate in UN Peacekeeping Operations (PKOs), increasing its presence in UN PKOs. According to the United Nations (UN), as of the end of January 2026, China had a total of 1,659 personnel including troops and police members—the largest number of peacekeepers among the permanent members of the UN Security Council—engaged in the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) and other UN PKOs. China’s share has remained the second largest in the UN PKO budget, after that of the United States, since 2016. Moreover, China has been actively participating in counter-piracy activities off the coast of Somalia and in the Gulf of Aden as well as humanitarian assistance and disaster relief activities. It is pointed out that factors behind such Chinese attitude include the growing need for protecting and promoting China’s national interests overseas following the expansion of national interests beyond its national borders, China’s attempt to verify military capabilities including units’ long-distance deployment through operations, its intent to raise its status by demonstrating its will to fulfill its responsibilities to the international community, its hope to diffuse the military’s peaceful and humanitarian images, and its attempt to enhance relations with PKO regions including African countries.

8 Education and Training In recent years, the PLA under the policy of building a military that “can fight and win a war” has promoted practical exercises including large-scale ones such as joint exercises led by theater commands, force-on-force exercises, landing exercises, inter-theater exercises, and large exercises including distant ones, as well as night-time exercises and joint exercises with other countries, in order to strengthen its operational capabilities. In the education spectrum as well, the PLA aims to train soldiers who have the ability to execute joint operations. It was reported in 2017 that the PLA National Defense University began training to develop human resources capable of directing joint operations. China has been developing defense mobilization systems and others in order to effectively utilize private resources in case of emergencies, including wars. The military use of civilian resources includes civilian ships’ transportation of military equipment. Also, in his speech at the 20th CCP Congress, General Secretary Xi raised the issue of deepening national defense education as a part of improving “Integrated National Strategic System and Capabilities.” In September 2024, China revised the National Defense Education Law and newly instituted the implementation of national defense education that is tied to patriotism. Such an initiative mobilizes society’s overall resources to the military and generally augments China’s forces available for military missions. As it is expected to proactively be promoted in the future, the initiative’s implications for the Chinese military forces’ operational capabilities must be watched closely.

In the education spectrum as well, the PLA aims to train soldiers who have the ability to execute joint operations. It was reported in 2017 that the PLA National Defense University began training to develop human resources capable of directing joint operations. China has been developing defense mobilization systems and others in order to effectively utilize private resources in case of emergencies, including wars. The military use of civilian resources includes civilian ships’ transportation of military equipment. Such an initiative mobilizes society’s overall resources to the military and generally augments China’s forces available for military missions. As it is expected to proactively be promoted in the future, the initiative’s implications for the Chinese military forces’ operational capabilities must be watched closely.

43 According to SIPRI Arms Transfers Database Russia relations had “reached the highest level in history.” Furthermore, in the Commemoration of the 80th Anniversary of the Victory in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War in September 2025, three leaders, President Xi, President Putin, and Chairman of the State Affairs Commission Kim Jong-un, were seen standing side by side. Furthermore, for example, amid growing tensions in U.S.- China and U.S.-Russia relations, China and Russia have consistently deepened their cooperation. Each country is believed to be planning to create an international environment favorable to itself by taking a united stance on security issues, such as Taiwan and issues surrounding NATO’s eastern expansion, which are in conflict with the United States and others. On the military front, since the 1990s, China has purchased modern weapons from Russia, including fighter aircraft, destroyers, and submarines. Russia is currently the largest supplier of weapons to China.43 Although China-Russia arms transactions in value in recent years have been lower than in some past period, China has apparently continued to indicate its strong interests in importing advanced Russian defense equipment and in joint equipment development with Russia. For example, China has introduced what are believed to be the latest fourth generation Su-35 fighter aircraft and the S-400 surface-to-air missile system from Russia. China has been reported as the first country to import the Russian S-400. Meanwhile, it is also suggested that Russia has concerns about competing with China in arms exports taking into consideration China’s improvement of technological power.

Military exchanges between China and Russia take place in such forms as routine mutual visits by senior military officers, as well as joint exercises, joint flights, and joint navigation. Both China and Russia have held the large-scale, joint naval exercise, Maritime Cooperation, since 2012, which includes joint minesweeping drills, blockade operations, raids, and seizure. Additionally, both China and Russia have implemented mutual participation in military exercises since 2018. The frequency of military cooperation has been increasing, including military from both China and Russia mutually participating in exercises organized by each country in September 2024. China likely regards these exchanges as an opportunity to learn about how to operate Russian-made weapons and the operational doctrine of the Russian Armed Forces, which have combat experiences. Since 2019, China and Russia have held joint flights over long distances using bombers a total of ten times. The joint flight in May 2022 was with stronger provocation than ever because it was intended to demonstrate force against Japan, which was holding a Japan-U.S.-Australia-India summit meeting at that time. Their activities are seen as diversifying. During joint flights in November 2024, the President Xi Jinping, President Putin, and Chairman of the State Affairs Commission Kim Jong-un attending the military parade in September 2025 [China News Service/Jiji Press Photo]

The repeated joint flights of bombers and joint navigations of vessels between China and Russia are obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan and are a grave concern for Japan’s security. Since 2021, China and Russia have held joint navigations by vessels a total of six times. The joint statement issued after the China-Russia summit meeting in March 2023 specified that the two countries would regularly conduct “joint patrols” and “joint exercises” at sea and in the air. Their activities are seen as diversifying. For example, during the joint navigation in August 2025, the two countries conducted simultaneous joint navigations in two directions for the first time, navigation from the Sea of Japan to the western Pacific Ocean via the Sea of Okhotsk, and navigation from the Sea of Japan to the East China Sea. Submarines also participated in the navigation for the first time. The repeated joint flights of bombers and joint navigations of vessels between China and Russia are obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan and are a grave concern for Japan’s security. In this way, China and Russia are demonstrating actions to enhance cooperation further even while aggression against Ukraine is ongoing. There is a possibility for the two countries to enhance military cooperation further, and these developments, including the strengthening of military cooperation between China and Russia, not only have a direct impact on the security environment surrounding Japan, but may also have strategic effects on the United States and Europe, and should be watched with concern. Since 2021, China and Russia have held joint navigations by vessels a total of six times. The joint statement issued after the China-Russia summit meeting in March 2023 specified that the two countries would regularly conduct “joint patrols” and “joint exercises” at sea and in the air. Their activities are seen as diversifying. For example, during the joint navigation in August 2025, the two countries conducted simultaneous joint navigations in two directions for the first time, navigation from the Sea of Japan to the western Pacific Ocean via the Sea of Okhotsk, and navigation from the Sea of Japan to the East China Sea. Submarines also participated in the navigation for the first time. The repeated joint flights of bombers and joint navigations of vessels between China and Russia are obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan and are a grave concern for Japan’s security. In this way, China and Russia are demonstrating actions to enhance cooperation further even while aggression against Ukraine is ongoing. There is a possibility for the two countries to enhance military cooperation further, and these developments, including the strengthening of military cooperation between China and Russia, not only have a direct impact on the security environment surrounding Japan, but may also have strategic effects on the United States and Europe, and should be watched with concern. 3 Relations with North Korea China has kept close relations with North Korea under the 1961 Sino-North Korean Mutual Aid and Cooperation Friendship Treaty. In June 2019, General Secretary Xi became the first Chinese president to visit North Korea in 14 years and held his fifth summit meeting with Chairman Kim. In September 2025, General Secretary Xi invited Chairman Kim to the so-called Commemoration of the 80th anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War and held the first China-North Korea summit meeting for the first time in approximately six years. China, while agreeing to UN Security Council resolutions until 2017 to enhance sanctions on North Korea, cooperated with Russia in proposing a draft resolution including lifting some of the sanctions based on UN Security Council resolutions in 2019. In May 2022, China exercised its power of veto with Russia to a draft resolution for sanctions proposed by the United States in response to North Korea’s launching of ICBM-class ballistic missiles. Although China has vowed to have seriously observed its international obligations, it has been pointed out that Chinese ships have been involved in illicit ship-to-ship transfer prohibited by the UN Security Council resolutions.

5 International Transfer of Weapons China is expanding its exports of missiles, tanks, aircraft including drones, and vessels, and was the world’s fourth-largest arms exporter in the decade from 2015 to 2024. Specifically, China’s major arms export destinations are believed to include Pakistan and Bangladesh, but it is also said to export weapons to Algeria, Nigeria, and other African countries, countries in Southeast Asia such as Thailand and Myanmar, and Middle Eastern countries such as Saudi Arabia.44 Some claim that China has transferred weapons to foreign countries in order to strengthen its strategic relationships with friendly nations, enhance its influence in the international community, and secure natural resources. China has not participated in some of the frameworks for international arms export control, and some point out that missile-related and other technologies have been transferred from China to other countries. SUGIURA Yasuyuki, Senior Fellow, China Division, National Institute for Defense Studies In recent years, the Chinese military has been intensifying its military activities in the area around Taiwan using combat aircraft and warships. There was no change to this trend in 2025 either; on the contrary, those actions seem to have been reinforced. In particular, the large-scale Chinese military exercises Strait Thunder-2025A, held in April, and Justice Mission-2025, held in late December, have drawn significant attention from the international community. It can be pointed out that the characteristics of military activities by the Chinese military in the area around Taiwan consist of the following three points: “combat readiness,” which means it conducts practical training with a Taiwan contingency in mind, “propaganda,” which means it actively provides information about the details of the training in a form which mixes together truths and falsehoods, and “normalization” which means that in addition to conducting large-scale exercises, it is also continuously developing a variety of other military activities in the area around Taiwan. From the perspective of combat readiness, the following points are of interest: (i) joint operations training in anticipation of precision guided attacks on the major cities and ports of Taiwan, (ii) joint sea and airspace blockade operations training targeting Taiwan, (iii) law enforcement training by the China Coast Guard coordinated with the military, (iv) simulation training of “decapitation strikes” targeting Taiwanese leaders and key targets, and similar. In particular, the Chinese military is gradually increasing the exercise sites in (ii) and aiming to reinforce its blockade systems (below figure). China is reinforcing a variety of capabilities with a Taiwan contingency in mind.

There was no change to this trend in 2025 either; on the contrary, those actions seem to have been reinforced. In particular, the large-scale Chinese military exercises Strait Thunder-2025A, held in April, and Justice Mission-2025, held in late December, have drawn significant attention from the international community. It can be pointed out that the characteristics of military activities by the Chinese military in the area around Taiwan consist of the following three points: “combat readiness,” which means it conducts practical training with a Taiwan contingency in mind, “propaganda,” which means it actively provides information about the details of the training in a form which mixes together truths and falsehoods, and “normalization” which means that in addition to conducting large-scale exercises, it is also continuously developing a variety of other military activities in the area around Taiwan. From the perspective of combat readiness, the following points are of interest: (i) joint operations training in anticipation of precision guided attacks on the major cities and ports of Taiwan, (ii) joint sea and airspace blockade operations training targeting Taiwan, (iii) law enforcement training by the China Coast Guard coordinated with the military, (iv) simulation training of “decapitation strikes” targeting Taiwanese leaders and key targets, and similar. In particular, the Chinese military is gradually increasing the exercise sites in (ii) and aiming to reinforce its blockade systems (below figure). China is reinforcing a variety of capabilities with a Taiwan contingency in mind.

From the perspective of propaganda, the points that gained attention include (i) the distribution of videos through official announcements by the Chinese military and state-run media, (ii) explanations about the details and purposes of the exercises and assertions about the legality of conducting the exercises by researchers affiliated with Chinese military research institutes, and (iii) criticism of the Lai Ching-te administration by the spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of National Defense. It is believed that the objectives of the military activities by the Chinese military in the area around Taiwan are the following. The first objective is to strongly criticize the Lai Ching-te administration which is considered to be more in favor of Taiwanese independence than the Tsai Ing-wen administration. The second objective is to restrain the United States, which is reinforcing its security relationship with Taiwan. The third objective is to further divide Taiwanese society and isolate the Lai Ching-te administration by combining a hardline stance of military action with a moderate stance centered on promoting economic relations between China and Taiwan. This strengthening of military pressure on Taiwan by the Chinese military amounts to an attempt to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion, and there are concerns that it could lead to destabilization of the security environment in the Indo-Pacific region. For that reason, it is necessary for Japan to continue to closely monitor these moves by the Chinese military. Section 3 Relations between the United States and China, Etc.

1 Relations between the United States and China (General Situation) With regard to the relationship between the United States, the world’s largest economic power, and China, the second largest, competitions between the two countries across the political, economic, and military realms have become increasingly apparent in recent years. This is due to various concerns such as changes in the balance of power caused by China’s growing national power, trade issues, issues concerning the South China Sea, the Taiwan issue, the Hong Kong issue, and human rights issues in China regarding Uighur and Tibet. In particular, since the first Trump administration, the moves of the United States and China that had kept each other in check have come to the surface. Subsequently, there has been strong interest in the irreversible developments in the strategic competition between the two countries. In December 2025, the second Trump administration released its National Security Strategy (NSS). Concerning China, it stated that previous attempts to facilitate China’s entry into the so-called “rules-based international order” were a mistake, and mentioned that the United States would rebalance its economic relationship with China, prioritizing reciprocity and fairness to restore American economic independence. The National Defense Strategy (NDS) released in January 2026 states that China is already the second most powerful country in the world, presents the perception that the speed, scale, and quality of China’s military buildup is historic, and then presents the idea that the United States will build and maintain strong denial defense along the First Island Chain, collaborate with its allies and partners to enhance the effectiveness of collective defense, establish deterrence, and maintain a favorable balance of military power in the Indo-Pacific to ensure that neither China nor anyone else can dominate the United States or its allies.

Taking a strict attitude toward China is becoming common nonpartisan policy. For example, a nonpartisan Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party was established in January 2023 and a resolution to extend the committee’s term, which was originally scheduled to be until the end of 2024, until the end of 2026 was passed in the U.S. House of Representatives in January 2025. On the other hand, regarding this posture of the United States, China says that it desires stable development of U.S.-China relations while at the same time emphasizing that it will resolutely defend its own sovereignty, security, and development interests, and resisting the U.S. posture, saying that the United States should stop portraying China as a military threat and whipping up antagonism among opposing camps. China shows a non-compromising attitude over its own “core interests and material concerns,” and uses special caution regarding involvement with the United States especially in regard to Taiwan issues that China values as “the core of core interests.” When Nancy Pelosi, then Speaker of the House of Representatives, visited Taiwan in August 2022, China conducted large scale military exercises in various areas around Taiwan, and showed an uncompromising attitude against the United States. For example, China announced countermeasures that included suspending various discussions between the two countries. Furthermore, when the United States decided in December 2025 to carry out what is said to be its largest ever weapons sale to Taiwan, China expressed its opposition later in the same month by conducting large-scale military exercises around Taiwan, among other responses.

Exchanges between the United States and China, including between their military authorities, slowed down against the backdrop of House Speaker Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in August 2022 and the detection and downing by the U.S. military of a Chinese reconnaissance balloon over U.S. homeland airspace in February 2023, but efforts have been made to resume exchanges since then. In November 2023, then President Biden held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping for the first time in about a year. They agreed to resume high-level dialogue between military authorities, which the Chinese side appears to have suspended in response to the shooting down of its spy balloon. Additionally, they agreed to resume consultations between their military authorities, which had been suspended by China as a countermeasure when House Speaker Pelosi visited Taiwan. Under the second Trump administration, immediately after inauguration of the administration, the United States imposed additional tariffs on China, citing the influx of fentanyl and other illicit substances as the reason for the tariffs. It also imposed reciprocal tariffs designed to correct trade imbalances. China retaliated with countermeasures, including additional tariffs on the United States and strengthened export controls on rare earth-related items. In this context, in June 2025, the first U.S.-China Summit Meeting since the inauguration of the administration was held in the form of a telephone summit. The leaders primarily consulted on trade issues, and in addition President Xi conveyed his firm position on the Taiwan issue. Subsequently, retaliations between the United States and China continued, including China’s announcement of strengthening of export controls on new rare earth-related items. However, in October of the same year, following a summit in the Republic of Korea (ROK)

Exports, etc. of goods, software, or technologies necessary for production or development to companies and other entities on the list require authorization from the BIS. the United States and its allies. During the second Trump administration, in March 2025, the United States added business entities in China and other countries to the Entity List,2 making them subject to regulations on exports from the United States, in order to restrict the CCP’s acquisition of high-performance computing capabilities and quantum technology that could be used for military purposes and hinder its development of hypersonic weapons. On the other hand, in May of the same year, the United States repealed the regulations strengthening export controls on semiconductors for artificial intelligence (AI) that had been established by the former Biden administration, on the grounds that they were hindering U.S. innovation. In September of the same year, the United States also announced measures to expand the application of export regulations to subsidiaries of business entities named on the Entity List, but taking into account the U.S.-China Summit Meeting held at the end of October of the same year, it decided to suspend these measures for one year from November 10. China has criticized these U.S. initiatives as a malicious blockade against Chinese companies and, since 2020, has enforced a series of laws and regulations which constitute countermeasures to the strengthening of regulations by the United States and other foreign countries.

Competition in the technology and critical minerals field between the United States and China is likely to intensify further in the future as both sides continue to reciprocate each other’s efforts to set forth new regulations. For example, the United States made a move to enhance bilateral and multilateral cooperation, the effects of which can be seen to be spreading internationally.

1 General Situation The second Trump administration, in the NSS, which presented its commitment to a Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP), stated that it would build a military capable of denying aggression anywhere in the First Island Chain, and in addition would focus on pressing its allies and partners to allow the U.S. military greater access to their ports and other facilities, to increase their own defense spending, and most importantly to invest in capabilities aimed at deterring aggression. Furthermore, the NDS advocates deterring China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, not confrontation. The Department of War, while placing importance on strategic stability, deconfliction, and de-escalation, stated it would engage in broader forms of dialogue with its Chinese military counterparts, while also erecting and maintaining a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain, urging and enabling key regional allies and partners to do more for our collective defense, and maintaining the ability to conduct devastating strikes and operations against targets anywhere in the world, including directly from the U.S. homeland. The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2026 continues to place importance on deterring China, etc. as in the previous year. It includes initiatives aimed at strengthening the posture and capabilities of U.S. Forces in the Indo-Pacific, such as extension of the Pacific Deterrence Initiative to enhance the deterrence and defense posture of U.S. Forces in the Indo-Pacific region and increased investment in the innovative technologies necessary to deter China, such as hypersonic technologies, AI, autonomous systems, cyber technologies, and others.

Section 1-1-2 (Defense Policies) Regarding relations with Japan, in the Japan-U.S. Summit Meeting during President Trump’s visit to Japan in October 2025, the two leaders concurred to advance a broad range of security cooperation in order to further enhance the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. Alliance. They acknowledged Japan’s significant strengthening of its defense capabilities and mentioned that Japan and the United States are “an ally at the strongest level.” In addition, in the Japan-U.S. Defense Ministerial Meeting in January 2026, the Ministers confirmed and agreed to make further efforts for expansion of their bilateral joint presence in the southwestern region of Japan and to work more closely together with regard to defense equipment and technology cooperation. On the other hand, China resists this U.S. posture, saying that the United States should stop portraying China as a military threat and whipping up antagonism among opposing camps. It is seen that China is wary of the growth of initiatives, such as those by Japan, the United States, Australia, and India, into strong alliances, as well as with the growing involvement of the United States in the Indo-Pacific region. Furthermore, the military power balance between the United States and China in the Indo-Pacific region is changing because China is rapidly strengthening its military power against a background of economic growth and other factors. China is out of the framework of the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty and the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) and has been enhancing ground-launched missile power unilaterally. Although the United States has insisted that China should be included in arms control negotiations and expressed its intention to apply certain brakes to China’s missile power build-up, China consistently refuses to participate in negotiations,3 asserting that it is maintaining its own nuclear forces at the minimum level necessary for its national security and that its nuclear forces are nowhere near the same scale as those of the United States and Russia. The changes in the military power balance between the United States and China can affect peace and stability of the Indo-Pacific region. Thus, the U.S.-China military trends in the region including the South China Sea and Taiwan will require further attention.

On the other hand, China resists this U.S. posture, saying that the United States should stop portraying China as a military threat and whipping up antagonism among opposing camps. It is seen that China is wary of the growth of initiatives, such as those by Japan, the United States, Australia, and India, into strong alliances, as well as with the growing involvement of the United States in the Indo-Pacific region. Furthermore, the military power balance between the United States and China in the Indo-Pacific region is changing because China is rapidly strengthening its military power against a background of economic growth and other factors. China is out of the framework of the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty and the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) and has been enhancing ground-launched missile power unilaterally. Although the United States has insisted that China should be included in arms control negotiations and expressed its intention to apply certain brakes to China’s missile power build-up, China consistently refuses to participate in negotiations,3 asserting that it is maintaining its own nuclear forces at the minimum level necessary for its national security and that its nuclear forces are nowhere near the same scale as those of the United States and Russia. The changes in the military power balance between the United States and China can affect peace and stability of the Indo-Pacific region. Thus, the U.S.-China military trends in the region including the South China Sea and Taiwan will require further attention.

2 South China Sea With regard to the issues over the South China Sea, the United States is concerned about such dimensions as obstruction to the freedom of navigation in sea lines of communication, restrictions on the activities of U.S. Forces, and the worsening security situation in the entire region. The United States has requested China to comply with international norms, and has repeatedly criticized China’s unilateral and assertive actions. On the other hand, China expresses opposition saying the United States is the largest threat to peace and stability in the South China Sea, and confrontation between these two countries is deepening. China has been advancing into the South China Sea by taking advantage of the power vacuum there since the 1950s, and promoting the militarization of the Paracel Islands. It has also been conducting rapid reclamation of the Spratly Islands on a large scale since 2014. Even after the illegality of the Chinese activities such as land reclamation was determined at the Philippines-China arbitration in 2016, China has made it clear that it would not comply with the decision and has been promoting its plan to militarize the area.

Section 2-2-6 (5) (Trends of Activities in the South China Sea), Section 7 (Southeast Asia) The United States has been condemning China’s action about issues concerning the South China Sea hitherto and has conducted Freedom of Navigation Operations and other activities. The second Trump administration also highlighted in the NSS the importance of the South China Sea from economic and security perspectives, stating that strong measures must be developed along with the deterrence necessary to ensure that this sea area is not subject to arbitrary closure by one country. In response to the clashes between the Philippines and China that have continued even after the Philippines-China arbitration award, the United States again issued a statement demanding that China comply with the obligations of international law. In addition, in January 2022, the U.S. Department of State released a study examining China’s maritime claims in the South China Sea in light of international law. The study concluded that China’s claims over most of the South China Sea are inconsistent with international law and gravely undermine the rule of law in the ocean. In February 2023, during a defense ministerial meeting between the United States and the Philippines, the two countries agreed to add four new cooperation bases within the Philippines, in addition to the existing five, under the “Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA)” to facilitate the rotational deployment of U.S. Forces. In addition, since April 2024, the United States has been deploying its ground-launched, mid-range missile system Typhon in the Philippines. In this way, the administration is showing its stance to further enhance cooperation with countries bordering the South China Sea.

Additionally, the United States has enhanced military efforts in the South China Sea. It has continuously conducted the Freedom of Navigation Operations, carried out joint exercises in July 2020 by deploying two Carrier Strike Groups for the first time since 2014, and subsequently conducted similar exercises several times in order to confront excessive claims by China and other countries over maritime interests. The United States has also conducted joint training with partner countries including Japan, the United Kingdom, Australia, the Netherlands, Canada, Singapore, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Responding to these American efforts, China has criticized the United States for hindering the peace and stability of the region. Going forward, while forming a free and open order based on the rule of law is important in the South China Sea, the military tensions may rise. Japan, which promotes a FOIP with the United States, will have to pay great attention to the situation.

1 Relations with China President Lai of the Democratic Progressive Party, who took office in May 2024, has declared his stance on cross-strait relations at every opportunity; namely, he wants to maintain the status quo and seek exchanges and dialogue on an equal footing, while rejecting the “One China” principle and “1992 Consensus”5 claimed by China. Furthermore, in March 2025, President Lai labelled China a “foreign hostile force” for the first time, and in addition, in November of the same year, he stated that Taiwan’s security was a “struggle about defending ‘democratic Taiwan’ and refusing to submit and become ‘Taiwan, China’” and presented a stance of bolstering Taiwan’s defense capabilities. He also reiterated that the “one country, two systems” model that China intends to apply to Taiwan is unacceptable, saying that the “‘One country, two systems’ model crosses a red line.” Even after the inauguration of the Lai administration, there has continued to be no dialogue between the Chinese and Taiwanese authorities, while China continues to exert pressure on Taiwan in various areas. On the military front, China has intensified its everyday military activities, including increasing the number of Chinese military aircraft entering the airspace surrounding Taiwan, and has conducted military exercises around Taiwan when President Lai has made statements regarding Taiwan’s sovereignty. Furthermore, in June 2024, the Chinese government issued judicial guidelines under which the death penalty may be imposed as the maximum punishment for “acts of secession committed by diehard ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists.” It also continued to add people, including Taiwan Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim, to its list of “diehard ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists,” and suspended the preferential tariff measures under the cross-strait Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement (ECFA) for 134 items from Taiwan, including its petrochemical products. Moreover, in September of the same year, it added pressure in political and economic areas, for example by suspending tariff exemptions for 34 Taiwanese agricultural and fishery products.

According to media reports, an unpublished report submitted by the Ministry of National Defense of Taiwan to the Legislative Yuan in December 2021 outlines the following process for an invasion of Taiwan by China: In the initial stage, China would concentrate its troops along the Chinese coast under the guise of exercises, employ “cognitive warfare” to cause panic among the Taiwanese people, and then concentrate its naval vessels in the Western Pacific to prevent foreign military intervention. Then, naval vessels would be gathered in the Western Pacific to prevent foreign military intervention. Next, under the strategy of transformation from exercises to war, the Rocket and Air Forces would launch ballistic and cruise missiles to attack Taiwan’s key military facilities, while the then Strategic Support Forces would carry out cyberattacks on Taiwan’s key military systems. Finally, after gaining sea and air superiority, landing operations by amphibious assault ships, transport helicopters, and more will be carried out, thus achieving total control of Taiwan before foreign forces intervene. Furthermore, the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR) published by the Ministry of National Defense of Taiwan in March 2025 indicated combat patterns are changing in the Taiwan Strait; specifically, that it is becoming more difficult to clearly identify signs of invasion by the Chinese military, that the transition from peacetime to wartime has become relatively rapid and ambiguous, that China’s development of long-range precision strike capabilities is blurring the boundary between the front and the rear, and that after the outbreak of the conflict, China will employ traditional, hybrid, and irregular warfare forces to inflict multi-domain attacks on Taiwan.

(3) China has strong offensive power of missiles including short-range ballistic missiles (SRBMs) and multiple launch rockets with enough range to attack Taiwan. In response, Taiwan has strengthened its missile defense capabilities by introducing PAC-3 missiles from the United States and increasing the number of Taiwan’s own Tien Kung III missile sites. However, limitations to this response have been pointed out when it comes to dealing with a saturation attack. In addition, Taiwan is attempting to enhance its enemy territory attack capabilities, including by possessing long-range cruise missiles such as the Hsiung Sheng surface-to-surface missile, which are said to have a range of approximately 1,200 km, and deciding to introduce AGM-84H long-range air-to-surface missiles from the United States. Comparison of military capabilities should be made based not only on the troop strength and the performance and quantity of equipment but also on various other factors such as the purpose and aspects of assumed military operations, operational arrangements, the skill level of personnel, and logistics. Nevertheless, the overall military balance between China and Taiwan is rapidly tilting to China’s favor. Concern over peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait which is vital for international security and prosperity is rapidly heightening not only in the Indo-Pacific region, but also among the whole international community, because China is activating threatening military actions around Taiwan. Recognizing that China’s attempts to make unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion are a challenge not only for the Indo-Pacific region but one common to the entire world, Japan, in cooperation with its ally, the United States, like-minded nations, and the international community, will closely monitor related developments with a greater sense of crisis. In addition, Taiwan is attempting to enhance its enemy territory attack capabilities, including by possessing long-range cruise missiles such as the Hsiung Sheng surface-to-surface missile, which are said to have a range of approximately 1,200 km, and deciding to introduce AGM-84H long-range air-to-surface missiles from the United States. Comparison of military capabilities should be made based not only on the troop strength and the performance and quantity of equipment but also on various other factors such as the purpose and aspects of assumed military operations, operational arrangements, the skill level of personnel, and logistics. Nevertheless, the overall military balance between China and Taiwan is rapidly tilting to China’s favor. Concern over peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait which is vital for international security and prosperity is rapidly heightening not only in the Indo-Pacific region, but also among the whole international community, because China is activating threatening military actions around Taiwan. Recognizing that China’s attempts to make unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion are a challenge not only for the Indo-Pacific region but one common to the entire world, Japan, in cooperation with its ally, the United States, like-minded nations, and the international community, will closely monitor related developments with a greater sense of crisis. (2) Military Capabilities The North Korean Army comprises about 1.10 million personnel, and roughly two-thirds of them seem to be deployed along the DMZ. The main body of the army is infantry, but the army also maintains armored forces including at least 3,500 tanks and artillery. North Korea is believed to have deployed long-range artillery along the DMZ, such as 240 mm multiple rocket launchers and 170 mm self-propelled artillery guns, which can reach cities and bases in the northern part of the ROK including Seoul. The Navy retains about 790 ships and boats with a total displacement of approximately 100,000 tons and is chiefly comprised of small naval vessels. Meanwhile, in April and June 2025, North Korea launched a “new-type multi-mission destroyer,”7 which significantly exceeds the size of any warship previously possessed by North Korea. Chairman Kim stated that “we will execute this plan of building multi-mission destroyer year by year.”8 Also, it has about 20 of the former model Romeo-class submarines, about 30 midget submarines and about 140 air cushioned landing crafts, the latter two of which are believed to be used for infiltration and other actions of the special operations forces. In September 2023, the Navy launched a new submarine that appears to be a modified Romeo-class submarine and dubbed it a “tactical nuclear attack submarine.” The Air Force has approximately 550 combat aircraft, most of which are out-of-date models made in China or the former Soviet Union. However, some fourth-generation aircraft such as MiG-29 fighters and Su-25 attack aircraft are also included. North Korea has a large number of outdated An-2 transport aircraft as well, which are believed to be used for transportation of special operations forces.

North Korea also possesses a large special forces9 contingent as a so-called asymmetric capability. In recent years, it has been strengthening its cyber units as an asymmetric force. These units are believed to steal cryptocurrency to fund nuclear and missile development, while also engaging in the theft of military secrets from other countries and developing capabilities to attack critical infrastructure abroad.

4 Progress of Military Cooperation with Russia (1) Trends in Military Cooperation As Russia’s aggression against Ukraine continues, North Korea is rapidly developing its cooperative relationship with Russia. In June 2024, Russian President Putin visited North Korea for the first time in 24 years and held a summit meeting with Chairman Kim. During the visit, both signed the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, which included a provision to provide military assistance in the event of an armed invasion, and Chairman Kim stated that relations between North Korea and Russia had entered a new stage, that of an alliance. (The treaty went into effect in December 2024.) Furthermore, another summit meeting was held in Beijing in September 2025 on the occasion of Chairman Kim’s participation in the 80th anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. Chairman Kim noted that North Korea-Russia relations had expanded and advanced in all fields since the conclusion of the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, while President Putin also expressed that relations with North Korea “have assumed an allied character.” These statements highlighted the further deepening of North Korea-Russia relations. The moves to strengthen relations with Russia are particularly evident in the military sphere. For example, since 2023, weapons and ammunition, including ballistic missiles, have been supplied from North Korea to Russia. It has been pointed out that North Korean artillery shells have been used in Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and that North Korea supplied at least 100 ballistic missiles in 2024.48 Such support has significantly contributed to Russia’s sustained operational capability against Ukraine. With its ongoing missile development and repeated ballistic missile launches, North Korea’s actions are severely undermining the peace and security of the region and wider international community. Moreover, the seemingly significant deepening of its military cooperation with Russia causes concern that this cooperation will lead to North Korea’s military capabilities becoming further enhanced. Given that North Korea’s military actions now pose an even graver and more imminent threat to Japan’s national security than ever before, it is crucial to continue working in close cooperation with the United States and the Republic of Korea while carefully monitoring North Korea’s actions to understand its future plans for strengthening its military capabilities based on the various policies indicated by Chairman Kim this time. Although the value of the 2023 to 2025 contracts was down from the record-high value of 2022, the ROK Government is aiming for rapid progress to becoming one of “the world’s four leading defense industrial powers”64 by pursuing diverse projects and expanding government support. Defense spending in FY2026 (regular budget) increased by about 7.5% from the previous fiscal year to nearly KRW 65.8642 trillion, marking the 27th consecutive year of increases since 2000. Furthermore, in the Joint Fact Sheet of the U.S.-ROK summit meeting (held in October 2025), which was released in November of the same year, the ROK declared that it would “increase its defense spending to 3.5% of GDP as soon as possible.” Fig. I-3-4-10 (Changes in the ROK’s Defense Budget (Past 10 Years))

5 Relations with Countries and Regions (1) Relations with China China and the ROK have made continuous efforts to strengthen their relations. China opposes the deployment of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system75 to USFK, saying that it undermines the strategic security interests of China. Although both countries agreed in October 2017 to continue communicating on the THAAD-related issues that China was concerned about through channels established between their respective military authorities, conflicting views still remain.76 Furthermore, in recent years, confrontations have occurred in the China-ROK Provisional Measures Zone (PMZ) in the Yellow Sea,77 where China has been installed structures and the ROK has been demanding their removal. While these kinds of concerns exist, since the inauguration of the Lee Jae Myung administration, two China-ROK summit meetings have been held, and there are signs of a recovery in economic relations. Concerning the China-ROK PMZ, the ROK Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced in February 2026 that it had confirmed that one of the three structures installed by China78 had been moved outside the PMZ, and the ministry also said that it was continuing to seek further progress on the issue through constructive consultations with China.79 With momentum building for improved China-ROK relations in this way, attention will continue to be focused on developments going forward.
