(2) Relations with Russia The ROK and Russia have agreed on cooperation in the areas of military technology, defense industry, and military supplies. Both countries held Defense Strategy Dialogue in August 2018 and agreed to promote the dialogue to vice minister level and, in November 2021, also agreed to set up hotlines between Navies and between Air Forces. The ROK has implemented sanctions against Russia and provided military supplies and other resources to Ukraine in a show of solidarity with the international community following Russia’s aggression against Ukraine since February 2022. In addition, when it was confirmed in October 2024 that North Korean soldiers had been dispatched to Russia, a government delegation of the ROK visited Belgium to provide information to NATO and the EU. At the same time, even as North Korean soldiers dispatched to Russia participate in fighting against Ukraine, the ROK maintains a cautious stance regarding the provision of lethal weapons to Ukraine. As the Lee Jae Myung administration places importance on maintaining a diplomatic balance with four neighboring countries (Japan, the United States, China, and Russia), attention will continue to be focused on how it will maintain stable relations with Russia, given the situation in Ukraine.

1 General Situation President Vladimir Putin, who has been seeking the revival of Russia as a strong and influential power, commenced full aggression against Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Russia’s aggression against Ukraine undermines the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, and it is also a serious violation of international law including the Charter of the United Nations, which forbids the use of force. The aggression shakes the foundations of the international order and is understood as the most serious and direct threat to defense in the European area. Russia also makes clear its stance that it continues to work on the modernization of strategic nuclear weapons, and repeats speech and behavior that can be taken as nuclear weapons threats in the middle of the aggression against Ukraine. In recent years, Russian forces around Japan have introduced new types of equipment and continued active operations. In addition, there has been movement to further enhance military cooperation with China, such as joint flights by Russian and Chinese bombers, joint navigation of warships, and continued mutual participation in exercises. Military trends of Russia in the Indo-Pacific region including Japan, combined with this strategic cooperation with China, are strong concerns for security. Also taking into account movements in the aggression against Ukraine, close observation of the situation is required. Chapter 2 (Russia’s Aggression and Defense by Ukraine)

1 Strategic and Policy Documents Russia set out its objectives and strategic priorities of domestic and foreign policies in the “National Security Strategy” revised in July 2021. The National Security Strategy states that Russia’s policies through now to strengthen its defense capabilities, domestic unity, and political stability, and modernize its economy, and develop its industrial base, have strengthened Russia as a sovereign state capable of pursuing an independent domestic and foreign policy and effectively opposing external pressures. This indicates Russia’s awareness of the existence of external threats and its belief that it is a “strong state” that will not succumb to them. It also states that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s (NATO) military activities around Russia are a military threat and that the deployment of U.S. intermediate- and short-range missiles in Europe and the Asia-Pacific region is a threat to strategic stability. In the defense section, the Strategy commits to giving continued priority to the role fulfilled by Russia’s military force, and to ensuring strategic deterrence and preventing military conflict by maintaining a sufficient level of nuclear deterrent capability and combat readiness of Russian military forces, including the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (AFRF). The Military Doctrine, revised in December 2014 as a document substantiating the principles of the National Security Strategy in the military sphere, states the existing view that while the probability of an outbreak of a large-scale war is decreasing, military risks to Russia are increasing, such as the movement of NATO’s military infrastructure closer to Russia’s borders including the expansion of NATO, and the establishment and deployment of strategic missile defense (MD) systems. In addition, the doctrine expresses growing alarm, defining the following as new military risks: NATO’s military buildup; the realization of the U.S. Global Strike concept; the rise of global violent extremism (terrorism); the formation of governments in neighboring countries that carry out policies threatening Russia’s interests; and the incitement of ethnic, social, and religious confrontations in Russia.

It also states that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s (NATO) military activities around Russia are a military threat and that the deployment of U.S. intermediate- and short-range missiles in Europe and the Asia-Pacific region is a threat to strategic stability. In the defense section, the Strategy commits to giving continued priority to the role fulfilled by Russia’s military force, and to ensuring strategic deterrence and preventing military conflict by maintaining a sufficient level of nuclear deterrent capability and combat readiness of Russian military forces, including the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (AFRF). The Military Doctrine, revised in December 2014 as a document substantiating the principles of the National Security Strategy in the military sphere, states the existing view that while the probability of an outbreak of a large-scale war is decreasing, military risks to Russia are increasing, such as the movement of NATO’s military infrastructure closer to Russia’s borders including the expansion of NATO, and the establishment and deployment of strategic missile defense (MD) systems. In addition, the doctrine expresses growing alarm, defining the following as new military risks: NATO’s military buildup; the realization of the U.S. Global Strike concept; the rise of global violent extremism (terrorism); the formation of governments in neighboring countries that carry out policies threatening Russia’s interests; and the incitement of ethnic, social, and religious confrontations in Russia.

In addition, the doctrine raises characteristics of modern military warfare as being the massive use of precision weapons, hypersonic weapons, electronic warfare equipment, all types of autonomous vehicles, and the like, as well as the phenomena of automation and centralization of operations through a network of automatic management systems. In addition, without using the phrase “hybrid warfare,” the doctrine also points out the integrated use of military force and political, economic, informational and other non-military measures, as well as participation in hostilities by irregular armed groups and private military companies. The Military Doctrine positions nuclear weapons as an essential component for preventing the outbreak of nuclear wars and military conflicts that use conventional weapons. document, “Basic Principles of State Policy of the Russian Federation on Nuclear Deterrence,” which is equivalent to the so-called nuclear doctrine. 2 Defense Budget Russia’s defense budget had generally remained at around 3% of GDP since FY2017. However, following the aggression against Ukraine, Russia has continued to increase its defense budget, and in FY2025, the revised budget reached an all-time high of approximately 13.5 trillion rubles (approximately 6.3% of GDP). The defense budget for FY2026 (initial budget) was approximately 12.9 trillion rubles, which represents the first decrease following the aggression against Ukraine; however, national security spending on paramilitary organizations amounted to approximately 3.9 trillion rubles, an increase of approximately 13% compared to the previous year.1 Fig. I-3-5-1 (Changes in Russia’s Defense Expenditure)

3 Military Reform By 2021, Russia established joint strategic commands for four military districts (the Western, Southern, Central, and Eastern Districts) as well as the Northern Fleet (in charge of units facing the Arctic), and the military forces have been jointly operated under each District Commander in this system. However, since the commencement of the aggression against Ukraine in February 2022, Russia has shown some movements to increase strength as well as to enlarge and reorganize units. Then Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu proposed increasing the total strength to 1.5 million troops, establishing two military districts in Moscow and Leningrad, reorganizing several existing brigades into divisions, deploying one new corps to the Finland border region, and other measures to President Putin at an expanded meeting of the Defence Ministry Board in December 2022. At a meeting in December 2023, it was reported that the number of military personnel had reached 1.15 million during the year and that two combined arms armies, a mixed aviation corps, four divisions, 18 brigades, and 28 regiments had already been newly formed. In February 2024, President Putin signed a presidential decree to create the Moscow Military District and Leningrad Military District, resulting in the Northern Fleet losing its status as a joint strategic command and military district. In September 2024, he signed another presidential decree to increase the number of military troops to 1.5 million.

Furthermore, in November 2025, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that it had established a new branch, the “Unmanned Systems Forces.” Regarding the Navy and the Aerospace Forces, although military districts maintain operational command during wartime, naval fleets and naval aviation units are excluded from their jurisdiction during peacetime according to a presidential decree which enetered into force in February 2025 to amend the “regulations on military districts,” and this move is a reversion to the system that Russia used in and before 2010. This is believed to be because the Russian Navy and Aerospace Forces placed more importance on establishing unified operation by each General Headquarters than on a unified operation system at the military district level. It will be necessary to continue to closely monitor the trends in the Russian military’s chain of command, organizational restructuring, and changes in its joint operational posture since the aggression against Ukraine from the perspective of how the Russian military will reflect the lessons it learned in Ukraine in its operational posture.

3 Military Posture and Trends Russia’s military forces are comprised of forces such as the AFRF, the Border Guard Service of the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation (FSB), and the Federal National Guard Service of the Russian Federation. The AFRF consists of three services and two independent forces: Ground Forces; Navy; Aerospace Forces; Strategic Missile Forces; and Airborne Forces. In developing its military capabilities, Russia is conscious of the United States and, while ensuring a balance in its nuclear forces, is expanding its equipment similar to that of advanced nations, such as land-attack cruise missiles capable of being precision-guided and drones, for its conventional forces that it perceives as inferior to those of advanced nations. As for its asymmetric responses, it is believed that Russia places importance on improving its so-called Anti-Access/ Area-Denial (A2/AD) capabilities through long-range surface-to-air and surface-to-ship missile systems and electronic warfare equipment. 1 Nuclear and Missile Forces Russia places a strong emphasis on its nuclear forces not only to maintain its international status and ensure a proper balance with U.S. nuclear capabilities, but also to compensate for the significant attrition of its conventional forces amid the ongoing aggression against Ukraine. To that end, it is working to maintain a high state of readiness while modernizing various platforms and early warning systems. Regarding strategic nuclear forces, Russia possesses intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs), and long-range bombers comparable to the United States in scale. In 2011, Russia started deploying the ICBM “Yars,” which is considered a multi-warhead version of the ICBM “Topol-M.” It was pointed out that the large ICBM “Sarmat,” intended to replace the ICBM “Voyevoda” which was made in Ukraine during the Soviet era, may have repeatedly failed in its launch tests between 2023 and 2025. However, the Russian government announced a successful launch in May 2026, and the missile is reportedly scheduled for deployment by the end of 2026. Eight Borey/Borey-A class Nuclear-Powered Ballistic Missile Submarines (SSBN), which carry the new-type SLBM Bulava, were commissioned. Five such vessels have already been deployed to the Pacific Fleet, and in the future, Russia plans to deploy five to the Northern Fleet as well. The modernization renovation of Tu-95 bombers and the new production of Tu-160 bombers continues, and the Russian Ministry of Defence has announced that two new Tu-160 bombers were delivered in 2025. As for non-strategic nuclear forces, Russia is working to deploy various non-strategic missiles such as the land attack missile system “Iskander,” which is believed to be capable of carrying either conventional or non-strategic nuclear warheads, the sea-launched cruise missile system “Kalibr,” the air-launched cruise missile (ALCM) “Kh-101,” and the air-launched ballistic missile (ALBM) “Kinzhal.” Russia places these missiles as “non-nuclear deterrence by precise guided weapons,” and considers

4 Space and Electromagnetic Domain The AFRF has also been stepping up its activities in the fields of space and the electromagnetic spectrum in recent years. Russia is believed to be promoting the development of anti-satellite weapons such as the “Nudol” anti-satellite missile system. In November 2021, Russia announced that it would conduct a satellite destruction test using an anti-satellite missile. Since 2013, Russia has put satellites into both low and geostationary orbits to conduct rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO), which have repeatedly been observed engaging in frequent RPO with other countries’ satellites on geostationary orbits. In the electromagnetic spectrum domain, since 2009, the AFRF has established an Electronic Warfare (EW) Unit, and many new EW systems have been procured and distributed or allocated to each service and force. In particular, it has been pointed out that in Ukraine, various electronic warfare equipment, including the Pole-21, are being deployed on the front lines and used against the Ukrainian military’s GPS-guided artillery shells and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). 5 Trends Related to the AFRF (General) Since 2010, the AFRF has been conducting large-scale round-robin exercises in each military district, with the objective of verifying the combat readiness of the military districts, etc.6 These exercises are helping to improve the long-distance mobilization capability of the AFRF. In September 2025, the Russia-Belarus joint strategic exercise “Zapad 2025” was held in the Leningrad Military District and the Moscow Military District (originally scheduled for 2023, but it was canceled). Approximately 10,000 personnel participated in the exercise, which included joint training with multinational forces involving personnel from India, Iran, and other countries. The training incorporated lessons learned in Ukraine, such as tactics for dealing with UAVs and unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), and ammunition drop training using first-person view (FPV) drones. Among exercises for nuclear and missile forces, in February 2022, just prior to the start of the aggression against Ukraine, a large-scale missile exercise was conducted across Russia using strategic nuclear forces such as ICBMs and SLBMs as well as missile forces capable of carrying conventional or tactical nuclear warheads (Iskander, Kalibr, Kinzhal, and Zircon). In addition, similar missile exercises for strategic nuclear forces were also conducted in October 2022, October 2023, and October 2024. In October 2025, the Russian Ministry of Defence also announced that it had conducted a missile exercise involving live launches of ICBM “Yars,” SLBM “Sineva” and ALCMs. Furthermore, the Russian Ministry of Defence took steps to maintain the readiness of its units and conducted exercises to test non-strategic nuclear forces for the first time since the collapse of the Soviet Union in response to provocative statements and threats from Western officials. These exercises were conducted in three stages, specifically in the Southern Military District in May 2024, the Leningrad Military District and Belarus in June 2024, and the Central Military District and Southern Military District in July 2024, and activities conducted during each exercise included simulated “Iskander-M” missile launches. In the Arctic Region, Russia is developing coastal surveillance radar networks for enhanced warning and surveillance. 31 interceptor fighters, while also deploying surface-to-air missiles and surface-to-ship missiles to develop sufficient preparedness for dealing with airborne threats from the north and attacks from ships. Along with these developments, Russia has built a large-scale residential facility for personnel at the base in two places within the Arctic Region. For example, the comprehensive Arctic expedition “Umka- 2022” was held in the Chukchi Sea in 2022. 6 Russian Forces in the Vicinity of Japan Russia newly established the Eastern Military District and the Eastern Joint Strategic Command in 2010. Ground Forces, the Pacific Fleet, and the Air Force and Air Defense Units have been placed under the Military District Commander, who conducts unified operation of these services. Meanwhile, regarding the Navy and Aerospace Forces, as mentioned earlier, the presidential decree to revise the countries “regulations on military districts” has excluded naval and air units from their military districts’ jurisdiction during peacetime, marking a return to the system Russia had used before 2010. Even as Russia’s aggression against Ukraine continues, Russia is strengthening its nuclear forces. In the vicinity of Japan, it appears to be intensifying its focus on defending the area around the Sea of Okhotsk, which is the operational zone of its strategic nuclear-powered submarines. The current presence of the AFRF in the Far East region is significantly smaller than it was at its peak. However, a considerable scale of military forces, including nuclear forces, still remains in the region. In recent years, Russia has also been deploying the latest equipment in the Far East. It announced that the percentage of new equipment in the Eastern Military District was 56% as of December 2021. Given that the AFRF has set their basis of operation on maintaining the combat readiness of their strategic nuclear units and dealing with conflicts through the inter-theater mobility of its round-the-clock readiness units, it is necessary to keep our attention on the trends of the AFRF in the Far East region while also keeping in mind the trends of units in other regions.

The fleet consists of approximately 50 major surface combatants and 20 submarines, roughly 10 of which are nuclear-powered. In addition, warships equipped with the Kalibr cruise missile, a precision-guided weapon capable of carrying both tactical nuclear and conventional warheads, have also been deployed successively to the Pacific Fleet since 2021. As of the end of FY2025, deployed warships included one Udaloy III-class destroyer and four improved Kilo-class submarines in Vladivostok as well as one Steregushchiy III-class frigate and two Yasen-M-class nuclear-powered submarines in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskiy. (4) Air Forces In the Eastern Military District, Russia deploys approximately 290 combat aircraft from its Aerospace Forces and Navy combined. Existing models are being modernized, and in addition to the Su-35 fighters and the Su-34 fighter-bombers, the new Su-57 is being introduced to improve their capabilities.

(5) Operations in the Vicinity of Japan In the vicinity of Japan, the AFRF has been actively continuing its activities, including exercises and drills which are believed to be conducted for objectives such as verifying the results of the military reform. The number of exercises carried out by the Russian Ground Forces in the areas adjacent to Japan has decreased from the peak. With regard to naval vessels, their activities are generally increasing in recent years. For example, various exercises and long-distance voyages have been carried out by Pacific Fleet vessels, along with patrols by nuclear-powered submarines. In April 2023, the commander of the Pacific Fleet was replaced for the first time in 11 years, and the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that a surprise inspection of the Pacific Fleet was conducted with the participation of more than 25,000 personnel and more than 160 vessels. Defence Minister Shoigu explained that the objective of this inspection was to “prevent the aggression of an enemy into the southern Sea of Okhotsk,” indicating that Russia intended to show off the capability of the Russian Navy to actively operate in the Sea of Okhotsk, which Russia considers crucial as an operating area for strategic nuclear submarines even while engaged in aggression against Ukraine. In addition, President Putin stated during a related exercise that military power “can be used in conflicts on all fronts.” It is believed that his statement aimed to emphasize that the naval forces in the Far East are maintaining the combat readiness even while ground forces are dispatched from the Eastern Military District to Ukraine.

4 Russian Forces in Japan’s Northern Territories Since 1978 during the former Soviet Union era, Russia has redeployed Ground Forces units on Kunashiri, Etorofu, and Shikotan Islands of the Northern Territories, which are inherent territories of Japan. While the Russian troop strength is thought to be far less than that at peak times, one division, which belongs to a corps still stationed in South Sakhalin, is located on Kunashiri and Etorofu Islands. Furthermore, tanks, armored vehicles, various types of artillery, anti-air missiles, and unmanned reconnaissance vehicles are deployed. In recent years, Russia has been upgrading the facilities of its troops located in the Northern Territories. It is also deploying new equipment such as surface-to-ship missile systems belonging to its Navy and fighter aircraft belonging to its Aerospace Forces, conducting large-scale exercises, and continuing its vigorous military activities under the illegal occupation of the Northern Territories, which are inherent territories of Japan. Some point out the background for such moves as being the rising military importance of all of the Sea of Okhotsk, an operating area of SSBN. The Russian military continues to conduct active operations not only in the Northern Territories, but also in South Sakhalin and the Chishima Islands, whose jurisdiction has not been determined. In recent years, the deployment of major new equipment in the Northern Territories has included the announced deployment of surface-to-ship missile systems to Etorofu and Kunashiri Islands in 2016, and in August 2018, three Su-35 fighters were reportedly deployed at the new civilian airport on Etorofu Island, which was opened to military and civilian dual use in January of that year.

In this document, Russia condemns Western countries for adopting anti-Russian policies and emphasizes cooperation with countries such as China and India, while stating that it aims to build a multipolar international order. 2 Relations with the United States President Putin has striven to deepen cooperative relations with the United States in the economic domain, while opposing the United States on any action Russia considers as “a U.S. attempt to encroach on Russia’s strategic interests.” On the military front, feeling that the United States’ installation of missile defense systems both at home and abroad—including in Europe and the Asia-Pacific— undermines global and regional security, Russia has criticized these moves for upsetting the strategic balance. Russia is also moving forward with the development of new strategic weapons that are said to be capable of reliably penetrating missile defense systems. In regard to arms control between the United States and Russia, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty ended in August 2019 during the first Trump administration after having gone through a series of processes originating from the withdrawal announcement of the United States side. In November 2020, the United States pulled out of the Open Skies Treaty, which was signed by the Western countries and Russia allowing its participants to mutually conduct unarmed observation and surveillance flights, and this was followed by Russia announcing its withdrawal in January 2021. On the other hand, with regard to the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which set the upper limit of strategic nuclear forces for Russia and the United States, although both countries agreed on its unconditional extension for five years in January 2021, just before the expiration of the treaty in February 2021, President Putin unilaterally declared “holding the treaty in abeyance” in February 2023, which is not stipulated in the treaty. In September 2025, President Putin stated that it was prepared to maintain central quantitative limits on weapons regulated by the treaty for one year following February 2026 if the United States did so as well, but the treaty expired during the same month without seeing any concrete progress.

5 Relations with Former Soviet Republics Russia positions the development of bilateral and multilateral cooperation with former Soviet republics as one of its most important foreign policy objectives. Russia considers its vital interests to be concentrated in this region. It stations its troops in the Collective Security Treaty Organization7 (CSTO) member states Armenia (which declared its intention to withdraw from the CSTO in February 2024), Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Belarus, as well as Moldova (Transnistria), Georgia (South Ossetia, Abkhazia), and Ukraine (Crimea). Through the conclusion of an alliance and strategic partnership treaty with Abkhazia in November 2014, the conclusion of an alliance and integration treaty with South Ossetia in March 2015, and other efforts, Russia has been working to ensure its military influence. However, today, after more than 30 years have passed since the collapse of USSR, none of the former Soviet Union countries except Belarus support Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Some consider that Russia’s influence on the former Soviet area will decline still further in the wake of the aggression against Ukraine. requested support from President Putin for the modification of Belarusian Air Force aircraft to specifications for equipment of nuclear weapons in June 2022, and President Putin agreed. It was announced in February 2023 that Belarus deployed an “Iskander” surface-to-surface missile system received from Russia. In July 2023, it was announced that the defense ministers of the two countries had signed documents regarding procedures for storing Russian tactical nuclear weapons on Belarusian territory. In December 2023, Belarusian President Lukashenko stated that the deployment of tactical nuclear weapons that Russia had delivered to the Belarusian territory was completed in October 2023. Under Russia’s revised Basic Principles of State Policy of the Russian Federation on Nuclear Deterrence (the so-called nuclear doctrine), Russia added attacks on Belarus to the conditions under which it would use nuclear weapons. In addition, in December 2024, the leaders of Russia and Belarus signed a security treaty that imposes an obligation on the countries to mutually defend each other, including the use of Russian tactical nuclear weapons deployed in Belarus. Furthermore, in September 2025, Russia and Belarus conducted the joint strategic exercise Zapad 2025, which was announced to have included training in the operation of Russia’s non-strategic nuclear weapons and the new intermediate-range ballistic missile “Oreshnik.” In December 2025, the Russian Ministry of Defence released a video to show that it had deployed a Strategic Missile Forces unit equipped with the “Oreshnik” system to Belarus. In the Caucasus region, Azerbaijan launched a military operation in September 2023 to make Armenian forces withdraw from the “Nagorno Karabakh Republic,” which had unilaterally declared independence on Azerbaijan’s territory and had been exercising effective control over the region. After being attacked by Azerbaijani forces, the “Nagorno Karabakh Republic” surrendered in September and signed an agreement to dissolve the republic by January 2024. As a result of this conflict, the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, which had been exercising effective control over part of Azerbaijan’s territory for more than 32 years since the end of the Soviet Union, was dissolved. The Russian armed forces, stationed as peacekeeping forces in the republic (withdrawn from the republic in June 2024), were unable to prevent the military conflict, which caused Armenia, a CSTO member state and Russia’s military ally, to lose trust in Russia,8 and some believe this has exposed the decline of Russian influence in the region.

In the Caucasus region, Azerbaijan launched a military operation in September 2023 to make Armenian forces withdraw from the “Nagorno Karabakh Republic,” which had unilaterally declared independence on Azerbaijan’s territory and had been exercising effective control over the region. After being attacked by Azerbaijani forces, the “Nagorno Karabakh Republic” surrendered in September and signed an agreement to dissolve the republic by January 2024. As a result of this conflict, the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, which had been exercising effective control over part of Azerbaijan’s territory for more than 32 years since the end of the Soviet Union, was dissolved. The Russian armed forces, stationed as peacekeeping forces in the republic (withdrawn from the republic in June 2024), were unable to prevent the military conflict, which caused Armenia, a CSTO member state and Russia’s military ally, to lose trust in Russia,8 and some believe this has exposed the decline of Russian influence in the region.

6 Relations with Other Countries (1) Relations with Asian Countries Russia recognizes that the significance of the Asia-Pacific region is increasing within its multi-pronged foreign policy and considers it strategically important to strengthen its status in the region from the viewpoint of socioeconomic development in Siberia and the Far East, and security. In Asia, in addition to its relations with China, Russia assigns an important role to its Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership with India and continues to pursue wide-ranging military cooperation. Furthermore, Russia is working to strengthen its relations with ASEAN countries and conducted its first-ever joint maritime exercise with such countries in the inshore waters of Indonesia in December 2021. From November to December 2023, vessels from the Russian Pacific Fleet visited eight countries in Southeast Asia and South Asia. With Myanmar in particular, Russia co-hosted an anti-terrorism tabletop exercise within the framework of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in August 2023 and then conducted the first joint maritime exercise between the two countries, the Myanmar-Russia Maritime Security Exercise (MARUMEX), in November 2023. From October to November 2024, Russia visited five countries from Southeast Asia to East Asia. In November, in particular, Russia conducted ORRUDA, its first-ever bilateral naval exercise with Indonesia, and PASSEX, its first-ever bilateral naval exercise with Thailand. In addition, from February to June 2025, Russia visited nine countries from Southeast Asia to South Asia and conducted bilateral exercises, among other activities. Section 8-1-3 (3) (Relations with Russia) (2) Relations with European Countries Through the framework of the NATO-Russia Council (NRC), Russia has worked with NATO as an equal partner in the areas of common interest, such as by participating in certain decision-making processes. However, following the Ukrainian crisis in 2014, NATO and European countries suspended their practical cooperation with Russia thereafter, including that in the military domain, except for the NRC’s ambassador-level meetings. Moreover, with the aggression against Ukraine, the relationship between Russia and European countries is the tensest it has been since the Cold War era. In particular, in September 2025, Poland announced that it had shot down Russian drones that had violated Polish airspace, but the Russian Ministry of Defence denied any intention to attack Polish territory. That same month, NATO announced that it had bolstered its eastern flank defense posture, with the United Kingdom and other NATO members deploying aircraft and naval vessels under the framework of “Eastern Sentry.”

Chapter 2, 3-2 (How NATO Member States and Other Countries Deal with the Situation) (3) Relations with Middle Eastern and African Countries In the Foreign Policy Concept published in March 2023, comprehensive mutual cooperation with Iran, total support for Syria, and deepened partnerships with Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other countries are stated definitely. Above all, for Syria, the AFRF has continued to secure the Tartus Naval Base and Khmeimim Air Base in Syria since September 2015 to conduct operations to support the Assad administration. In operations in Syria, Russia has conducted bombings using fighter bombers and long-range bombers, as well as attacks using cruise missiles from surface ships and submarines deployed in the Caspian Sea and the Mediterranean Sea. After the collapse of the Assad administration in December 2024, Russian Presidential Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov stated that no final decision has been made regarding Russian military bases in Syria and that this decision will be made based on consultation by the powers that control the country. In addition, in January 2025, President Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership covering a wide range of fields, including security and energy. However, although this treaty includes military-technical cooperation, it does not include any regulations on the provision of military assistance

In recent years, Russia has actively tried to sell not only to conventional importers of its products but also to U.S. allies and U.S. friendly countries such as Türkiye. Russia appears to be reinforcing its nuclear forces even as it continues its aggression against Ukraine. In the area surrounding Japan, Russia is considered to be further focusing on the defense of the area surrounding the Sea of Okhotsk, which is its waters of operation for strategic nuclear-powered submarines. Regarding strategic nuclear submarines, a new type of Borey A-class SSBN was deployed every year between 2022 and 2024, bringing the current total of Borey/Borey A-class SSBNs to five, and some of the existing nuclear submarines have been modernized and upgraded. In recent years, the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (AFRF) has newly deployed “Bastion” and “Bal” surface-to-ship missile systems and S-400 surface-to-air missile systems in the Kamchatka Peninsula, which is in the vicinity of the Sea of Okhotsk, Russia’s waters of operation for nuclear-powered submarines; in the Chishima Islands and South Sakhalin, which are disputed territories; and in Japan’s Northern Territories. These moves are thought to be part of Russia’s so-called “bastion” strategy, in which it seeks to prevent other countries’ militaries from approaching the area around the Sea of Okhotsk, the waters where it operates its strategic nuclear-powered submarines. In addition, from the perspective of strengthening the “bastion” strategy, the AFRF is considered to be advancing the development and utilization of naval and air forces based in Primorsky Krai and the Kamchatka Peninsula. Specifically, Russia is in the process of upgrading the Pacific Fleet with ships armed with “Kalibr” cruise missiles, which are precisionguided munitions capable of carrying tactical nuclear and conventional warheads.

Furthermore, in recent years, Russia has further reinforced its military cooperation with China. Specifically, Russia has been conducting joint navigation of naval vessels, joint flights of bombers, and various types of training with China. Regarding the joint navigation of naval vessels, along with a trend toward expanding the sea areas in which these activities take place, diversification in the range of naval activities has been seen, such as the participation of submarines in an August 2025 joint navigation for the first time. Moreover, regarding joint flights of bombers, expansion of the airspace in which the activities take place and an increase in aircraft types other than bombers participating in the activities have been seen. In December 2025, Chinese and Russian bombers flew a long distance from the East China Sea, passing through the airspace between the main island of Okinawa and Miyakojima Island, and reaching the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Shikoku for the first time in a joint flight. Moreover, regarding the various trainings, in September 2024 the militaries of China and Russia each participated in exercises organized by the other country and conducted in the same timeframe. We must watch Russia’s military developments in the Indo-Pacific region, including the area surrounding Japan, as well as Russia’s increasing naval and air forces and trends in Russia’s military cooperation with China, with strong concern. YAMAZOE Hiroshi, Head of America, Europe, and Russia Division, National Institute for Defense Studies Since February 2022, Russia has continued its intense aggression against Ukraine involving attacking and occupying its territory, which has resulted in countless human rights violations. Despite the economic sanctions imposed on the country, Russia appears to be raising funds for the war effort by switching to new oil and gas export markets, along with increasing taxes and issuing government bonds, which indicates a certain degree of resilience against the sanctions. Moreover, in addition to strengthening the production capabilities of military supplies through prioritizing allocation of resources to the arms industry, it is also focusing on recruiting new contract soldiers and continually sends large quantities of military supplies and personnel to Ukraine. In particular, Russia also receives support from overseas for military supplies. For example, it has been reported that the country produces military supplies using foreign currency and technical resources such as communications devices and sensors obtained through trade with China. In addition, Shahed drones, which it produces using manufacturing technology from Iran, have been deployed on the battlefield. According to the Government of Ukraine, Russia is mass-producing Geran drones, an upgraded version of Shahed drones that use components from China. Russia has also been supplied with artillery shells and ballistic missiles by North Korea, and there are reports that over half the artillery shells used by Russia originate from North Korea. This foreign support is what has enabled Russia to continue its intense aggression. Meanwhile, it is believed that military aid to Russia does not only benefit the recipient, but also the provider. For example, in cases where Russia uses military technology or different types of weapons on the battlefield, there is a possibility that data on the experience or effectiveness thereof will also be shared with the technology provider.

The Review of Australia’s Defence Capabilities conducted in 1986 assessed itself as “one of the most secure countries in the world” and indicated that it would receive at least 10-years’ warning before any major attack on Australia. This outlook defined Australia’s defense policy even after the Cold War. However, Australia recognized that its strategic environment has been deteriorating more rapidly than anticipated since 2020 due to military modernization in the Indo-Pacific region and intensifying competition between major powers, including the United States and China. Given the situation, Australia released the 2020 Defence Strategic Update to reconsider its defense strategy, stating that Australia’s defense plan based on the aforementioned 10-year warning time was no longer appropriate. The Albanese’s Labor Party Government, which was established in May 2022 and began its second term in May 2025, has been developing the National Defence Strategy (NDS) and the Integrated Investment Program (IIP) biennially since April 2024. The NDS2026, released in April 2026, states that the international system is trending away from rules toward the exercise of power, and that Australia’s exposure to force projection and military coercion will reach levels not seen since World War II. In addition, while building on the Strategy of Denial1 adopted by the previous NDS, the updated NDS aims to (1) develop greater self-reliance; (2) prioritize capability acquisition and sustainment plans drawing on lessons learned from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East; (3) strengthen Australia’s sovereign defense industrial base and build stronger, more diverse international industrial partnerships;

(4) improve national civil preparedness and national resilience to help shield Australia from regional or global disruption; and (5) increase coordination with regional partners to shape a region governed by rights and rules. The IIP outlines the priority capability area for investment areas and other specific measures necessary to achieve the capabilities set out in the NDS. It states that investments will be made in areas such as maritime capabilities, long-range strike capabilities, the accelerated introduction of integrated air and missile defense, and the expanded adoption of autonomous and uncrewed systems across the land, maritime, and air domains. In addition, Australia has been conducting monitoring and surveillance activities against illicit maritime activities, including ship-to-ship transfers with North Korean-flagged vessels in waters around Japan since 2018. From late February to mid-March 2026, Royal Australian Navy frigate HMAS Toowoomba conducted monitoring and surveillance activities. (2) AUKUS Initiatives In September 2021, then Prime Minister Scott Morrison, along with the leaders of the United States and the United Kingdom, announced the establishment of a new trilateral security cooperation framework, AUKUS, aimed at deepening diplomatic, security and defense cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region. Under the announced joint statement, Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States will promote the following concrete initiatives: (1) support for Australia to acquire at least eight nuclear-powered submarines2 and (2) technical cooperation for advanced capabilities (cyber, artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technology, and undersea capabilities). In April 2022, Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States announced in relation to aforementioned (2) that they would deepen their cooperation regarding hypersonics and counter-hypersonic capabilities, electronic warfare, defense innovation and information sharing.

(2) Relations with China China is Australia’s largest trading partner, and the two countries have conducted various exchanges in the defense area such as dialogues between the defense authorities, bilateral exercises, and mutual visits of vessels, in addition to exchanges and cooperation in the political areas. Meanwhile, Australia has been clearly showing its wariness toward China by explicitly conveying its position on China given the military use of the South China Sea and its expansion to Pacific island countries. The Australian government has been expressing strong concerns over China’s reclamation and construction activities in the South China Sea and opposing any unilateral attempt to change the status quo through militarization or coercive actions on disputed features. It has also expressed its intent to continue exercising its rights to freedom of navigation and overflight. In 2020, Australia, which was under the former Morrison government at the time, suggested the necessity of an independent investigation into the origin of the COVID-19 outbreak in China. China successively imposed trade blockages on Australian beef and other products, leading to a rapid deterioration of Australia-China relations. Subsequently with the change of government in Australia, the two countries resumed diplomatic and security dialogue and removed all trade blockages in December 2024.

2 New Zealand New Zealand is located in the Indo-Pacific Region and is an important strategic cooperative partner that shares fundamental values with Japan. In July 2022, the Ministry of Defence announced that the government would conduct a Defence Policy Review to formulate the country’s long-term defense strategy based on issues such as the growing impacts of climate change and intensifying strategic and geopolitical competition, including Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. In August 2023, the New Zealand government announced the country’s first-ever five-year security policy guidelines, New Zealand’s National Security Strategy 2023-2028 (NSS), analyzing the security challenges it faces. The country also announced the Defence Policy and Strategy Statement (DPSS), which specifies the country’s objectives and defense strategy under its defense policy as the first phase of the Defence Policy Review, as well as the Future Force Design Principles (FFDP), which guides the New Zealand Defence Force’s (NZDF) investment plans for the next 15 years. In the DPSS, it was noted that the heightened competition and tensions in the disputed areas of the Indo-Pacific region pose potentially significant impact for New Zealand’s interests and that the impact of climate change will exacerbate existing fragilities within Pacific Island countries and across the region which in turn could increase economic and governance risks. On China, New Zealand observed that the country is using all its instruments of national power in ways that can pose challenges to existing international rules and norms. Also, it is assessed that China continues to invest heavily in growing and modernizing its military, and is increasingly able to project its military and paramilitary force beyond its immediate region, including across the wider Indo-Pacific.

3 Pacific Island Countries The Pacific Island countries, a collective term for island nations and regions located in the Pacific Ocean, are important to Japan for their abundant marine resources as they possess vast exclusive economic zones and serve as transport routes for energy resources. Pacific Island countries face challenges regarding their small size and land distribution, distance from major international market, and the vulnerabilities to natural disasters and climate change. In addition, the number of Pacific Island countries with their own military forces is limited to just three: Fiji, Papua New Guinea, and Tonga. Given these circumstances, these countries consider climate change to be the single greatest threat to their security and sees the loss of national territory due to rising sea levels and the increasing scale of natural disasters as the matter of serious concern. Traditionally, these countries have deep relationships with Australia, France, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. However, China’s increasingly active approach in recent years has made geopolitical competition between major powers become even more prominent. For example, in April 2022, China concluded an agreement on security cooperation with the Solomon Islands that reportedly includes provision that allows deployment of Chinese police and military to the island, also allowing the port call and replenishment of Chinese vessels. Meanwhile, in May 2023, the United States and Papua New Guinea signed a Defense Cooperation Agreement that enables the U.S. military to access ports and airports in the Papua New Guinea. Furthermore, amid China’s effort to expand its influence through large-scale infrastructure development and deployment of hospital ships, the United States is striving to maintain and enhance its military presence in the region. Australia has also been actively expanding its regional presence, notably through substantial increase in its budget for supporting Pacific Island

In addition, the number of Pacific Island countries with their own military forces is limited to just three: Fiji, Papua New Guinea, and Tonga. Given these circumstances, these countries consider climate change to be the single greatest threat to their security and sees the loss of national territory due to rising sea levels and the increasing scale of natural disasters as the matter of serious concern. Traditionally, these countries have deep relationships with Australia, France, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. However, China’s increasingly active approach in recent years has made geopolitical competition between major powers become even more prominent. For example, in April 2022, China concluded an agreement on security cooperation with the Solomon Islands that reportedly includes provision that allows deployment of Chinese police and military to the island, also allowing the port call and replenishment of Chinese vessels. Meanwhile, in May 2023, the United States and Papua New Guinea signed a Defense Cooperation Agreement that enables the U.S. military to access ports and airports in the Papua New Guinea. Furthermore, amid China’s effort to expand its influence through large-scale infrastructure development and deployment of hospital ships, the United States is striving to maintain and enhance its military presence in the region. Australia has also been actively expanding its regional presence, notably through substantial increase in its budget for supporting Pacific Island

countries. In 2023, it concluded the security agreement with Papua New Guinea and the Falepili Union Treaty with Tuvalu and signed the Nauru-Australia Treaty in 2024. In October 2025, Australia and Papua New Guinea signed the Pukpuk Treaty, which serves as a mutual defense treaty, and agreed to upgrade their relationship to that of an alliance. Furthermore, in December 2025, the three countries of Australia, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea held their inaugural Trilateral Defence Minister’s Meeting, and agreed to hold it annually from 2026 onward. The growing competition for engagement in the region, primarily among the United States, China, and Australia, has drawn great attention. 1 General Situation Southeast Asia is the center of the Indo-Pacific region, located at the intersection of the Pacific Ocean and the Indian Ocean and occupies a strategic position for traffic, linking the Pacific and the Indian Oceans, such as the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea. Therefore, it is an important region for Japan, which relies on maritime transport for many of the supplies needed for economic activities and the lives of the Japanese people. Meanwhile, this region still has destabilizing factors, including the territorial disputes in the South China Sea, ethnic minority issues, disputes over land borders, and separatist and independence movements. Moreover, there have also been problems with Islamic extremist groups and piracy incidents obstructing the safe passage of ships. In order to cope with these issues, the countries in Southeast Asia are working to build military forces for national defense and the maintenance of domestic public security, as well as for addressing new security issues that include counterterrorism and counter-piracy. Each country is also pursuing cooperation respectively with countries such as the United States, China, Russia, and Australia to this end. In recent years, against the backdrop of factors such as economic growth, they have increased their defense expenditure and advanced the modernization of their militaries and strengthening of their maritime law enforcement capabilities.

2 Cambodia In 2022, Cambodia released its first defense white paper in 16 years since 2006, identifying the following key challenges in its national defense policy: modernizing equipment, developing military infrastructure, enhancing cyber security capabilities, etc. With regards to Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base, located in southwestern Cambodia, the possibility of China’s exclusive use of a portion of the base has been pointed out. In June 2021, Cambodia’s Minister of National Defence acknowledged that China had contributed to the development of the base. However, he stated that access to the base facilities was not limited to China alone. Amid these circumstances, in December 2023, two Chinese naval vessels reportedly entered the Ream Naval Base to conduct “training” for the Royal Cambodian Navy and participated in the bilateral exercise “Golden Dragon 2024” in May 2024. Although the vessels are replaced sometimes, Chinese naval vessels are believed to be permanently anchored there. In April 2025, an inauguration ceremony was held to commemorate the completion of upgrade work at the naval base and the establishment of the “Cambodia-China Joint Logistics and Training Center” followed by the bilateral exercise Golden Dragon 2025 in May. The Cambodian Prime Minister has stated that the establishment of foreign military bases in Cambodia is against its Constitution and it welcomes all friendly countries. Naval vessels from Japan and Viet Nam have made port calls at the naval base following the upgrade. In January 2026, a U.S. Navy littoral combat ship (LCS) has also made a port call. In April 2026, one Chinese naval vessel was provided to Cambodia, and it has been suggested that another vessel may be provided in the future. Further movements pertaining to the Ream Naval Base continues to draw attention.

From May 2025, military clashes have occurred in the vicinity of the un-demarcated border between Cambodia and Thailand, escalating tensions between the two countries. In July of the same year, with the mediation of Malaysia (then the Chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)), the United States, and other countries, the two countries agreed on an immediate ceasefire and a mechanism for implementing the ceasefire. Moreover, in October, the two countries signed a Joint Declaration on the border conflict. However, subsequently, clashes continued to occur, resulting in numerous casualties, refugees, and damage to civilian facilities in both countries. In December, it was announced that an immediate ceasefire had been agreed once again. Tensions remain high near the border, so attention will be focused on developments going forward.

3 Indonesia As part of its military modernization plan, Indonesia aims to achieve the Optimum Essential Force (OEF), accordingly announcing an increase in defense expenditure as well as a policy to bolster its deployment of assets to the Natuna Islands, the South China Sea, and other locations. It has been reported that Indonesia has deployed an integrated unit, air squadron, etc. to the Natuna Islands and that the transfer of its naval combat command headquarters to Natuna is almost completed and is now capable of operating fighter jets, surface vessels, and submarines in the area. In addition, Indonesia pursues non-aligned and omnidirectional diplomacy, and it conducted exercises with Russia, Australia, and China after the inauguration of the Prabowo administration in October 2024. With the United States, Indonesia is strengthening its cooperative relationship in such fields as military education and training and military equipment procurement. In addition, Indonesia has carried out bilateral training including army exercise Garuda Shield, naval exercise Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training (CARAT)1 and counter terrorism exercise Southeast Asia Cooperation Against Terrorism (SEACAT)2 with the United States. Since 2022, the Super Garuda Shield, a multilateral exercise expanding both the military services and participating countries of the original Garuda Shield, has been conducted. Although Indonesia does not recognize the “nine-dash line” claimed by China, it has enhanced its patrol activities in the area keeping in mind the fact that the “nine-dash line” overlaps with part of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) claimed by Indonesia in the vicinity of the Natuna Islands.

4 Laos Under the defense policy released in 2013, Laos adopted self-defense as the core of its approach and stated its intention to strengthen the integration of national defense with politics, diplomacy, and economics, while promoting peace, friendship, and collaboration at both the global and regional levels. Furthermore, its basic policy is good neighborly and omnidirectional diplomacy based on the five principles of peace: mutual respect for territory and sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence, and it maintains good relationships with ASEAN member states, China, Russia, and others. In September 2025, President Thongloun Sisoulith participated in the military parade for the Commemoration of “the 80th anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War,” and in October of the same year, he visited North Korea on the occasion of the 80th anniversary of the founding of the Korean Workers’ Party, and met with Chairman Kim. Although there was a military confrontation between Laos and Cambodia over an un-demarcated border area in 2019, there have been no other military conflicts between Laos and neighboring countries ever since.

7 The Philippines In the National Security Policy 2023-2028 (NSP) released in August 2023, it identifies that the South China Sea issue remains a primary national interest of the Philippines, all the while strengthening cooperation with allies and partner countries and developing a comprehensive national security policy encompassing a wide range of areas including the economy, energy, and climate change. The Philippines, with a historically close relationship with the United States, has maintained a cooperative relationship with the United States under the Mutual Defense Treaty and Military Assistance Agreement, even after the withdrawal of the U.S. Forces in 1992. In February 1998, the two countries signed a Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA), which prescribed the legal status of U.S. military personnel when the U.S. Forces conducts combined military exercises or other related activities in the Philippines. Furthermore, in April 2014, the two countries signed the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), which allows enhanced cooperation in disaster relief, rotational deployment of the U.S. Forces, construction and improvement of agreed locations in the Philippines by the United States, and U.S. Forces’ prepositioning of equipment and others. In March 2016, under EDCA, the two countries agreed on designating five bases of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) as sites for the rotational deployment of the U.S. Forces. Since President Marcos took office in June 2022, the Philippines has further strengthened its cooperation with the United States. In February 2023, the U.S. and the Philippine defense ministers jointly announced the designation of four new bases for the EDCA. These four bases consist of three in northern Luzon Island near Taiwan and one on Palawan Island facing the South China Sea. Furthermore, in May 2023, the U.S.-Philippines Bilateral Defense Guidelines were adopted and released for the first time, which serve as a roadmap of modernization of alliance cooperation and deepening interoperability between the United States and the Philippines.

Moreover, in September 2023, a U.S.-Philippines joint navigation in the South China Sea was held under the Marcos administration, followed by the Maritime Cooperation Activity (MCA) in seas and air space surrounding the Philippines, including the South China Sea in November of the same year. Furthermore, the U.S. Army’s ground-launched, mid-range missile system, Typhon, has been deployed in the Philippines since April 2024. Also, in addition to the aforementioned Typhon, during the multilateral joint exercise Balikatan 25, conducted from early April to early May 2025, hosted by the United States and the Philippines, the U.S. Marine Corps’ Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and the Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) were deployed in the Philippines. Moreover, in the Balikatan 26 conducted from late April to early May 2026, the U.S. Marine Corps deployed the NMESIS and the MADIS, following on from the previous year, and the U.S. Army launched a Tomahawk cruise missile from the Typhon. Furthermore, at the U.S.-Philippines defense ministers’ meeting held in October 2025, the establishment of the joint U.S.-Philippines “Task Force-Philippines,” a task force which will increase operational cooperation and enhance interoperability particularly in the South China Sea, was announced. In July 2016, the final award was rendered, accepting nearly all of the Philippines’ submissions. The government of the Philippines released a statement that it welcomed the Philippines-China arbitration award and strongly affirmed its respect for the decision, while China stated that it would not comply with this decision.

the Philippine warship Sierra Madre was stranded. According to the Philippine government, the Philippine supply ship was attempting to replenish the supplies of the stranded warship and the action by the China Coast Guard resulted in injuries to the Philippine personnel onboard and damage to the Philippine vessel. In response, President Marcos condemned the action by the China Coast Guard and the maritime militia against the vessels and personnel, pointing out that it was provocative and a clear violation of international law. The United States has reiterated that the U.S.-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty extends to both countries’ armed forces, public vessels, and aircraft of either country—including those of its coast guard—anywhere in the Pacific to include the South China Sea. In July 2024, the Philippine and Chinese governments announced that they had reached a “provisional agreement” concerning rotation and resupply missions to Sierra Madre. Nevertheless, the tension between the two countries in the South China Sea remains persistent, and several incidents occurred in 2025 as well that mainly resulted in injuries to the Philippine personnel onboard and damage to the Philippine vessel. In November 2024, the Philippines announced it had signed a domestic law aimed at defining its territorial waters and EEZ in accordance with international law. China condemned this as a serious infringement on its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights. In the same month, China established baselines for its territorial sea adjacent to Scarborough Shoal and published “standard names” for the features of the South China Sea. Moreover, in September 2025, China announced that it had designated a part of the Scarborough Shoal a “national nature reserve” and in response to this the Philippines and the United States issued statements calling for China to abide by the July 2016 Philippines-China arbitration award. 8 Singapore Singapore highly prioritizes its national defense, with defense spending accounting for about 3% of its GDP. In October 2022, the Digital and Intelligence Service was established as the fourth service of the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), integrating existing command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, and cyber capabilities. In addition, Singapore emphasizes the importance of cooperative relationships with ASEAN and the FPDA, and has concluded defense cooperation agreements with countries within and outside the region. With the aim of contributing to peace and stability in the region, Singapore supports the United States’ presence in the Asia-Pacific. Since signing the 1990 Memorandum of Understanding (November 1990), Singapore has been allowing the United States to use military facilities in the country. In addition to port calls to Changi Naval Base by U.S. aircraft carriers, the rotational deployment of littoral combat ships (LCSs) began in 2013. Since 2015, the U.S. P-8 patrol aircraft are regularly deployed. In addition, Singapore conducts combined exercises with the United States, such as CARAT and SEACAT. Singapore has strong economic ties with China. Both countries also conduct joint naval exercises. In October 2019, the two countries signed the revised Agreement on Defence Exchanges and Security Cooperation (ADESC), which formalized existing defense cooperation, including regularization of dialogue and exercises. Meanwhile, Singapore’s position differs from China’s in some areas such as the South China Sea, where Singapore has taken note of a resolution based on the Philippines-China arbitration award and it also reportedly has military relations with Taiwan. In March 2020, Singapore and Australia signed the “Treaty on Military Training and Training Area Development” in Australia. As part of this treaty, the expansion and development of the Shoalwater Bay Military Training Area were completed in November 2024. Moreover, in October 2025, they signed an MOU on Enhanced Defence Cooperation, including enhanced access to each other’s training facilities and enhanced cooperation in the cyber domain.

Meanwhile, Singapore’s position differs from China’s in some areas such as the South China Sea, where Singapore has taken note of a resolution based on the Philippines-China arbitration award and it also reportedly has military relations with Taiwan. In March 2020, Singapore and Australia signed the “Treaty on Military Training and Training Area Development” in Australia. As part of this treaty, the expansion and development of the Shoalwater Bay Military Training Area were completed in November 2024. Moreover, in October 2025, they signed an MOU on Enhanced Defence Cooperation, including enhanced access to each other’s training facilities and enhanced cooperation in the cyber domain.

9 Thailand Thailand’s defense policy includes: strengthening defense cooperation through ASEAN, international organizations, and other entities; defense that makes comprehensive use of political, economic, and other national strengths; and effective defense aimed at increasing the readiness of the Royal Thai Armed Forces (RTAF) and developing the defense industry. In the defense white paper released in 2023, Thailand identified cyber and space operations as capabilities that needed to be enhanced for the future national defense. In

October 2024, it reportedly established a dedicated cyber-command unit, reorganized existing cyber units within the Army, Navy, and Air Force, and created an institution for training cyber workforce. In addition, in terms of the space domain, Thailand plans to change the name of the Royal Thai Air Force to the “Royal Thai Air and Space Force.” Under its flexible omnidirectional diplomatic policy, Thailand pursues cooperation with other Southeast Asian countries and coordination with major countries. In particular, Thailand has an alliance with the United States based on the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty (Manila Treaty) (effective from February 1955), and the U.S. military has access to the Thai military’s U-Tapao Royal Thai Navy Airfield. Thailand has been conducting the U.S.- Thailand combined exercise “Cobra Gold” since 1982, which is currently one of the largest multilateral joint exercises in Southeast Asia. In addition, Thailand and the United States have continued to participate in joint exercises such as CARAT, involving the U.S. and Thai navies and others, and the counter-piracy and trafficking exercise SEACAT. Thailand and China have conducted joint training such as Blue Strike between their navies and Falcon Strike between their air forces. From May 2025, military clashes have occurred in the vicinity of the un-demarcated border between Cambodia and Thailand, escalating tensions between the two countries. In July of the same year, with the mediation of Malaysia (then the ASEAN Chair), the United States, and other countries, the two countries agreed on an immediate ceasefire and a mechanism for implementing the ceasefire. Moreover, in October, they signed a Joint Declaration on the border conflict. However, subsequently, clashes continued to occur, resulting in numerous casualties, refugees, and damage to civilian facilities in the both countries. In December, it was announced that an immediate ceasefire had been agreed once again. However, tensions remain high near the border, and efforts toward the development continues to draw attention.

11 Viet Nam Based on its viewpoint that the sea is closely associated with the national construction and defense, Viet Nam has established the objective of becoming a strong marine country, particularly prioritizing the modernization of its military forces and law enforcement forces at sea as well as ensuring the capability for maritime domain awareness, maritime independence, sovereign rights, jurisdiction and national interests at sea. Furthermore, Viet Nam deploys its omnidirectional diplomatic policy and intends to actively participate in international and regional cooperation in order to build friendly relations with every nation. The National Assembly held in April 2026 gave approval for the General Secretary of the Communist Party To Lam, to concurrently serve as President. Viet Nam and the United States have strengthened their military relations in recent years. This has taken such forms as joint training with the U.S. Navy and port calls by U.S. Navy vessels in Viet Nam. In 2023, during then U.S. President Biden’s first visit to Viet Nam as president, he met with then President Thưởng and agreed to upgrade the bilateral relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. Viet Nam and Russia have been strengthening cooperation in the area of national defense and actively engaging in high-level government exchanges. In May 2025, General Secretary of the Communist Party To Lam participated in Russia’s military parade to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the war victory over Germany. The Viet Nam military also participated in the parade, albeit on a small scale. Moreover, in a summit meeting held after the parade, the two countries declared their determination to advance their comprehensive strategic partnership to a new level. Section 5-5-6 (1) (Relations with Asian Countries) Viet Nam has been actively engaging in high-level government exchanges with China under their comprehensive strategic cooperation partnership. In April 2025, President Xi visited Viet Nam and met with General Secretary of the Communist Party To Lam. In addition, then See Timor-Leste officially joins ASEAN [ASEAN]

(ADMM). In September 2023, ASEAN held its first maritime exercise on its own in the waters surrounding Indonesia, including the North Natuna Sea. In addition, ASEAN attaches importance to expanding its relations with countries outside of the region. It holds the ADMM-Plus, a platform that adds eight non-ASEAN countries including Japan to ADMM. Moreover, ASEAN is conducting joint maritime exercises with major powers such as the United States, China, Russia, and India, and in December 2025, it conducted the ASEAN-U.S. Maritime Exercise for the second time since 2019. In addition, ASEAN and China have continued talks to discuss the formulation of the Code of Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (COC). In July 2019, China announced at the ASEAN-China Ministerial Meeting that they had completed the first reading of COC’s Single Draft Negotiating Text. Subsequently, a second reading was initiated. At the August 2021 ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, it was noted that a provisional agreement on the Preamble had been reached. Moreover, at the ASEAN-China Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in July 2023, the Guidelines for Accelerating the Early Conclusion of an Effective and Substantive COC were adopted. The third reading of the guidelines began in October of the same year, and the completion of the third reading was declared in the Press Statement by the Chair of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Retreat in January 2025. President Marcos of the Philippines, who is serving as the ASEAN Chair in 2026, has shown a willingness to conclude the COC in an accelerated manner. Furthermore, regarding the situation between Cambodia and Thailand, where tensions have escalated since 2025, ASEAN has been making efforts to de-escalate tensions, including by holding the special foreign ministers’ meetings.

1 General Situation India is the world’s largest democratic country. It has achieved rapid economic growth in recent years and has significant influence in the South Asian region. Also, it is located in the middle of the Indian Ocean, which is of strategic and geopolitical importance. India has also increased its presence as a geopolitical player, while the international community in return has high expectations for the country’s role. India has traditionally aimed at nonaligned and omnidirectional diplomacy while emphasizing the preserving of strategic autonomy. The Modi administration has maintained a neighborhood first policy, which emphasizes strengthening relations with South Asian countries, while expanding the focus of strengthening India’s external relations to the Indo-Pacific region in accordance with the “Act East” policy. In addition, the administration has carried out proactive foreign policy, prioritizing India’s relations with the United States, Russia, and Europe as well as the Middle East and Africa. On the other hand, India has non-demarcated border issues with China and Pakistan. There are also concerns about the activities of ultra-leftists and secession and independence movements, as well as activities of Islamic extremists. Accordingly, defending its land borders and tackling the threat of domestic terrorism are major concerns for India. In addition, in recent years, India has considered efforts for maritime security as an important focus point, strengthened its presence in the Indian Ocean, and clearly recognized China’s increased activity in the Indian Ocean.

It is considering the establishment of unified combatant commands with the aim of strengthening operational and organizational cooperation among military services. Under the “Make in India” and “Self-Reliant India” initiatives, the Modi government is actively working toward the domestic production and modernization of military equipment and taking measures to promote exports. 1 General Situation Wedged between the powerful South Asian nation of India and politically unstable Afghanistan, and sharing borders with China and Iran, Pakistan is placed in a geopolitically significant and complex position. Particularly in the border area with Afghanistan, extremist organizations are engaging in cross-border terrorist activities, and Pakistan’s actions in the fight against terrorism could significantly impact the stability of Afghanistan.5 Since October 2025, sporadic exchanges of attacks have occurred near the border between Pakistan and Afghanistan.

2 Military Pakistan takes the position that maintaining nuclear deterrence against attacks with nuclear and conventional weapons by India is essential to ensure national security and self-defense. It has been pointed out that Pakistan retains around 170 nuclear warheads as of January 2025. The development of ballistic missiles and cruise missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads is still continuing. Tactical nuclear missile “Nasr” and IRBM “Shaheen-II” are already operative. In addition, the flight test of ground-to-ground missile “Shaheen-III” with the range of 2,750 km was successfully conducted in April 2022. Pakistan has been enhancing its military capabilities, as evidenced by the October 2023 launch test of the purportedly MIRV-capable ballistic missile “Ababeel.” In recent years, Pakistan has also been promoting the modernization of equipment, and while it makes attempts at domestic production through joint development of equipment and technology transfer, it promotes its relationship with China in military fields, and rising dependence on China is observed. The Pakistan Army operates “Al-Khalid” tanks, which were jointly developed with China, as its main battle tanks. Pakistan is enhancing the Comprehensive Layered Integrated Air Defense (CLIAD) system by purchasing air defense systems such as “LY-80” and “HQ-9/P” from China, and Pakistan is also advancing the introduction of drones by procuring them from China and Türkiye and advancing the development of domestically produced drones. The Pakistan Navy is replacing or augmenting its aging warships, introducing submarines, and cooperating with China and Türkiye while also conducting bilateral exercises with both countries. The Pakistan Air Force operates JF-17 fighter jets, which were jointly developed with China and produced domestically, Chinese-made J-10CE fighter jets, and other aircraft. In November 2025, the constitution was amended, reorganizing the military by creating a new rank, Chief of Defence Forces, with unified command authority over the Army, Navy, and Air Force, and making the rank of Field Marshal a lifetime rank with immunity from prosecution. In December of the same year, Field Marshal Asim Munir, the Chief of Army Staff, was appointed Chief of Defence Forces.
