(2) Relations with China Pakistan and China maintain a close relationship under their “all-weather strategic partnership,” and mutual visits by their summit leaders take place frequently. Their cooperation in the military sector, including bilateral training, exporting weapons, and transferring military technology, is also deepening. As the importance of sea lines of communication increases for China, it is believed that the importance of Pakistan is rising for China accordingly, partly because, geopolitically, Pakistan faces the Indian Ocean. At the same time, there have been more and more terrorist attacks aimed at Chinese people in Pakistan in recent years, which is a serious issue. In response, Pakistan and China conducted their bilateral counterterrorism exercise “Warrior” in Pakistan from November to December 2024—the first such exercise in five years since 2019—and they conducted the same exercise from November to December 2025. In terms of military equipment, the introduction of the Chinese-made attack helicopter Z-10ME was announced in August of the same year, and the launch of the fourth Hangor-class submarine, manufactured in China, was announced in December of the same year.

2024. It has expanded the scope of its activities to conflict prevention and crisis management outside its area since the end of the Cold War. NATO’s three core tasks are deterrence and defense, crisis prevention and management, and cooperative security. Amid an increasing sense of crisis among member states in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, a new NATO Strategic Concept was adopted at the NATO Summit in June 2022 for the first time in 12 years since 2010. This new Strategic Concept states that the Euro-Atlantic area is not at peace and that the possibility of an attack against member states’ sovereignty and territorial integrity cannot be discounted. In addition, NATO placed Russia as the most significant and direct threat to member states’ security and to peace and stability in the Euro-Atlantic area. This new Strategic Concept mentioned China for the first time, stating that China’s ambition and coercive policies challenge NATO’s interests, security and values. The Washington Summit Declaration, issued at the NATO Summit in July 2024, newly referenced emerging cooperation between Russia and North Korea as well as between Russia and China. Regarding military cooperation between Russia and North Korea, the declaration stated that it is having a serious impact on Euro-Atlantic security and expressed grave concern. Regarding China, the declaration noted that the country is a decisive supporter of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. In addition, recognizing that the situation in the Indo-Pacific region could directly impact Euro-Atlantic security, NATO decided to advance cooperation with the Indo Pacific 4 (IP4) and its partners in the Indo-Pacific region (Australia, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea (ROK), and Japan), in flagship projects including support for Ukraine, cyber defense, measures against disinformation, and technology.

Through these actions, NATO has emphasized one of its core missions of defending member states while strengthening deterrence and defense capabilities based on the understanding that the security environment has drastically changed. For example, since 2014, NATO has overhauled its plans and structures to ensure member states can respond to any threat from any direction, with an agreement to establish a forward presence, particularly in the east. Following the initial deployment of multinational battalion-sized battlegroups in the three Baltic states and Poland in 2017, NATO decided to deploy battlegroups in Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania, and Slovakia in 2022 and in Finland in 2025. Note that at the NATO Summit in June 2022, it was agreed that these battlegroups would be expanded from battalion to brigade size as needed.1 Most recently, in September 2025, Poland announced that it had shot down Russian drones that had violated its airspace. Since then, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) of unknown nationality have continued to enter the airspace of various European countries. In response, NATO launched Eastern Sentry, an enhanced monitoring activity with the objective of strengthening its defense posture on its eastern flank from the Baltic states and Poland to the Black Sea. Regarding NATO member states’ defense spending, at the NATO Summit held in The Hague in June 2025, it was agreed that the member states would raise their target for defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035. Under this commitment, at least 3.5% of GDP is to be devoted to core defense expenditure, while up to 1.5% is allocated to broader defense- and security-related expenditure. Core defense expenditure is defined by NATO as payments made by an Allied national government specifically to meet the needs of (1) its own armed forces, (2) those of other Allies or (3) the needs of the Alliance as a whole. Moreover, it was stated that direct contributions to Ukraine’s defense and its defense industry could be included in NATO-standard defense spending. 3 Relations with China China’s recent rise has attracted attention from NATO as well. The 2022 NATO Strategic Concept states that “The People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) stated ambitions and coercive policies challenge our interests, security and values,” and mentioned China’s rapid enhancement of nuclear forces, absence of transparency, and malicious hybrid and cyber activities. On this basis, it mentioned that NATO will engage constructively with China for the alliance’s security interests, and protect against China’s coercive efforts to divide NATO. In June 2025, in a press conference before the NATO Summit held in The Hague, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that the massive build-up of the military capabilities of Russia and China was a direct threat to the territories of the NATO member states. Furthermore, he brought up China, along with North Korea and Iran, as countries supporting Russia and have plunged Ukraine into a conflict which affects the whole world. Moreover, since 2025, he has made multiple statements to the effect that China would seek Russia’s cooperation in future regional conflicts, and in addition he has continuously made statements about the impact and dangers of China-Russia cooperation. China’s relations with European countries, including NATO’s policy on engagement with China, should be continuously watched.

security ties with partners including Japan. In June 2025, the Keir Starmer administration announced the 2025 Strategic Defence Review (SDR 2025). With the recognition that Europe faces more serious and less predictable threats than any time since the Cold War, the review presents a policy which prioritizes strengthening the defense capabilities of Europe and continues to position Russia as “an immediate and pressing threat.” Furthermore, the review evaluates China to be “a sophisticated and persistent challenge,” and points out that China’s military exercises around Taiwan risk dangerous escalation in the Taiwan Strait, and that its aggressive actions are fueling tension in the South China Sea. Note that the review asserts that the Indo-Pacific is a strategically important region for the United Kingdom, and mentions cooperation with the IP4, NATO’s partner countries in the region. The United Kingdom is continuing its engagement with the Indo-Pacific region. According to an announcement from the U.K. Ministry of Defence, in July 2024, the United Kingdom participated in the Royal Australian Air Force’s Exercise Pitch Black 24. In 2025, the carrier strike group (CSG), with the aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales as its flagship, conducted deployment activities in the Indo-Pacific region for over approximately eight months. This CSG called at the ports of countries in the region, including Japan, and carried out joint exercises with the countries, including participation in the multilateral joint exercise Talisman Sabre 25 hosted by the United States and Australia. In addition, the United Kingdom has conducted monitoring and surveillance activities in waters around Japan in response to illicit maritime activities including ship-to-ship transfers with North Korean-flagged vessels since FY2018. In June 2025, HMS Spey, and in September, HMS Richmond conducted monitoring and surveillance activities.

The United Kingdom is continuing its engagement with the Indo-Pacific region. According to an announcement from the U.K. Ministry of Defence, in July 2024, the United Kingdom participated in the Royal Australian Air Force’s Exercise Pitch Black 24. In 2025, the carrier strike group (CSG), with the aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales as its flagship, conducted deployment activities in the Indo-Pacific region for over approximately eight months. This CSG called at the ports of countries in the region, including Japan, and carried out joint exercises with the countries, including participation in the multilateral joint exercise Talisman Sabre 25 hosted by the United States and Australia. In addition, the United Kingdom has conducted monitoring and surveillance activities in waters around Japan in response to illicit maritime activities including ship-to-ship transfers with North Korean-flagged vessels since FY2018. In June 2025, HMS Spey, and in September, HMS Richmond conducted monitoring and surveillance activities.

2 France Since the end of the Cold War, France has focused on maintaining independence of its defense policies, while having led initiatives to enhance the defense structure and capability in Europe. It has worked on the development of its military capacity by streamlining and integrating military bases, dealing with operational requirements to strengthen its defense capability, as well as enhancing its intelligence capabilities and modernizing equipment required in the future. In July 2025, the updated National Strategic Review 2025 was announced as a consequence of further deterioration in the global security environment. It stated that there is a high risk of a high-intensity conflict occurring in Europe by 2030, and presented the policies of acceleration of rearmament and strengthened cooperation with allies. It positioned Russia as the most direct threat to France and the countries of Europe, and pointed out that it is engaging in nuclear intimidation, cyberattacks, and attempts to interfere in electoral processes, and is strengthening its partnerships with China and North Korea. It states that China’s confrontation with the United States is unavoidable and China has the goal of becoming the world’s leading power, surpassing the United States, by 2050, and pointed out that China is strengthening its military exercises around Taiwan on an unprecedented scale and expanding its influence in Europe and Africa as well.

4 Canada In a National Defence Policy paper published in April 2024, the Department of National Defence of Canada indicated that the world is currently in a period of global uncertainty due to the three connected trends: climate change, the rise of autocracies and destructive states such as Russia and China, and the spread of new and disruptive technologies. Based on this recognition of the security environment, Canada has positioned the securing of its sovereignty in the Arctic and North American region as the core of its defense policy. To ensure a ready, resilient and relevant Canadian Armed Forces, Canada has decided to update its human resource base and equipment, procurement reform, renewing national defense infrastructure, promote digitalization, and building stronger defense industrial base. Furthermore, the Mark Carney administration inaugurated in March 2025 announced a plan to increase and accelerate defense investment in June of the same year, and planned to increase investment in the field of defense by approximately CAD 9 billion and achieve defense expenditure of 2% of GDP during FY2025. In addition to this, Canada announced its Arctic Foreign Policy in December 2024. This policy takes into account changes in the security environment surrounding the Arctic Circle, such as increased access to Arctic resources and shipping routes due to climate change, Russia’s strengthening military presence, and growing interest from China and other countries. Specific measures include appointment of an Arctic ambassador and establishing new consulates in Alaska and Greenland. Furthermore, Canada has been conducting the military exercise Operation Nanook in the Arctic region since 2007, and in addition it has been advancing industrial and other cooperation with the United States and Finland with the objective of strengthening icebreaker ship design and construction capabilities. Canada regards the United States as its most important ally and conducts air defense, space defense, and maritime monitoring and surveillance activities in North America jointly with the United States through the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD). Concerning its involvement in the Indo-Pacific region, in November 2022, Canada announced its first Indo-Pacific Strategy as a comprehensive road map to deepen its engagement in the region over the next decade. In the strategy, China is mentioned as an “increasingly disruptive global power” and that it is looking to shape the international order into a more permissive environment for China’s interests and values. The strategy also states that Canada will challenge China if it engages in behavior that undermines Canada’s national interests or those of its partners in the region. On the other hand, Canada has expressed a willingness to cooperate with China on the solutions for climate change and other global problems, and Prime Minister Carney visited China in January 2026 and announced a “new strategic partnership” with China. In addition, in the aforementioned Indo-Pacific Strategy, Canada has clarified its strategic objectives, such as promoting the peace, resiliency, and security of the region as well as expanding and deepening security relationships with allies and partners that include Japan. Canada has also stated its intention to continue monitoring and surveillance activities5 in response to illicit maritime activities, including ship-to-ship transfers with North Korean-flagged vessels, which started in April 2018. Canada conducted monitoring and surveillance activities using its Royal Canadian Air Force CP-140 patrol aircraft from late March to early April 2026. Moreover, in the strategy, it is stated that Canada will strengthen the presence of the Royal Canadian Navy in the Indo-Pacific region, for example by increasing the number of frigates deployed there. Note that since 2018, Royal Canadian Navy vessels have transited through the Taiwan Strait6 in accordance with international law.

4 Situation in Syria In November 2024, anti-government forces led by Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), which is based in Idlib in northwestern Syria, launched an offensive against the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and seized control of the capital city of Damascus in December of the same year. Then President Assad fled to Russia, and the Assad regime collapsed. On December 10, a “transitional government” centered on the anti-government forces was inaugurated, and on January 29, 2025, Ahmed al-Sharaa, commander of HTS, took office as transitional president. The president has presented a policy of unifying all of Syria and working toward establishing sovereignty under a single state authority, but clashes with armed groups and former regime supporters have occurred in various regions. For example, in March of the same year, an agreement was reached with the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) to integrate SDF-controlled regions into the government, but clashes continued repeatedly. On the other hand, progress toward unification has also been seen. For example, in January 2026, an agreement was reached to hand over two of the three northern governorates controlled by the SDF to the government. Furthermore, on October 5, 2025, the Syrian government held the first parliamentary elections since the collapse of the Assad regime, but elections were held only in the 11 of 14 governorates under Syrian government control; the holding of the elections in the remaining three governorates was postponed due to security concerns, among other reasons.

2 Relations between African Countries and Other Countries In terms of security, African countries have long and deep relationships with the United States, Europe, and Russia. Based on this, the relationship with Russia has been further deepening recently, and Chinese involvement in Africa has become prominent. (1) China and Russia China has been strengthening its economic ties with African countries for a long time, but in recent years, it has also increased its military involvement in the region. This includes intensive interactions among not only state leaders but also senior military officials as well as active arms exports and exchanges between military forces. China also actively dispatches personnel to undertake UN PKO in Africa. Some suspect that underlying these movements could be China’s aim to ensure a stable supply of natural resources and to secure additional overseas bases in the future. For example, in August 2017, China began to operate its first overseas military base in Djibouti, known as a “support base,” to provide logistical support to its military, and in July and October 2024, and April and October 2025, Chinese troops stationed at the “support base” conducted joint exercises with the Djibouti Armed Forces troops. There have also been activities in African coastal countries. On the west coast of Africa, from June to July 2023, Chinese naval counter-piracy units visited the Gulf of Guinea countries and conducted joint exercises. On the east coast as well, from July to August 2024, a two-week-long joint exercise was conducted along with Tanzania and Mozambique. Moreover, China conducted trilateral joint exercises with Russia and South Africa in November 2019 and February 2023, and in January 2026, it conducted a joint military exercise with South Africa, Russia, the UAE, and other countries off the coast of South Africa.

1 Trends Related to the “Principle of the Freedom of the High Seas,” etc. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)1 provides for the principles of freedom of navigation on the high seas and freedom of overflight. Nevertheless, in the waters and airspace surrounding Japan, especially in the East and South China Seas, it has become increasingly common for China to unilaterally assert its rights or take action based on assertions that are incompatible with the existing international order, creating situations where these principles are unjustly violated. In addition, North Korea’s repeated launches of ballistic missiles into the Sea of Japan and the Pacific Ocean, as well as launches using ballistic missile technology for the purpose of a satellite launch, not only violate related United Nations Security Council resolutions but are also problematic from the perspective of ensuring the safety of aircraft and ships. They also threaten the peace and security of Japan, the surrounding region, and the international community. Chapter 3, Section 2-2-6 (Maritime and Airspace Activities), Chapter 3, Section 4-1-3 (WMD and Missiles) Despite these numerous acts that could pose risks to securing the stable use of oceans and airspace, in recent years progress has been made in efforts to avert and prevent unintended consequences in the seas and skies. As for multilateral initiatives, navies of countries participating in the Western Pacific Naval Symposium (WPNS) adopted the Code for Unplanned Encounters at Sea (CUES).2 CUES sets forth a code of conduct, such as procedures and communication methods, for ensuring safety in the event of unexpected encounters by vessels or aircraft of the navies of these countries. In addition, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and China are continuing to hold official talks aimed at formulating the Code of the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (COC). It is strongly hoped that these initiatives designed to avert and prevent unintended consequences in the seas and skies will supplement the existing international order and that the countries concerned, including China, refrain from unilateral actions that add to tension and act on the basis of the principle of the rule of law. Part III, Chapter 3, Section 1-2-14 (China)

3 Trends in the Arctic Ocean and the Arctic Region In recent years, moves toward the utilization of the Northern Sea Route and the development of natural resources in the Arctic Ocean have gained momentum in line with a decline in sea ice. The eight arctic nations consisting of Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, and the United States established the Arctic Council in 1996 to promote cooperation for common challenges such as sustainable development and environment protection.5

From the perspective of security, the Arctic Ocean has traditionally been used for the deployment of strategic nuclear forces and as their transit route. With the decrease in sea ice in recent years, ships have been able to navigate for a longer period of time and more extensively than before. It has therefore been considered that the region could be used for deploying maritime forces or maneuvering military forces using military maritime transport capabilities in future. In this situation, moves to deploy new military capabilities in the ocean have been observed. Russia’s maritime doctrine, announced in July 2022, positioned the Arctic Ocean as an area of vital importance. Russia is promoting efforts to establish a system to protect its national interests in the Arctic region. Its various policy documents clearly state Russia’s interests and the role of the Russian military in the Arctic. Furthermore, Russia is proceeding to develop a radar surveillance network as well as reconstructing airfields and deploying surface-to-air and surface-to-ship missiles along the Arctic coast. Note that Russia possesses more icebreakers than any other country in the world and is also the only country to have operational nuclear-powered icebreakers. In connection with such incidents, it has been pointed out that intentional destruction could constitute an element of hybrid warfare. For example, in February 2023, submarine cables connecting the Matsu Islands to mainland Taiwan were cut, and Taiwanese authorities announced that it was believed to have been done by a Chinese fishing boat and cargo ship. In January 2025, submarine cables for international communication in the waters north of Taiwan were damaged, and, in February 2025, it was also announced that submarine cables connecting the main island of Taiwan to the Penghu Islands had been cut. As a result of this situation, in 2025, Taiwan enhanced its law enforcement and warning and surveillance efforts while also promoting legislation that included imposing stricter penalties for intentional damage. Meanwhile, in the Baltic Sea as well, a number of critical submarine cables have been damaged since November 2024 in particular. To enhance maritime presence and monitoring, NATO hosted a Summit of Baltic Sea Allies in January 2025, where the launch of a new military activity called “Baltic Sentry” was announced. In addition, in February 2025, the EU announced its EU Action Plan on Cable Security to ensure the resiliency of submarine cables. Given that submarine cables are essential infrastructure for people’s lives and economic activities, Japan must closely monitor any incidents related to submarine cables getting damaged. 2 Biological and Chemical Weapons Biological and chemical weapons are relatively inexpensive and easy to produce and disguise because many of the resources and technologies needed in their production are dual-use items. 4 Growing Concerns about Transfer and Proliferation of WMDs and Other Technologies Even weapons that were purchased or developed for self-defense purposes could easily be exported or transferred once domestic manufacturing becomes successful. Some of these states that seek WMDs do not hesitate to put their land and people at risk, and furthermore, due to their weak governance, terrorist organizations are active in their territories. Therefore, it is conceivable that in general, the possibility of actual use of WMDs would increase. The proliferation of WMDs and other related technologies has been noted in numerous instances. For example, it came to light in February 2004 that nuclear-related technologies, mainly uranium enrichment technology, had been transferred to North Korea, Iran, and Libya by Dr. A.Q. Khan and other scientists in Pakistan. There has been significant transfer and proliferation of ballistic missiles that serve as means of weapon delivery as well. The former Soviet Union and other countries exported Scud-B to many countries and regions, including Iraq, North Korea, and Afghanistan. China and North Korea also exported DF-3 (CSS-2) and Scud missiles, respectively. As a result, a considerable number of countries and other actors now possess ballistic missiles. Section 1 New Ways of Warfare Seen in Russia’s Aggression against Ukraine and Related Challenges

1 General Situation New ways of warfare and related challenges have emerged during Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. A mass quantity of diverse, inexpensive unmanned assets has been deployed on the battlefields of Ukraine, where they have been used to launch attacks on expensive equipment and basic infrastructure as well as large-scale coordinated attacks in combination with conventional shells and missiles. In addition, decision-making using artificial intelligence (AI) and networks has accelerated, and, in addition to attacks in the space, cyber, and electromagnetic domains, information warfare is also being combined with other kinds of attacks in sophisticated ways. Furthermore, compared to the past, equipment and tactics are being updated on an extremely short cycle. Russia has also demonstrated a certain level of ability to absorb economic sanctions, and as the aggression drags on, the forces of both Russia and Ukraine are rapidly depleting their equipment and ammunition, which has resulted in both countries viewing the stable procurement of such resources as a key challenge. In this situation, the importance of ensuring sustained operational capability (SOC) has become clear, including by stockpiling equipment and ammunition even during peacetime and further enhancing the defense production and technological bases that underpin the development, production, and maintenance of equipment. At the same time, with the help of equipment provision and training support from NATO member states and other countries, Ukraine has been able to resist protracted aggression by Russia. Withstanding initial attacks and receiving effective support from allies, like-minded countries, and others are critical to ensuring SOC. Drawing lessons from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, countries are accelerating efforts to adapt to new ways of warfare and prepare for lengthy wars. It is important to pay attention to future trends. Chapter 2 (Russia’s Aggression and Ukraine’s Defense)

1 Mass Deployment and Expanded Use of Unmanned Assets New ways of warfare that involve utilizing unmanned assets have emerged during Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Generally speaking, unmanned assets enable long-term operations in harsh environments while preserving manpower. As the battlefields of Ukraine transition to a war of attrition, unmanned assets are playing an important role in inflicting losses on adversary forces while minimizing casualties. Both Russia and Ukraine have been deploying a mass quantity of diverse, inexpensive unmanned assets, including unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), for a wide range of applications, such as searching for targets and attacking expensive equipment as well as basic infrastructure. In addition, UAVs are being used to launch large-scale coordinated attacks in combination with traditional shells and missiles. (1) Mass Operation of Unmanned Assets During its large-scale missile attacks against Ukraine, Russia has also been deploying a large number of one-way attack UAVs, including Shahed-type UAVs, capable of long-range flight to saturate Ukraine’s air defense network, thereby increasing the probability of Russian missiles penetrating the air defense network. In addition, since around October 2024, Russia has also expanded its use of decoy UAVs that are difficult to distinguish from one-way attack UAVs. By employing a combination of such lower-cost UAVs that can be produced in large quantities, Russia has been launching effective long-range attacks against Ukraine. On the other hand, it has been pointed out that it is necessary for Ukraine to destroy missile and UAV launch facilities, production plants, and other installations located in Russia, which are the source of the Russian attacks. In this regard, Ukraine is also using domestically produced UAVs See Trends in New Ways of Warfare

An apartment complex in Kharkiv that was destroyed by Russian UAVs [State Emergency Service of Ukraine] Shahed-type UAV [Defence Intelligence of Ukraine] (2) Expanded Applications of Unmanned Assets On the battlefields of Ukraine, the applications of unmanned assets are rapidly expanding and currently include reconnaissance and observation as well as long-range attacks and precision attacks on the front line. First of all, it has been pointed out that, by using a mass quantity of UAVs and other assets to conduct information gathering activities, both sides identify positions of hostile armored vehicles and infantry units, thereby increasing battlefield “transparency” and improving the situational awareness on the battlefield. In addition to their use for reconnaissance and observation purposes, both Russia and Ukraine are also increasingly using first-person view (FPV) drones on the front line to attack armored vehicles, enemy fortifications, and individual soldiers. In addition to large-scale attacks launched from national territory, there have also been examples of operations in which UAVs were employed from within enemy territory to maximize the element of surprise. For example, it has been reported that, in June 2025, Ukraine launched Operation “Spiderweb,” which involved 117 UAVs concealed in wooden cabins disguised as cargo, transporting them into Russia, and then remotely controlling them to attack multiple bases in the country, thereby damaging dozens of strategic bombers and other aircraft. During the same month, the Security Service of Ukraine announced that Operation “Spiderweb” had resulted in estimated total damages to Russia of approximately USD 7 billion, showing that inexpensive approaches can be utilized to destroy expensive equipment.

Unmanned assets are also being effectively utilized offshore. By combining unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) with UAVs and missiles, Ukraine has been preventing Russian ships from approaching its coast and forcing them to withdraw, thereby limiting the activities of Russian ships. For example, according to the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, by the end of May 2024, “Magura V5” USVs developed by Ukraine sank a total of eight ships belonging to Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, including large landing ships and patrol boats. Similarly, in December 2024, improved “Magura V5” USVs shot down two Russian military helicopters, and in May 2025, “Magura V7” USVs used anti-air missiles to shoot down two Russian military fighter jets. Based on the above, USVs are apparently functioning as anti-aircraft assets. In addition, in December 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine announced that “Sub-Sea Baby” unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) had been used to attack a Russian military submarine, and future trends in the utilization of UUVs by Ukraine will be a subject of attention. The military then instantly shares the results with each unit to facilitate prompt and accurate decision-making. In September 2024, President Vladimir Putin announced that approximately 140,000 UAVs had been supplied to the military in 2023 and that around ten times more would be supplied in 2024. In April 2025, he announced that over 1.5 million UAVs had been supplied to the military in 2024. Meanwhile, to ensure its own SOC, Ukraine has been depending on support from Western countries in terms of the supply of its equipment and ammunition. At the same time, Ukraine has been focusing on domestically producing such supplies and expanding its production capacity, and, in March 2025, Ukraine announced that it had produced at least 2.3 million UAVs in 2024. In addition, on the battlefields of Ukraine, equipment and tactics are being updated on an extremely short cycle compared to the past, and prompt, flexible technological innovations are becoming increasingly important. 6 Support from Allies and Like-Minded Countries In addition to providing a substantial amount of equipment to Ukraine, from man-portable missiles to fighter jets, Western countries have also been offering extensive support in terms of intelligence and training while also promoting co-production of equipment with Ukraine. In order for Ukraine to maintain its SOC, support from its allies and like-minded countries is essential. At the same time, Russia also seems to be maintaining its military capabilities by obtaining equipment from foreign sources. It has been reported that, in addition to Russia using UAVs originally developed by Iran to attack various targets in Ukraine, China has also been sending dual-use items to Russia to bolster its SOC. In addition, as Russia’s aggression against Ukraine continues, North Korea has been enhancing its military cooperation with Russia. For example, North Korea has been providing ammunition and weapons including ballistic missiles to Russia since 2023 while also deploying soldiers to Russia since the latter half of 2024 to participate in combat with Ukraine. It has been reported that North Korean shells have been used during Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and that there is a possibility that North Korea has been enhancing its tactical capabilities by taking advantage of its experience fighting against Ukraine, so it will be necessary to continue to closely monitor progress on military cooperation between Russia and North Korea. In addition, the Indian Army implements initiatives to have its units produce UAVs, and announced that they produced 819 UAVs for both monitoring and combat purposes by the end of 2025. India has also announced the intention to actively invest in AI as well as related policies. In 2018, India launched a task force to start researching and developing AI in the defense field. In July 2022, India’s Ministry of Defence organized and held AiDef, the country’s first AI-related exhibition, through which the country announced newly developed technologies, etc. and expressed its intention to actively utilize AI in the defense field.7 India has also developed AI-powered UAV swarm technology, and, in January 2021, the country released information on a swarm-attack demonstration involving the use of 75 UAVs. The country has announced that it also incorporates UAV swarm technology into certain Indian Army exercises.

In addition, in August 2025, the Indian military announced India’s Joint Doctrine for Multi-Domain Operations, thereby pointing out the importance of the space, cyber, and cognitive dimensions as new fields. It has also been pointed out that the impact of disinformation and psychological operations is increasing, leading to national cognitive restructuring and increased social divisions that could pose a challenge for traditional military forces, so India believes that achieving superiority in the cognitive dimension could be the most important factor during both peacetime and wartime. Regarding initiatives to ensure SOC, based on its Self-Reliant India policy, the country has announced the intention to increase its stockpile of ammunition up to its target level, establish at least two suppliers for each type of ammunition, and formulate a roadmap to establish a minimum of one domestic supplier for every type of ammunition required by the country.

5 Europe Based on lessons learned from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and other considerations, Europe is pursuing initiatives in fields that include unmanned assets, AI, cyber, information warfare, and SOC.

1 The United Kingdom One example of efforts in the United Kingdom is the announcement of the Defence Drone Strategy by the Ministry of Defence in 2024. This strategy has shown an awareness of the fact that, given that unmanned assets are being effectively utilized for a wide range of applications on the battlefields of Ukraine and the related technological innovation is extremely fast, past development and procurement methods are not sufficient for responding. Based on such lessons learned, the United Kingdom has clearly stated the need to achieve the mass operation of inexpensive unmanned assets, quickly procure them, and pursue development through fast and repeated improvements while also building a resilient supply chain to strengthen the U.K. industrial base. In the AI field, the United Kingdom announced its Strategic Defence Review 2025 in 2025, in which it identified further expansion of AI utilization as one of its priorities. For example, by introducing the Digital Targeting Web as AI infrastructure in 2027, the British military plans to comprehensively link everything from target acquisition to offensive action, thereby achieving an extremely rapid and optimal means of attacking targets based on information collected and organized using AI. In addition, in the cyber and electromagnetic spectrum domains, the United Kingdom officially launched the Cyber & Specialist Operations Command in September 2025 to unify land, sea, and air units. Furthermore, in the SOC field, the United Kingdom is emphasizing the need to ensure a stockpile of ammunition and equipment while also promptly replenishing it, and, to address this issue, they are expanding their production systems, including building new ammunition factories, radically reforming their equipment procurement process, and taking other steps.

3 Germany Based on lessons learned from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and other considerations, Germany is enhancing its investment in UAVs. At the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Defense Ministers’ Meeting in October 2025, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius supported NATO’s plan to enhance defense by using drones and expressed Germany’s intention to invest 10 billion euros in all kinds of advanced drones for attack and defense purposes in the next several years. In addition, in the air defense field, including responding to UAVs, Germany launched the European Sky Shield Initiative in October 2022 as a multilateral framework for countering

diverse airborne threats, including the kinds of missiles and UAVs seen during Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. The objective of this framework is for participating states to jointly procure, operate, and maintain air defense systems and to combine multiple air defense systems to strengthen the air defense network of various European countries in multiple layers, including everything from short-range air defense (several kilometers or less) to ballistic missile defense. At the present time, 21 European countries participate in this initiative, including Switzerland and Austria (current as of March 2025), and future trends will continue to be monitored. In addition, in the information warfare field, Germany is responding to the threat of disinformation based on examples of disinformation related to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine by providing the German people with information on how to identify disinformation, such as basic approaches that include the utilization of fact-checking and confirmation of information sources, thereby alerting them to such dangers. In the SOC field as well, Germany is working on strengthening its defense industrial base. Germany’s National Security and Defence Industry Strategy, which was formulated in December 2024, points out that there have been efforts to promote the development of innovative technologies during Russia’s aggression against Ukraine through digitization and increased battlefield transparency, indicating that it is necessary to respond to such rapid technological progress. In line with the country’s policy to maintain the production capacity of specific key industries under this strategy, Germany has specified AI, quantum technology, unmanned systems, and the like as especially important defense industry technologies, and the country is aiming to build systems offering domestic supply capabilities to avoid having to depend on foreign countries for such technologies.

Colonel KAWAMURA Kouki, Senior Fellow, Global Security Division, National Institute for Defense Studies To overcome the fog of war, it has long been understood that frontline units and headquarters need to share information, and units need to work together while using a common map of operations, thereby achieving a synergistic effect. This requires a network that enables information to be exchanged continuously between sensors, shooters, and decision-makers. It has long been believed that making this a reality would give commanders the advantage in terms of decision-making, while also enabling individual units to take autonomous actions toward exploiting an opponent’s weaknesses. From the Gulf War onward, the U.S. Forces worked toward a force design based on the concept of “network-centric warfare.” Underlining this was the concept of combining a huge number of satellites, radars, and other sensors to create an information infrastructure, which, if maintained in a stable manner, would naturally lead to an improved level of situational awareness. However, since radar-equipped information-gathering aircraft and ground combat platforms move at a fast pace across vast battlefields spanning tens to hundreds of kilometers, wireless communication tends to become the dominant means of connecting units with one another. This has also been a point of vulnerability that could be exploited to interrupt network operations. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq were fought on the premise that the opponent lacked the capability to disrupt U.S. Forces’ networks. In the 2010s, however, there was a real possibility that potential adversaries would disrupt networks using a variety of different means, including kinetic attacks, electronic interference, and cyber weapons. An example of this is the U.S. Forces’ airborne warning and control systems involved in the Syrian civil war, which were subjected to jamming by Russian electronic warfare units.

This requires a network that enables information to be exchanged continuously between sensors, shooters, and decision-makers. It has long been believed that making this a reality would give commanders the advantage in terms of decision-making, while also enabling individual units to take autonomous actions toward exploiting an opponent’s weaknesses. From the Gulf War onward, the U.S. Forces worked toward a force design based on the concept of “network-centric warfare.” Underlining this was the concept of combining a huge number of satellites, radars, and other sensors to create an information infrastructure, which, if maintained in a stable manner, would naturally lead to an improved level of situational awareness. However, since radar-equipped information-gathering aircraft and ground combat platforms move at a fast pace across vast battlefields spanning tens to hundreds of kilometers, wireless communication tends to become the dominant means of connecting units with one another. This has also been a point of vulnerability that could be exploited to interrupt network operations. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq were fought on the premise that the opponent lacked the capability to disrupt U.S. Forces’ networks. In the 2010s, however, there was a real possibility that potential adversaries would disrupt networks using a variety of different means, including kinetic attacks, electronic interference, and cyber weapons. An example of this is the U.S. Forces’ airborne warning and control systems involved in the Syrian civil war, which were subjected to jamming by Russian electronic warfare units.

This and similar incidents have brought about a sense of crisis on the U.S. side. An “unacceptable environment” for military operations is a situation in which information and communication lines cannot be used as intended due to disruption, interference, or similar actions by an opponent. Concerns spread within the U.S. Forces that ultimately, network-centric warfare may not be well adapted to such environments. What has emerged from this is the concept of “decision-centric warfare.” This is based on a disaggregated force design, and its aim is to create mosaic-like networks composed of multiple nodes, rather than bringing together all systems in a single network. Instead of sophisticated, high-quality information nodes that are vulnerable to attack, the concept prioritizes a kill web composed of low-cost sensors and expendable unmanned systems that can be maintained even in unacceptable environments for military operations. As Bryan Clark and Dan Patt of the Hudson Institute have noted, the objective of decision-centric warfare is to accelerate the U.S. Forces’ own decision-making processes, while at the same time posing enemies with an insoluble set of dilemmas to disrupt operations, thereby preventing them from reaching objectives in time. As such, attention has been drawn to a command and control structure that combines human commanders with AI-equipped machines. AI decision-support algorithms suggest courses of action that an opponent cannot predict, helping to determine the combination of forces and tactics necessary to accomplish a mission before field commanders issue orders. In contrast to network-centric warfare, which led to much more centralized decision-making, it has come to be expected that decision-centric warfare will encourage a level of autonomy and flexibility across subordinate units. Decision-centric warfare, which aims to flexibly combine various assets as a way of adapting to changes on the battlefield, is a new concept for overcoming the fog of war and frictions inherent to military operations. It can also be said that the concept supports Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2), whose goal is to enhance the capabilities of the U.S. Unified Combatant Command by strengthening coordination across air, land, marine, space, and cyberspace domains. SUGIURA Yasuyuki, Chief, Asia and Africa Division, National Institute for Defense Studies Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has drawn attention to warfare in the cognitive dimension; that is, information warfare and psychological warfare. Meanwhile, China appears to be using such warfare to validate its own military doctrine. Up to present, China has established “informationized local wars” as its military doctrine. This places importance on the elements in C4ISR: command, control, communication, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. Furthermore, as its next military doctrine, it envisions “intelligentized warfare” that incorporates AI, unmanned assets, quantum technology, and other technologies. With intelligentized warfare, there is a greater focus on the operation of unmanned assets and AI, as well as warfare in cyberspace and the cognitive dimension. China has traditionally focused on warfare in the cognitive dimension, employing the “Three Warfares” of “media warfare,” “psychological warfare,” and “legal warfare.” It appears that the country intends to integrate warfare in the cognitive dimension with the physical domains of land, maritime, air, and space, along with cyberspace and the information domain. 1 Space Domain and Security There is no concept of national borders in space, meaning that the utilization of satellites enables observation, communications, and positioning anywhere on Earth. Thus, major countries make efforts to enhance the capabilities of a variety of satellites and launch them for the purpose of enhancing C4ISR (command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance) functions. Such satellites include information gathering satellites that collect imagery and signals concerning various activities, early warning satellites for detecting the launch of ballistic missiles, positioning satellites for enhancing the precision of weapons systems, communication satellites used for communications relay. On the other hand, anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons to hinder the utilization of space by other countries are also under development. Regarding destructive Direct-Ascent Anti-SATellite (DA-ASAT) missiles, China and Russia conducted tests targeting their own satellites in 2007 and 2021, respectively. As a result, a large amount of space debris has been generated, raising concerns about the risk of such debris colliding with satellites and other space assets of various countries. Regarding China, it has been pointed out that the robot arm technologies being developed by China to inspect and repair in-orbit satellites can be repurposed as ASATs such as satellite-attack satellites (so-called “killer satellites”). As for Russia, it has been pointed out that the ejection of an object from its satellite against a nearby satellite was an ASAT experiment.1 Furthermore, it has been pointed out that China and Russia are developing jammers for interfering with communications between target satellites and ground stations, as well as high energy technology such as laser weapons designed to degrade or damage satellites. In addition, a Russian cyberattack on a satellite communication provider in 2022 disrupted satellite communications services, raising concerns about cyberattacks on space systems.

“Ensuring American Space Superiority,” which set out various objectives for ensuring the national and economic security of the United States in space, including returning to the surface of the Moon by 2028. More specifically, based on the executive order “The Iron Dome for America,” the United States is aiming to develop and demonstrate next-generation missile defense technologies by 2028, ensure the ability to detect, characterize, and counter threats to the United States from very low-Earth orbit and through cislunar space, including placing nuclear weapons in space, create a national security space architecture by promoting acquisition reform that integrates commercial space capabilities, and enhance collective space security for both the United States and its allies, etc. In addition, “Ensuring American Space Superiority” calls for relevant government agencies to identify technology and supply chain gaps related to strengthening U.S. air and missile defense and formulate a detailed improvement plan to address them within 90 days, and to formulate a national security strategy related to space within 180 days. Based on these policies, in May 2025, the U.S. Department of War announced a plan to develop a “Golden Dome,” which will be capable of intercepting hypersonic, ballistic, and advanced cruise missiles launched both within and outside of Earth’s atmosphere. This system will include both space-based interceptors and sensors, and it will offer interoperability with existing interceptors to function alongside them. The current plan is for the “Golden Dome” to be operational within three years. In addition, in November 2025, the United States announced the plan to deploy new weapons capable of jamming Chinese and Russian intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance satellites all over the world.

Chapter 3, Section 1-2 (Military Posture) (2) China China has been promoting space development since the 1950s and is investing in space systems aimed at strengthening the country’s C4ISR and targeting capabilities. China has been further intensifying its space activities in recent years, including completing the Tiangong space station and advancing plans for a lunar base. In 2024, China accelerated its efforts to build a satellite constellation for rapid information gathering and communication, including starting to launch Guowang and Qianfan, low-Earth orbit Internet satellite groups. It has been reported that China has over 1,000 satellites and plans to launch thousands more by 2030. In addition, these satellite groups will apparently be deployed as megaconstellations, which are intended to compete with Starlink as alternative providers of global Internet service.4 Furthermore, efforts in lunar exploration are advancing. In June of 2024, the unmanned lunar probe Chang’e 6 successfully completed the first-ever sample collection and return mission from the far side of the Moon. While traditionally emphasizing international cooperation and the peaceful use of space, it is pointed out that China proactively used space for military purposes, including information gathering, communications and positioning through satellites. For example, the possibility of military use has been pointed out with respect to BeiDou for aircraft and vessel navigation and guidance of missiles, and with respect to Yaogan for electronic and image reconnaissance.

(3) Russia While Russian space activity has been reduced since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia has continued to be active in space in recent years, even after its aggression against Ukraine. For example, Russia continues to launch a large number of various types of satellites, including the Kosmos series, and sends Progress series cargo aircraft to the International Space Station (ISS). Furthermore, Russia has revealed a development plan for its own space station, with each module scheduled to be launched between 2028 and 2033. Note that, in terms of ASATs, the U.S. Government has concluded that the Kosmos 2576 satellite launched by Russia in 2024 is in fact a counter-space weapon with the capability to attack other satellites. There have also been claims that Russia is planning to deploy a nuclear-armed anti-satellite system in space. However, the Russian Government has denied these allegations. In regard to Russian policies, Russia released in 2016 the Federal Space Program for 2016-2025 as a specific future

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) indicated its recognition that space is the fifth operational domain alongside land, sea, air and cyberspace and that armed attacks in space could trigger NATO’s right to collective self-defense. In its new strategic concept published in 2022, NATO stated that it would strengthen its ability to operate effectively in the space and cyber domains. In October 2024, some NATO members agreed to the promotion of the “NORTHLINK initiative,” which is a plan to build a military-satellite communication network in the Arctic, as well as the start of the “STARLIFT initiative,” which is a plan to secure rocket launch capabilities. The United Kingdom, in its Defence Space Strategy announced in 2022, stated that it will invest GBP 1.4 billion over the next 10 years in areas such as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) and satellite communications. In addition, U.K. Space Command, which was officially established in 2021, successfully launched Tyche, its first information gathering satellite, in 2024. France announced the Space Defence Strategy in 2019, stating that it aimed to establish a space command and strengthen its threat recognition and space situation monitoring capabilities. In the same year, France established a space command under the Air Force. In 2020, the Air Force was renamed the Air and Space Force, adding activities to ensure free access to space and freedom of action in space to its duties. In addition, under its Military Programming Act 2024-2030, France has stated its intention to increase its defense budget for the space domain by EUR 3.9 billion by 2030, increase communication connectivity and resilience, enhance the country’s information gathering methods, accelerate or expand its ability to act both in outer space and in terms of efforts aimed at outer space, and pursue other goals.

1 Cyberspace and Security Cyberspace, which is formed by various services and communities, including the Internet, is becoming increasingly important as a new social domain. Therefore, cyberattacks that compromise information assets and networks in cyberspace are real threats to security because they can have serious impacts on society. Additionally, typical cyberattacks include unauthorized access, information leakage and disruption of computer functions by malware (malicious software), information falsification and theft, and distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks that impair networks by transmitting large amounts of data simultaneously. When cyberattacks target electric power systems, medical systems, and other critical infrastructure, they can also cause damage that includes system failures. The methods of attack are also becoming increasingly advanced and sophisticated, and it has been pointed out that AI can be used to launch cyberattacks that are faster and more sophisticated than anything people could do without it. For military forces as well, cyberspace forms the foundation of command and control, which extends from central command to ground-level forces, as well as the foundation for operating unmanned assets, including unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and critical infrastructure, which makes cyberspace essential in many fields. In this regard, the dependence of military forces on cyberspace is further increasing. There is a high probability of cyberattacks being launched on such infrastructure not only in peacetime but also before traditional forms of invasion through air, sea, and land, so it is necessary to promptly and accurately respond to threats in the cyber domain. In addition, since cyberattacks do not require weapons and it is not easy to identify the attackers and ascertain the damage, such attacks are recognized as an asymmetrical means to impede military activities of adversaries at low cost. It is believed that many foreign armed forces are establishing or enhancing their cyberattack capabilities.

2 Threat Trends in Cyberspace Cyberattacks have frequently been carried out against not only government organizations and military forces but also business corporations and academic organizations in various countries, targeting their critical technology, confidential information and personal data. In addition, advanced persistent threats (APTs), which are relentless cyberattacks on specific organizations, are also considered to be organized activities because they require abundant resources, arrangements, and capabilities for long-term activities. Amid this situation, the United Kingdom has also identified cyberattacks by China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran as “real and enduring threats.”10 (1) China In China, it was once believed that units responsible for cyber warfare were organized under the Strategic Support Force, but it has been pointed out that the Strategic Support Force was dissolved in 2024 and that its subordinate Cyberspace Force was elevated to a service arm. Taiwan has pointed out that, in terms of cyberattack methods used by China, China attempts to infiltrate Taiwan’s core infrastructure networks through combined approaches that include attacks on hardware and software vulnerabilities, DDoS attacks, and social engineering,11 and that China also launches cyberattacks targeting Internet-based logistics, command and control, communications, commercial activities, and military infrastructure, thereby attempting to disrupt Taiwan’s activities.12 China’s 2019 defense white paper, released in July 2019 and titled “China’s National Defense in the New Era,” stated that China’s armed forces are accelerating the building of their cyberspace capabilities. 21 According to “Beyond Hacktivism: Iran’s Coordinated Cyber Threat Landscape,” CSIS (January 2026) (4) Iran In Iran, the principal actors behind cyberattacks are believed to include state-sponsored APT groups that cooperate with the Islamic Republic of Iran Army and are associated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is under the direct command of the Supreme Leader, and the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), which is under the jurisdiction of the President, as well as hacktivists that act independently of the government. These groups carry out a wide range of attacks, including DDoS attacks, website falsification, and sophisticated destructive activities that target industrial control systems and operational technologies. In general, hacktivist groups are categorized differently than APT groups, but, as Iran expands its cyber operations, hacktivists are starting to emulate tactics and methods used by APT groups, raising concerns that include tool and capability sharing as well as command and control relationships.21 In the last several years, Iran has been launching more frequent cyber operations against critical U.S. infrastructure. For example, a group of hacktivists who call themselves the CyberAv3ngers and emerged in October 2023 to resist the actions of Israel in Gaza has been primarily targeting Israeli infrastructure but also launches attacks against U.S. water and sewer services. In March 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and NSA issued a warning that hacker groups allegedly affiliated with Iran’s IRGC had launched cyberattacks targeting industrial control systems. In addition, it has been reported that, during the exchange of attacks with Iran in June 2025, cyberattacks were launched by Iran.

3 Initiatives against Cyberspace Threats Given these growing threats in cyberspace, various initiatives are under way. Because the United States, Europe, Japan, and other countries support the free, fair, and safe use of cyberspace, they hold discussions on how international law should be applied as well as putting norms into practice. In contrast, Russia, China, and similar countries call for the possibility of new, legally binding treaties and are continuing to hold discussions due to differing views. Starting in 2021, the UN held a five-year Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG) in which all UN members participated. The OEWG discussed a wide range of topics, including cyberspace threat perceptions, norms, the application of international law, and confidence-building measures, and, in 2025, they submitted their final report, including the establishment of the Global Mechanism, a framework for continuing with OEWG work, to the UN General Assembly, which approved it. Strategically speaking, the United States announced its Cyber Strategy in March 2026, under which the country will protect its critical infrastructure and identify and disrupt the networks of adversaries through defensive and offensive cyber operations, thereby preventing attacks directed at the United States. The government has also announced a “Zero Trust23 Strategy” to strengthen cybersecurity at federal agencies, calling on each department and agency to implement security measures based on the Zero Trust model. In addition, the government has announced a National Cyber Workforce and Education Strategy to secure cyber workforce, which sets out its intention to address the long-term issue of acquiring basic cyber skills for the public and reforming cyber education. In terms of security, the Department of Defense’s Cyber Strategy 2023 stated that the department would track the organizations, capabilities, and intentions of attackers, disrupt and degrade malicious cyber activities and defend against them, and support the Unified Combatant Command’s operations in the cyber domain and cooperate with allies and related countries to defend against them. In addition, under the National Defense Strategy set forth by the second Trump administration, the Department of War is prioritizing enhanced cyber defense aimed at protecting the U.S. Forces and specific civilian targets, while also developing other options for deterring and weakening cyber threats directed against the U.S. homeland. At the Japan-U.S. “2+2” Meeting in 2019, the two countries agreed to strengthen cooperation in the field of cyberspace, affirming that international law applies in cyberspace and that a cyberattack could, in certain circumstances, constitute an armed attack for the purposes of the Japan-U.S. Security Treaty. The U.S. Forces include Cyber Command, which was elevated to a Unified Combatant Command in 2018 to control cyberspace operations. The U.S. Cyber Command, with 6,200 personnel, comprises teams that protect the Department of Defense’s information networks, monitor and defend against adversary cyber activities and support the Unified Combatant Commands’ operations. The U.S. military also conducts operations to defend against and disrupt malicious cyber activities on critical networks in partner nations such as Latvia and Lithuania.

Electronic jamming includes electromagnetic interference (jamming), electromagnetic wave deception (spoofing), and physical destruction using high-power electromagnetic waves (such as lasers and microwaves). EP includes thwarting detection by adversaries and reducing or neutralizing adversary EA against communications and radar equipment by changing the frequency of electromagnetic waves used or increasing their power. ES consists of activities designed to collect information relating to electromagnetic waves used by adversaries. To effectively achieve EA and EP, it is necessary to continuously monitor and analyze what kinds of electromagnetic waves are used and how by the adversary’s communications equipment, radar, and EA aircraft. Electromagnetic spectrum management is to grasp how electromagnetic waves are used in the battle area and to appropriately adjust frequencies, directions and durations of electromagnetic waves used by friendly forces and equipment to avoid electromagnetic wave interference. Major countries recognize EA as an asymmetric means of attack similar to cyberattacks that effectively prevent adversaries from demonstrating their military capabilities. 2 Each Country’s EW Initiatives (1) The United States In its “Electromagnetic Spectrum Superiority Strategy” announced in 2020, the United States states that ensuring freedom of action in the electromagnetic spectrum, at the time, place and parameters of its choosing, is a prerequisite for successful operations across all domains. In 2021, an implementation plan for the strategy was approved, which— the United States says—paves the way for initiatives such as establishing procedures to develop, integrate and strengthen integrated electromagnetic spectrum operations and develop guidance for acquiring electromagnetic spectrum capabilities. The U.S. Army has deployed a Multi-Domain Task Force with space, cyberspace, and EW functions in the U.S. homeland (2017), Germany (2021), and Hawaii (2023). Furthermore, in 2021, the U.S. Air Force established the 350th Spectrum Warfare Wing to operate and maintain electronic warfare. In 2023, the Strategic Command officially opened the “Joint Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations Center,” which is intended to serve as the center of the U.S. military’s electromagnetic spectrum operations, including force management, planning and situational monitoring. It conducts a space-domain EW exercise called “Black Skies,” and a command-and-control exercise under electromagnetic interference called “Heavy Rain.”

(2) China The Chinese military considers EW to be an essential element of modern warfare. It appears that the Chinese military seeks to achieve information dominance in a conflict by aligning EW and cyber warfare to protect its own information networks and prevent the enemy from using the electromagnetic spectrum.25 The Chinese military’s EW strategy is reportedly focused on suppressing, degrading, disrupting and deceiving enemy electronic equipment. Its EW units are said to be routinely training to conduct jamming and anti-jamming operations against multiple communication and radar systems and GPS receivers during exercises, which are believed to evaluate operational units’ proficiency in EW weapons and other aspects.26 On the organizational front, the Strategic Support Force, which is considered to have been responsible for EW, was dissolved in April 2024, and its subordinate Aerospace Force and Cyberspace Force were reportedly elevated to service arms. The Cyberspace Force now appears to be responsible for EW.27 In addition, it has been reported that China has deployed electronic jamming equipment on Mischief Reef in the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea,28 and, around Japan, flights by Y-8 and Y-9 EW aircraft and other aircraft have been confirmed. 2 High-Power Energy Weapons High-power energy weapons, such as railguns, high-power laser weapons, and high-power microwave weapons, are being developed as a means to counter various airborne threats. A railgun is a kind of weapon that shoots bullets using a magnetic field generated from electrical energy. Unlike missiles, the bullets used for railguns have no propulsion device. For this reason, the bullets are smaller, cost less, and require less space for storing. Therefore, railguns are said to be capable of coping effectively with attacks involving a large number of missiles. Laser weapons, which use high-power laser energy to destroy targets, are being developed by the United States, China, Russia and other countries as low-cost, effective means of intercepting a large number of small UAVs and small vessels. High-power microwave weapons are weapons to destroy or cause the malfunction of electronic equipment in UAVs, missiles, and the like. (1) The United States The United States is developing several laser weapons. In June 2025, the U.S. Army conducted a live-fire test of the 50kW-class vehicle-mounted laser weapon DE M-SHORAD (Directed Energy Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense) by targeting a UAV swarm, which resulted in the swarm being successfully neutralized. In addition, in 2023, the United States concluded a contract to develop 300kW-class laser weapons. In 2022, the U.S. Navy also equipped the Arleigh Burke-class missile destroyer USS Preble with the 60kW-class laser weapon HELIOS (High Energy Laser and Integrated Optical-dazzler with Surveillance), and, in January 2026, it used this to successfully fire at and neutralize four UAVs. Note that the plan is to eventually increase the output of HELIOS to 150kW, which will make it effective against UAVs that do not have exposed sensors or engines. THOR (Tactical High-power Operational Responder) against numerous UAVs to simulate swarm flights, effectively disabling many of them. The U.S. Marine Corps is also assessing the integration of AI-based UAV detection and tracking capabilities with high-power microwave weapons. (2) China China unveiled the LW-60, a vehicle-mounted laser weapon with an unknown power output that is designed to counter small UAVs, at the 2024 China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition. There are also indications that China has deployed anti-satellite laser weapons that appear to be designed to interfere with or damage the optical sensors of low-earth orbit satellites and that it is developing laser weapons with even higher power output. (3) Russia Russia has deployed the 10kW-class Peresvet laser weapon system, and it is reportedly developing a megawatt-class chemical laser weapon system for attacking satellites. (4) Israel In September 2025, Israel finished developing the Iron Beam, a vehicle-mounted air defense laser weapon with a 100 kW-class power output, and the country demonstrated that the weapon is capable of intercepting rockets, mortar rounds, UAVs, and a wide range of other threats while also announcing the successful completion of a series of related tests. In December 2025, the Iron Beam was given to the first unit to ever use it, and Israel plans to deploy the new weapon to more units. (5) The United Kingdom In November 2025, the U.K. Ministry of Defence announced that it had used the DragonFire laser, its first ever high-power laser weapon, to successfully shoot down a UAV flying at a speed of 650 km/h. The DragonFire laser is inexpensive to fire, costing just £10 per shot, and it is apparently accurate enough to hit a target the size of a £1 coin from a kilometer away. In addition, the United Kingdom has already concluded contracts for Royal Navy Type 45 destroyers to be outfitted with the new weapon in 2027. The United Kingdom is also considering equipping British Army vehicles and Royal Air Force fighter aircraft with the laser.33

3 AI Technology AI technology is one area where rapid development is taking place, including generative AI, which can generate natural text and images in response to instructions, AI agents that can autonomously analyze information necessary to achieve objectives and act accordingly, and physical AI systems that use AI as a brain in combination with a physical body in the real world to take autonomous action and learn. It has been pointed out that this rapid AI progress has been exerting a great impact on the military field, including its applications for UAVs and the cyber domain as well as support for command and decision-making and improving data processing capabilities. (1) Utilization of AI to Support Command and Decision-Making, Etc. a. The United States and Europe One example of AI utilization in the United States is the use of the AI-powered Maven Smart System developed through the Project Maven initiative advanced by the U.S. Army to enable the rapid assessment of combat spaces, collection of large volumes of data, and analysis of the collected data using AI to identify and attack targets. In May 2024, the U.S. Department of Defense announced a contract with a private company to develop the system, and, in 2025, the contract amount limit up through 2029 was increased to approximately USD 1.3 billion. In addition, in April 2025, NATO also announced that it had agreed to a contract to purchase this system.34 b. China China announced in 2020 that an AI Military Simulation Competition was held by the Central Military Commission with the purpose of researching and developing next-generation command information systems. The U.S. DoD has pointed out that China’s goal is to pass Western countries in terms of AI research and development by 2025 and to become the world’s leader in the AI field by 2030.35

has built a 4,600 km quantum cryptographic communication network consisting of the quantum cryptographic communication satellite Mozi and a ground communication network between Beijing and Shanghai. In addition, in July 2022, China launched its Jinan-1 quantum-secured microsatellite, which costs 1/20th as much as the Mozi. In March 2025, China announced that it had used its Jinan-1 satellite to achieve quantum-key distribution between South Africa and a station in Beijing, located 12,900 km apart. On the other hand, the possibility of transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), which is difficult to decrypt using quantum computers, continues to be researched in many countries, and the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced the first PQC standards in August 2024. In the EU, the European Commission has requested that member states formulate strategies aimed at transitioning to PQC. In June 2025, the European Commission announced a roadmap related to this, based on which the goal is for the EU’s important systems to finish transitioning to PQC by the end of 2030. Note that China has introduced PQC and is apparently researching its own algorithm that differs from the NIST standards.

5 Additive Manufacturing Technology Additive manufacturing technology, as typified by 3D printers, is expected to be applied to each military sector in various countries, due to low manufacturing cost and parts procurement that does not rely on inventory. The United States, in announcing the “Use of Additive Manufacturing Technology” in 2021, stated that it would enhance the independence and readiness of its military services and has installed 3D printers on some of its surface ships and submarines. As an example of an initiative pursued by a specific military branch, the U.S. Army utilizes additive manufacturing technology to proactively resolve supply shortages, and field units also use this technology to manufacture metal parts on site, thereby eliminating the need to transport them. In addition, to train personnel in the use of sophisticated manufacturing technologies, the United States is significantly enhancing training courses related to them.39 China is also utilizing 3D printers to manufacture parts for military aircraft. Ukraine is similarly utilizing 3D printers to manufacture UAV parts, etc.

5 Trends in the Cognitive Dimension Information warfare in the international community begins even before the outbreak of conflict, as it aims to shape a favorable security environment by influencing people’s perception through disinformation and strategic messaging, thereby affecting public opinion and decision-making in other countries, while also preventing external influence on one’s own decision-making. For example, as has been pointed out in the cases of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, the 2023 clashes between Israel and the Palestinian militants, and the presidential elections

in Taiwan and the United States, concerns over information warfare, including the dissemination of disinformation and the proliferation of information aimed at eroding trust in the target government or dividing society using social media and influencers, have been growing. In particular, in recent years, advances in AI technology are making deepfakes and generative AI-created videos, images, and documents even more of a serious threat, as they are highly realistic and can be created in a short time with inexpensive, easily accessible tools. It is believed that Russia and China are waging information warfare both domestically and abroad, aiming to build an information environment favorable to them. It has also been noted that China is spending billions of dollars to promote propaganda, spread disinformation, and conduct censorship by investing in the media of other countries. In addition, the U.S. Department of War has pointed out that China has positioned cognitive-dimension operations as a core element of its so-called “pressure campaign” against Taiwan, with the aim of weakening Taiwan’s will to resist China and deepening social divisions there. In addition, China utilizes the infosphere to disseminate specific political narratives, adversely affect the Taiwanese people, and emphasize activities of the PLA around Taiwan.40 Meanwhile, ever since Russia’s aggression against Ukraine started, Russia has been expanding its range of information-based influence operations as part of its hybrid warfare efforts, and it has been reported that the country is even using agents stationed in other countries.
