YAMAGUCHI Shinji, Senior Fellow, China Division, National Institute for Defense Studies In recent years, the battle in the cognitive dimension has intensified, with countries attempting to disrupt and have an impact on the politics and societies of adversary countries through information manipulation and influence operations. China and Russia are attempting to take advantage of the characteristics of free and open political and social systems in democratic countries to disrupt the politics of adversary countries and lead them in a direction which is desirable for themselves, by carrying out information manipulation using disinformation and other techniques and influence operations against the democratic countries. As part of such techniques, China carries out promotion, propaganda, information manipulation on social media, and united front (influence) operations. Promotion and propaganda refer to activities by China’s state-controlled media, such as Xinhua News Agency and others, to communicate the narrative of China to the world, transmit government views and Chinese culture, and rebut the propaganda of foreign countries. Next, there is the spread of disinformation through social media and other channels. We are seeing cases in which the governments of other countries deliberately spread disinformation with the aim of causing disruption and division in the domestic politics and societies of adversary countries. China is also expanding these kinds of activities. Its united front operations are one type of influence operation to create external collaborators in order to achieve the political goals of the Chinese Communist Party. It targets people who are favorable to the Chinese government, who hold views close to China on certain issues, and who have cultural or ethnic ties to China, and attempts to lead them in a direction advantageous to China’s political objectives.

What China is trying to achieve through these activities is, firstly, to enhance China’s image and expand support for its policies; secondly, to rebut the claims and information of foreign countries that are disadvantageous to China; and thirdly, to increase social divisions and create political and social disruption in adversary countries. The targets of China’s operations are mainly Taiwan and the countries in the Global South. China is aiming to disrupt politics in Taiwan and form advantageous conditions for itself and is scheming to increase support for itself by trumpeting the shortcomings and problems of the United States and Europe to the Global South countries. It has been thought that China has not been directing its activities against Japan very actively, but recently, these activities have been intensifying. In particular, since President Xi Jinping mentioned the “historical ties between Fujian Province and Okinawa” in June 2023, China’s operations surrounding Okinawa Prefecture have intensified. The number of Chinese government and party officials visiting Okinawa Prefecture is increasing, and activities such as fake accounts on social media attempting to spread false videos inciting “Ryukyu independence” have been seen. The activities of China, Russia, and others have not necessarily been highly effective. However, this kind of cognitive warfare can pose a serious challenge to democracy as it attempts to incite division by taking advantage of areas of disagreement in the adversary’s politics and society. It is necessary for various government departments, companies, and society as a whole to cooperate to respond to it. Colonel KAWAMURA Kouki, Senior Fellow, Global Security Division, National Institute for Defense Studies As long as you have a smartphone, you can exchange messages and videos with people from all over the world at anytime and from anywhere. For this to happen, there needs to be a communication facility within signal range close by. A prime example of an operation that took advantage of this kind of information infrastructure for smart devices was Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb (June 2025), which targeted military bases deep within Russia’s vast territory. During the operation, drone operators in Ukraine carried out a simultaneous attack on multiple Russian military bases located as far as 1,000 to 5,000 kilometers away using 117 small drones. Known as Osa (Ukrainian for “wasp”), the drones destroyed numerous large bombers and other equipment (causing damage estimated in the region of 1.03 trillion yen). So, how were these small drones with a range of only 10 or so kilometers able to attack Russian military bases located thousands of kilometers away? The first step was to hide dozens of drones in the roofs of storage containers on the back of large trailers, which were driven to within a 10-kilometer radius of the targets by drivers recruited locally in Russia. It has been reported that the drones, equipped with the same type of SIM card used in cell phones, were capable of being remotely controlled from within Ukraine, located thousands of kilometers away, through control signals received via Russia’s mobile communication network (4G/LTE networks we use each day) (see figure). In addition, GNSS receivers were also necessary for enabling operators to track information on the drones’ positions in real time.

Remote control using standard mobile networks can be affected by traffic signal delays and radio interference. For this reason, drones were equipped with open-source flight control software available to the public (ArduPilot). This meant that drones could stably maintain autopilot operation along a pre-set flight path. In addition to flight stabilization, drones were also equipped with a “fail-safe” function that would activate in the event of traffic signal delays or a drop in communication. Since the drones were being flown over enemy territory, it was naturally anticipated that they would be subject to radio jamming from the Russian side. To combat this, drones were equipped with a pre-trained AI module. Consequently, even if a drone was no longer under an operator’s control, the module’s object recognition algorithm enabled autonomous terminal guidance, meaning that the drone could identify target vulnerabilities pre-trained in advance. A computer is required to run the AI module, so the Osa drones were equipped with Raspberry Pi 5s (commonly known in Japan as “Razu-pai”), a micro PC about the size of a business card. Operation Spiderweb was so named because it extended so far into Russia’s territory; places that were once believed to be beyond the reach of Ukraine’s offensive capabilities. What made this possible was the ability to use Russia’s domestic mobile communications network. This contrivance is achievable just by connecting a SIM card to a computer via USB memory (dongle). In fact, it has been reported that Russian Forces are also leveraging local mobile communication networks in the country’s almost daily airstrikes on Ukraine. With just a smartphone, we can enjoy the convenience of communication from anywhere in the world. In the same way, provided they can be covertly transported close to their target, small drones equipped with microcomputers and SIM cards can be used for sabotage operations, regardless of the origin or destination. With such examples of recent conflicts, it feels like we are being compelled to face this new reality. Regarding AI technologies, in January 2026, the U.S. DoW announced the Artificial Intelligence Acceleration Strategy. This strategy positions AI as a destructive technology and calls for all units to become AI-first combat units so as to enable the United States to rapidly achieve military-AI dominance. July 2025, China expressed its support for the Global South to help ensure universal access to AI.9 Various nations are also pursuing research and development related to quantum technologies, including quantum computing and quantum cryptographic communication. In 2018, the United States established the National Quantum Initiative (NQI) Act, and then the U.S. Senate introduced a bill to reauthorize it in January 2026. Based on the NQI Act, the federal government is promoting initiatives to pursue research and development related to quantum information science in cooperation with industries and academia. In connection with this, as phase 2 of the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI), DARPA has published research results on applications that could have an impact on the quantum advantage.10 In China, during a speech given by President Xi Jinping in June 2024, he stated that quantum technology is a Chinese priority and that the government is offering various kinds of large-scale support. In terms of quantum computing, China also introduced the Tianyan-504, a 504-qubit superconducting quantum computer, during the same year. Similarly, in terms of quantum cryptographic communication, China has already introduced its Quantum Experiments at Space Scale (QUESS) project, and, in 2027, the country plans to launch a high Earth orbit quantum communication satellite as part of its efforts to achieve long-range communication.11 Moving on, various nations are treating advanced semiconductors as important strategic goods. In July 2025, the United States established the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). This act is aimed at helping the United States to expand its semiconductor manufacturing base by expanding tax credits related to investment in semiconductor manufacturing facilities and equipment while also offering preferential treatment related to associated depreciation.12 Meanwhile, the European Union (EU) has enforced the European Chips Act, which positions semiconductors as essential for economics, social functions, defense, and national security. This act promotes capacity building aimed at enabling next-generation semiconductor technology design, manufacturing, and system integration.13 Furthermore, the foreign countries recognize the defense production base as an essential element of national defense and organize the systems to implement their policies through the publication of policy documents related to defense industry policies and the establishment of organizations in charge of the defense industry. They also take on a variety of initiatives such as supporting the participation of domestic companies in government programs and promoting exports to sustain and strengthen their defense production base.

Furthermore, the Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA) announced a policy to procure equipment taking into consideration the ripple effects for domestic industries, and a policy to promote cooperation between foreign companies and domestic companies as well as the use of domestic products by foreign companies.14 Each country exports military equipment strategically because trading equipment strengthens the relationship between two trading countries as well as the defense production and technological bases. For example, the United Kingdom announced in its Defence and Security Industrial Strategy (DSIS) that it would support exporting with cross-ministerial effort from different government offices, such as the Department for International Trade and the Home Office. The United States, Russia, Europe and China are still the top four in terms of export value of military equipment, while Australia formulated its export strategy.15 The ROK established an export support organization,16 and financially supports research and development for export. The first-ever DBP was formulated in 2022 in accordance with the NDS as a medium- to long-term plan that establishes the level of Japan’s defense capabilities, the JSDF’s structure which is based on the capability level roughly a decade into the future, and the total expenditures and the quantity of major equipment to be acquired over a five-year period. The future level of Japan’s defense capabilities had been previously established in the NDPG, while the total expenditures for the buildup of defense capability over a five-year period were set forth in the Medium Term Defense Program (MTDP), which was in turn based on the NDPG. However, the level of Japan’s defense capabilities as well as the total expenditures over a five-year period have now been integrated into a single, unified defense buildup program. Section 4 Revision of the Three Strategic Documents Compared with 2022, when the current National Security Strategy (NSS), National Defense Strategy (NDS), and Defense Buildup Program (DBP) (hereinafter the “Three Strategic Documents”) were formulated, changes in the security environment are accelerating across a wide range of fields. First, challenges to the free and open international order based on the rule of law are intensifying. Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, in particular, is an outrageous act that shakes the very foundation of the international order. Russia has continued its aggression against Ukraine for more than four years and has repeatedly engaged in words and actions that could be interpreted as threats involving nuclear weapons. Second, the Indo-Pacific is seeing China and North Korea further strengthen their military capabilities, along with closer cooperation between China and Russia and between Russia and North Korea. China has sustained high-level growth of its defense expenditure and engaged in broad, rapid improvement of its military power without sufficient transparency. Even since 2022, China’s growth in defense expenditure has far outpaced that of Japan. China also continues its attempts to unilaterally change the status quo in the East China Sea and South China Sea, including intrusions into Japanese territorial waters around the Senkaku Islands. Furthermore, in addition to the activities of two aircraft carriers in the Pacific Ocean in June 2025, China commissioned its third aircraft carrier “Fujian” in November of the same year, thereby steadily developing operational capabilities in distant waters and airspace. Additionally, although cooperation between China and Russia had already been observed before the formulation of the current Three Strategic Documents, in the three years since then, the two countries have steadily enhanced their strategic coordination. Military cooperation between Russia and North Korea has also deepened significantly.

Third, based on lessons learned from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, countries are hurrying to prepare to defend against new ways of warfare that include the mass operation of unmanned assets and possible prolonged wars. Regarding new ways of warfare, developments observed in Russia’s aggression against Ukraine include the mass deployment of diverse, inexpensive unmanned assets, as well as large-scale coordinated attacks that combine these assets with conventional shells and missiles. In addition, both sides are making full use of elements such as electronic warfare, AI, space, cyber, and information warfare, with the role of AI on the battlefield expanding particularly rapidly. Hybrid warfare combining these elements is becoming increasingly sophisticated. At the same time, in terms of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, alongside preparing for new ways of warfare, it has also been important to incorporate conventional equipment, including tanks, artillery, and trench warfare, thereby combining modern combat approaches with traditional ones. Moreover, equipment and tactics on the battlefield are being updated on an extremely short cycle compared to the past, and prompt, flexible technological innovations are becoming increasingly important. The fact that Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has continued for more than four years has also brought into sharp focus the importance of maintaining regular stockpiles and ensuring sustained response capabilities by further enhancing defense production and technological bases. Against this backdrop of accelerating changes in the security environment across various fields, the Government of Japan has brought forward the goal to achieve the defense budget level of 2% of GDP outlined in the current NSS in FY2025 with a combination of initial and supplementary budget. It is also conducting internal deliberations toward revising the Three Strategic Documents in 2026.

In addition, both sides are making full use of elements such as electronic warfare, AI, space, cyber, and information warfare, with the role of AI on the battlefield expanding particularly rapidly. Hybrid warfare combining these elements is becoming increasingly sophisticated. At the same time, in terms of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, alongside preparing for new ways of warfare, it has also been important to incorporate conventional equipment, including tanks, artillery, and trench warfare, thereby combining modern combat approaches with traditional ones. Moreover, equipment and tactics on the battlefield are being updated on an extremely short cycle compared to the past, and prompt, flexible technological innovations are becoming increasingly important. The fact that Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has continued for more than four years has also brought into sharp focus the importance of maintaining regular stockpiles and ensuring sustained response capabilities by further enhancing defense production and technological bases. Against this backdrop of accelerating changes in the security environment across various fields, the Government of Japan has brought forward the goal to achieve the defense budget level of 2% of GDP outlined in the current NSS in FY2025 with a combination of initial and supplementary budget. It is also conducting internal deliberations toward revising the Three Strategic Documents in 2026.

In addition, in order to weather the severe security environment surrounding Japan, it is important to respond by combining various policy means while strengthening Japan’s comprehensive national power, namely its diplomatic, defense, economic, technological, intelligence, and human resource capabilities. From this perspective, it has been deemed necessary not only to reinforce defense capabilities centered on the equipment and activities of the Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF), but also to organize cross-governmental initiatives, including maritime safety capabilities, research and development, public infrastructure development, cybersecurity, and international cooperation aimed at enhancing the deterrence capabilities of Japan and like-minded countries, and to examine how Japan’s security should be ensured from the standpoint of comprehensive national power, including the aforementioned initiatives. In doing so, it is also considered essential to strengthen technological capabilities and the industrial base through cross-governmental initiatives, while advancing economic security policies and fostering economic fundamentals so that Japan’s credibility and the lives of its citizens will not be harmed even in times of contingency. From this perspective, it has also been deemed necessary to examine both the reinforcement of deterrence and response capabilities and the appropriate approach to economic and fiscal policy. Based on this recognition, in April 2026, the Expert Panel to Consider National Security from the Perspective of Comprehensive National Power was established within the Cabinet Secretariat, and its inaugural meeting was held by the Prime Minister. The NDS comprehensively presents Japan’s defense objectives and approaches and the means by which Japan accomplishes those objectives. The outline is as follows. The most important responsibility of the Government of Japan is to resolutely defend to the end the lives of Japanese nationals and their peaceful livelihoods, as well as Japan’s territorial land, airspace, and waters. This constitutes the foundation of Japan’s national security. The international community, of which Japan is a member, is facing serious challenges, and has entered into a new era of crisis. One cannot rule out the possibility of serious events taking place in the future in the Indo-Pacific region, particularly in East Asia, that might shake the foundation of the stable postwar international order. Amid the most challenging and complex security environment since the start of the postwar period, Japan needs to directly face up to the grim reality and fundamentally reinforce its defense capabilities, with a focus on the capabilities of its opponents, to protect the lives and peaceful livelihoods of Japanese nationals. The military background for Russia’s aggression against Ukraine was that Ukraine did not possess sufficient capabilities to deter Russian aggression. There has also been a renewed recognition that no nation can possibly safeguard its security on its own and that cooperation with allies who possess the will and capability to jointly counter invasions is integral. Another point worth noting in this case is that a nation with powerful military capabilities had developed the intention to launch aggression at some point in time. While threats materialize through a combination of capability and intention, it is difficult to accurately ascertain another party’s intention from the outside. If a state’s decision-making process is opaque, there will always exist conditions under which threats may materialize. To protect one’s nation from such states, it is necessary to possess deterrence capabilities that alert others to the difficulty of making unilateral changes to the status quo by force, as well as to develop defense capabilities that are focused on the capabilities of opponents. (2) Second Approach: Joint Deterrence and Response by the Japan-U.S. Alliance The second approach is to further strengthen the Japan-U.S. Alliance. The Alliance with the United States is a key pillar of Japan’s security, and fundamental reinforcement of Japan’s defense capabilities will lead to more effective employment of U.S. capabilities and will further strengthen deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. Alliance. By demonstrating such joint resolve and capability, Japan and the United States will deter unilateral changes to the status quo by force and such attempts. In addition, if an invasion of Japan occurs, a Japan-U.S. joint response will disrupt the invasion. The first measure to this end is to strengthen Japan-U.S. joint deterrence and response capabilities. Japan’s NDS and the United States’ National Defense Strategy are well aligned in prioritizing the prevention of unilateral changes to the status quo by force through integrating all approaches and means. Accordingly, Japan will further deepen discussions with the United States on their respective roles, missions, and capabilities, and further reinforce Japan-U.S. joint deterrence capabilities in an integrated manner from the perspectives of enhancing readiness and resiliency, imposing a cost on opponents, and deterring invasion against Japan. The next is to reinforce alliance coordination functions. To conduct aligned joint responses of Japan and the United States, Japan will further upgrade the overall coordination functions centered on the Alliance Coordination Mechanism (ACM). In addition, in order to enhance collaboration with like-minded countries and others centered around the Japan-U.S. Alliance, Japan will promote closer operational coordination by leveraging the ACM and others. Furthermore, Japan will reinforce the foundational elements that support effective allied response in all phases, including information security, cybersecurity, and equipment and technology cooperation. The last is measures to support the stationing of the U.S. Forces Japan (USFJ). Japan will promote various measures to provide stable support for the stationing of the USFJ, such as steady implementation of the realignment of the USFJ and the initiatives to reinforce the readiness and resiliency of the USFJ, while optimizing the bilateral joint posture to respond to the severe security environment.

(3) Third Approach: Collaboration with Like-minded Countries and Others In order to respond to unilateral changes to the status quo by force and such attempts and to ensure Japan’s security, it is extremely important to reinforce collaboration with not only our ally but also as many countries as possible. From such a perspective, Japan will promote efforts that contribute to realizing a Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP). Moreover, Japan will proactively promote multilateral and multilayered defense cooperation and exchanges, taking into account regional characteristics and situations of various countries. While promoting collaboration with like-minded countries and others, Japan will pay attention to communication with China and Russia.

• Future of the JSDF The NDS lays out basic concepts with regard to a number of aspects, including the roles of each service of the JSDF in the seven priority areas of key capabilities for fundamental reinforcement of defense capabilities, the joint operations system based on these roles, and the development of the architecture of each service of the JSDF. Given the need for strategic and agile defense policy planning and making, the NDS states that the JSDF will fundamentally reinforce its functions concerned. Fig. II-2-2-2 (Concept for Developing the JSDF’s Architecture) See ARAKAKI Hiromu, Head, Global Security Division, National Institute for Defense Studies Deterrence is the act of ensuring that your opponent is prevented from taking a specific action. A key objective of Japan’s defense policy is to deter another party from unilaterally changing, or attempting to change, the status quo in the Indo-Pacific region through the use of force or coercion. Deterrence is important because when strengthened, it can prevent situations that would threaten or compromise Japan’s national security, including military invasions such as Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. There are two different approaches to deterrence: deterrence by denial and deterrence by punishment. Deterrence by denial involves preventing specific actions by an aggressor by making it impossible for them to successfully carry out those actions. For example, the act of possessing sufficient missile defense capabilities can convince an aggressor that it would not be able to achieve its objectives even with a missile attack, thereby deterring them from such actions.

In order to reinforce the infrastructure to support effective joint response capabilities, Japan will also reinforce efforts related to information security and cybersecurity, as well as equipment and technology cooperation. In addition, measures to support the stationing of the U.S. Forces Japan will be steadily implemented. Furthermore, in order to actively promote multi-faceted and multi-layered defense cooperation and exchanges in line with a Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP), Japan will further promote the development of institutional frameworks for various agreements, while also promoting initiatives including bilateral training and exercises as well as defense equipment and technology cooperation. Lastly, in fundamentally reinforcing defense capabilities, Japan will, while adhering to the scrap-and-build approach, optimize the JSDF’s organization and authorized strength as well as equipment. We will also further our ongoing efforts toward more efficient procurement, which have achieved significant cost reductions. In addition, to account for Japan’s aging population with a declining birth rate, Japan will robustly promote automation, labor-saving and optimization.

In addition, a new maritime transport unit will be established as a joint unit to improve the mobile deployment capabilities to the southwestern region.2

2 Joint Operations System of the JSDF In order to rapidly and effectively fulfill the duties of the JSDF, the MOD/JSDF has adopted the joint operations system in which the GSDF, the MSDF, and the ASDF are operated integrally. Furthermore, it works toward building an architecture that is capable of realizing cross-domain operations in domains such as space, cyberspace and the electromagnetic spectrum. The Japan Joint Staff is responsible for joint operations of the JSDF. It is headed by the Japan Joint Staff Chief of Staff, Japan Joint Staff, who develops a joint operations concept for JSDF operations, and centrally supports the Defense Minister on JSDF operations from a military expert’s perspective. The Defense Minister’s commands concerning the operations of the JSDF are delivered through the Japan Joint Staff Chief of Staff, Japan Joint Staff, and the Defense Minister’s orders concerning operations of the JSDF are executed by the Japan Joint Staff Chief of Staff, Japan Joint Staff. In doing this, the Defense Minister’s commands and orders are delivered through the Japan Joint Staff Chief of Staff, Japan Joint Staff not only in cases where two or more JSDF units are employed, but also in cases where a single JSDF unit is employed to respond. The Japan Joint Staff undertakes functions relating to the operations of the JSDF, while the Ground, Maritime and Air Staff Offices undertake functions for unit maintenance, such as personnel affairs, building-up defense capability, and education and training.

3 The JSDF Joint Operations Command The National Defense Strategy and the Defense Buildup Program call for the establishment of a permanent Joint Headquarters that facilitates the centralized command of the GSDF, the MSDF, and the ASDF units. The aim is to build a system that enables seamless cross-domain operations at all stages from peacetime to contingency, with the aim of strengthening the effectiveness of joint operations of all JSDF services. To this end, in March 2025, the MOD/ JSDF established the JSDF Joint Operations Command (JJOC) in Ichigaya as the permanent Joint Headquarters, which is headed by the Commander, JSDF Joint Operations Command (C-JJOC). Part II, Chapter 2, Section 2 (Outline of the National Defense Strategy (NDS)) Section 1 Responses to Invasion of Japan Surrounded by water and possessing an extensive coastline, Japan has numerous remote islands far from the main island, a vast exclusive economic zone (EEZ), and a broad continental shelf. It is a challenge to defend to the end the lives, physical well-being, and property of Japan’s people, as well as its territorial land, airspace, and waters, and abundant resources widely distributed in these areas. In addition, as Japan relies on overseas trade for much of its resources and food, it is essential to reinforce the free and open maritime order and ensure the freedom and safety of navigation and flight. In the event that deterrence fails and an invasion of Japan occurs, Japan will respond swiftly and flexibly according to the nature of the situation, taking primary responsibility for countering the invasion while receiving support from its ally. In such a situation, the Ministry of Defense (MOD)/JSDF will organically integrate operation capabilities across land, sea, and air domains, as well as space, cyberspace, and the electromagnetic spectrum under the centralized command of the JSDF Joint Operations Command (JJOC). By coordinating Ground Self-Defense Force (GSDF), Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF), and Air Self-Defense Force (ASDF) units to conduct joint operations, they will deter and eliminate any invasion of Japan. In addition, in the event of a large-scale terrorist attack or an attack on critical infrastructure that poses a serious threat to the lives, physical wellbeing, and property of Japanese citizens, Japan will cooperate with related organizations to take effective countermeasures.

1 Joint Operations of the JSDF In the event of an invasion of Japan, JSDF units work together through joint operations under the centralized command of the Commander, JSDF Joint Operations Command (C-JJOC). In particular, in modern warfare, it is important to organically integrate operation capabilities in the space, cyberspace, and the electromagnetic spectrum domains in addition to the land, sea, and air domains. It is also necessary to respond swiftly and appropriately to a wide range of situations that are neither peacetime nor contingency, such as gray zone situations, as well as to hybrid warfare. To that end, in accordance with the Minister’s orders on JSDF operations, the C-JJOC is eligible to command centrally major units of Ground, Maritime and Air Self-Defense Forces, as well as units operating in the Space and Cyber domains from peacetime, so that the JSDF will be able to establish a flexible defense posture quickly depending on the situation. The C-JJOC takes control of the overall operations, assigns missions to the necessary subordinate commanders, and allocates the required forces to each commander in order to conduct joint operations quickly and effectively. Major joint operations include amphibious operations to retake islands, operations utilizing counterstrike capabilities, and missile defense operations. For example, in amphibious operations, the GSDF amphibious units and MSDF transportation units work in coordination to land forces from the sea on remote islands. 6 Responses in the Electromagnetic Spectrum Domain Electromagnetic spectrum is used for command and communication, warning and surveillance, information gathering, precision guidance of missiles, and other purposes. Because the use of electromagnetic spectrum spans not only the land, sea, and air, but also outer space and cyberspace, in order to gain the advantage in operations across all domains, it is essential to secure superiority in the electromagnetic spectrum domain by strengthening electronic warfare capabilities and properly managing the electromagnetic spectrum. To this end, the JSDF conducts operations such as disrupting enemy use of electromagnetic spectrum and gathering and analyzing information related to electromagnetic spectrum through the use of the Network Electronic Warfare System (NEWS), multi-purpose EP-3 aircraft, and RC-2 signals intelligence aircraft. (3) Violations of Japanese Territorial Airspace by Chinese and Russian Aircraft In August 2024, one Chinese military Y-9 intelligence-gathering aircraft violated Japanese territorial airspace over the waters off the Danjo-gunto Islands (Nagasaki Prefecture). In the following month, one Russian military IL-38 patrol aircraft violated Japanese territorial airspace north of Rebun Island (Hokkaido) three times. The ASDF scrambled fighters to respond and used flares for the warning for the first time in countermeasures against airspace violation. Furthermore, in May 2025, a China Coast Guard helicopter, which took off from a China Coast Guard vessel that had intruded into Japanese territorial waters around the Senkaku Islands, violated Japan’s territorial airspace. JCG vessels issued warnings directing the helicopter to leave the airspace, while the ASDF scrambled fighters in response. This was the first case where a Chinese helicopter violated Japan’s territorial airspace. Such airspace violations not only constitute a serious infringement of Japan’s sovereignty but also pose a threat to the safety of its people and are utterly unacceptable. The Government of Japan lodged strong protests with the Chinese and Russian governments and firmly demanded the prevention of any recurrence. 3 Responses to Submarines Navigating Underwater in Japanese Territorial Waters (1) Basic Concept The Defense Minister will issue an order for Maritime Security Operations to deal with foreign submarines submerging in Japanese territorial waters.16 Such submarines will be required to navigate on the surface and show their flags17 in accordance with international law. If they do not comply, they will be required to leave Japanese territorial waters. (2) Response by the MOD/JSDF The MSDF conducts warning and surveillance of the waters surrounding Japan using patrol aircraft and vessels. When there is detection of submerged navigation by a foreign submarine within Japan’s territorial waters, it works to identify and track the submarine. It strives to maintain and enhance its capabilities to demonstrate its intent not to permit submerged navigation in violation of international law, as well as to respond even in shallow-water maritime areas. In 2004, the MSDF observed a submerged Chinese nuclear-powered submarine navigating under Japanese territorial waters around the Sakishima Islands (Okinawa Prefecture). In response to this incident, the MSDF issued an order for Maritime Security Operations and continued to track the submarine with MSDF vessels until it entered the high seas.18 The MOD/JSDF will continue to maintain a warning and surveillance posture and enhance response capabilities in order to address submerged navigation by foreign submarines within Japan’s territorial waters.

18 In addition, in 2018, underwater navigation by a Chinese submarine was confirmed for the first time through Japan’s contiguous zone in the vicinity of the Senkaku Islands. Furthermore, in 2021, a submarine presumed to be Chinese was confirmed to be navigating underwater through the Japanese contiguous zone in the vicinity of Amami Oshima Island (Kagoshima Prefecture), and warning and surveillance were carried out by MSDF destroyers and patrol aircraft.

This includes dissemination of disinformation and the spread of information aimed at eroding trust in government and dividing society. 6 Responses to Ship-to-Ship Transfers (1) Basic Concept Pursuant to UN Security Council Resolution 2375, UN member states are prohibited from engaging in ship-to-ship transfers of goods at sea involving North Korean vessels. This is intended to prevent North Korea from smuggling to evade sanctions imposed based on the UN Security Council resolution. Japan is committed to ensuring the effectiveness of the UN Security Council resolution by responding to ship-to-ship transfers in close cooperation not only with the United States and ROK but also with the international community, toward the realization of North Korea’s dismantlement of all weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missiles in a complete, verifiable and irreversible manner. (2) Response by the MOD/JSDF The MOD/JSDF has the MSDF gather information on vessels suspected of violating the UN Security Council resolution, and cooperates closely with relevant ministries and agencies, countries, and international organizations. As a result, during the period from 2018 onward to the end of March 2026, there has been confirmation of 24 cases of seaborne rendezvous between North Korean-flagged tankers and foreign-flagged tankers, etc. on the high seas of the East China Sea. Given the strong suspicions that these vessels engaged in ship-to-ship transfers, Japan shared the information with relevant countries and made public announcements on the subject. In recent years, there has been growing international concern about these illicit maritime activities, including ship-to-ship transfers with North Korean vessels. Since April 2018, the United States and the ROK, as well as Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, France, Germany, the Netherlands, and Italy, have dispatched naval vessels and aircraft in the waters surrounding Japan to conduct monitoring and surveillance activities. The MOD/JSDF will continue close cooperation with relevant countries to ensure the effectiveness of the UN Security Council resolution.

3 Points of the FY2026 Budget The MOD/JSDF has allocated approximately 277.3 billion yen in FY2026 for initiatives to enhance unmanned defense capabilities. Major projects include the reinforcement of intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting (ISRT) functions and the research and development of unmanned assets. In particular, the MOD/JSDF takes circumstances surrounding unmanned assets into consideration and plans to acquire a large number of low-cost UAVs, USVs and UUVs in an aim to establish the Synchronized, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defense (SHIELD) with unmanned assets within FY2027. Specifically, we will acquire first-person view (FPV) modular UAVs for short-range information gathering, small attack UAVs for searching for and identifying vehicles, craft and the like and attacking them by ramming, ship-launched UAVs for strike against enemy vessels, small multi-purpose USVs, ship-based small UAVs capable of improving the information gathering and warning and surveillance capabilities of surface vessels and of striking enemy vessels and so forth, land-launched anti-ship UAVs for long-range strike against surface vessels, radar site defense UAVs to defend radar sites against hostile UAVs and small multi-purpose UUVs for information gathering against naval assets. With these assets, we will establish a defense system capable of implementing asymmetric and multi-layered measures by fully leveraging the characteristics of unmanned assets. These include coordinating manned and unmanned assets to counter adversary invasion forces comprising highvalue assets such as surface vessels at sea, while integrating stand-off defense capabilities. In addition, along Japan’s coasts, we will utilize a large number of various unmanned assets to effectively counter landing forces. At the same time, the MOD/JSDF plans to acquire the MQ-9B (Sea Guardian) long-endurance unmanned aircraft to implement seamless ISRT. The MSDF will commence the operation of the MQ-9B in FY2028; however, as part of an early introduction project, two aircraft will be used at Kanoya Air Base starting in FY2027 for flights conducted by a private company. At the same time, in order to further enhance the effectiveness of measures against airspace violations, including from a cost-effectiveness perspective, we will utilize this early introduction project to examine operational guidelines necessary for the use of long-endurance unmanned aircraft in such measures.

2 Cyber Domain (1) Basic Concept Cyberspace, as used on the Internet and other platforms, encompasses a variety of services and communities, which has become an indispensable part of citizen’s daily lives. Furthermore, it is a critical infrastructure even for military purposes including command and control and organization’s network. It is also a vital domain for the national defense to execute cross-domain operations. Therefore, cyberattacks that compromise information assets and networks in cyberspace can have a significant impact on society and pose serious threats to national security. In the cyber domain, it is important to gather and share information from peacetime to contingencies through cooperation with other countries, relevant ministries and agencies and the private-sectors, as well as to strengthen Japan’s overall response capabilities in the field of cybersecurity. In coordination with the whole-of-government efforts in the field of cybersecurity, the MOD/JSDF will promote initiatives that strengthen cooperation with related ministries and agencies, critical infrastructure operators and the defense industry, while enhancing the level of its cybersecurity. Section 3-3 (Cybersecurity), Part I, Chapter 4, Section 3-2 (Trends in Space Domain)

(2) Initiatives of the MOD/JSDF The MOD/JSDF will coordinate with whole-of-government initiatives in the field of cybersecurity, including active cyber defense, even in peacetime, with a view to ensuring mission assurance in the event of a contingency. In doing so, the MOD/JSDF will establish a posture where persistent risk management is implemented, primarily on information and other systems critical in conducting joint operations. We will also leverage external human resources to further enhance our cybersecurity. The MOD/JSDF will protect its information systems and the like from all cyber threats with its high level of cybersecurity capabilities and also will use these capabilities to strengthen the national cybersecurity as a whole.

2025. Under this legislation, the JSDF has been granted the legal authority to conduct “Remote Access and Neutralization Measures” to prevent damage from certain serious cyberattacks that pose security concerns to JSDF command, control, and information systems, as well as to government and core infrastructure. The ability to respond to cyberattacks that fall short of armed attack during peacetime significantly contributes to the JSDF’s mission assurance in a contingency and represents a major step toward improving Japan’s overall cyber response capabilities. Furthermore, the MOD/JSDF will contribute to ensuring cybersecurity across Japan by supporting government-wide initiatives prescribed in the Cyber Response Capability Strengthening Act, including “Enhancement of Public Private Partnership” and “Utilizing I.D.C. (Information and Data under Communications).” These efforts will also lead to protecting the economic activities of Japanese citizens. With a view to ensuring the successful execution of missions under any circumstances, the MOD/JSDF will continue to strengthen its cyber defense capability to respond seamlessly to increasingly sophisticated and advanced cyber threats, including expanding the organizational structure of the JSDF Cyber Defense Command, which is responsible for the new missions related to active cyber defense. Defense Minister Koizumi and the Commander of the JSDF Cyber Defense Command Commentary New Missions in Cyberspace

The ability to respond to cyberattacks that fall short of armed attack during peacetime significantly contributes to the JSDF’s mission assurance in a contingency and represents a major step toward improving Japan’s overall cyber response capabilities. Furthermore, the MOD/JSDF will contribute to ensuring cybersecurity across Japan by supporting government-wide initiatives prescribed in the Cyber Response Capability Strengthening Act, including “Enhancement of Public Private Partnership” and “Utilizing I.D.C. (Information and Data under Communications).” These efforts will also lead to protecting the economic activities of Japanese citizens. With a view to ensuring the successful execution of missions under any circumstances, the MOD/JSDF will continue to strengthen its cyber defense capability to respond seamlessly to increasingly sophisticated and advanced cyber threats, including expanding the organizational structure of the JSDF Cyber Defense Command, which is responsible for the new missions related to active cyber defense. skills. The MOD/JSDF will continue its efforts to recruit and develop talented cyber workforce toward the fundamental reinforcement of its cyber defense capabilities. Part V, Chapter 2, Section 2-2 (Initiatives to Reinforce the Human Resource Base) b. Security Enhancement As cyberattacks and other threats are becoming more advanced and sophisticated every day, MOD/JSDF has shifted its approach to information system security measures from temporary “risk elimination” to continuous “risk management,” and has introduced the Risk Management Framework (RMF),which continuously analyzes and evaluates risks and implements necessary security measures even after the start of the information system operation. Additionally, the MOD/JSDF will shift away from the traditional mindset that perimeter security16 is sufficient to maintain the safety of the organization’s network, and will promote the introduction of the new security controls based on the “Zero Trust” concept.17 These will improve the cybersecurity level of the MOD/JSDF and establish a posture that can safeguard information assets against any intrusion into the organization’s network. In order to strengthen the protection posture of information systems, the MOD/JSDF will develop a cloud system that integrates and standardizes the JSDF systems, implement centralized cybersecurity measures, improve defense posture of equipment and facility infrastructure systems, enhance the threat hunting function that continuously hunts for and detects potential internal threats based on the assumption that threats have already penetrated inside the network, and develop the support system by making use of AI to enable rapid situational awareness and response to cyberattacks. In addition, defense-related companies are upgrading their information systems and implementing other security control measures in accordance with the Standards on Cybersecurity Measures for Defense Industry. Fig. III-1-2-11 (Risk Management Framework (image)), Part IV, Chapter 2, Section 1-2-4 (Strengthening Defense Industrial Security)

Education and Research To fundamentally strengthen cyber defense capabilities, it is necessary to develop workforce that possess sophisticated knowledge and skills about cybersecurity, including the expansion of education and the utilization of knowledge from private sectors. In this context, the MOD/JSDF has developed cyber workforce through continuous and by stages assignment to the cyber units that are in charge of responding to cyberattacks, and by providing them with both in-house and external education. Regarding education, the GSDF System and Signal/Cyber School has provided cybersecurity education as a common program across all JSDF services. Personnel have been dispatched to the U.S. National Defense University’s College of Information and Cyberspace International Fellows and the U.S. Army’s Coalition Cyber Operations Planner course, and the specialized course in system and cyber engineering has been established at the GSDF High Technical School. At the National Defense Academy, the Department of Information Engineering has been reorganized into the Faculty of Cyber and Information Engineering. In terms of research, the MOD/JSDF is strengthening the research organization of the Cyber Security Division in the National Institute for Defense Studies and Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency’s Future Capabilities See See REFERENCE: The MOD/JSDF’s “I Want to Know About This!”: JSDF Measures against Cyber Attacks URL: https://www.mod.go.jp/j/press/shiritai/cyber/index.html

Development Center18 is conducting research into cyber protection technology for equipment systems to prevent the spread of damage caused by cyberattacks and enable various equipment systems to remain in operation in the event of cyberattacks. (3) Cooperation with Private Companies and Other Countries, and Others To respond to cyberattacks in a swift and appropriate manner, it is necessary to keep abreast of the latest information, including risks related to cybersecurity, countermeasures and technological trends, through cooperation with private companies, and strategic talks, joint training and other opportunities with our ally and other parties. For this purpose, the MOD/JSDF will effectively cooperate with private companies, and foreign countries, including the United States. a. Cooperation with Private Companies and Others Through the Cyber Defense Council (CDC), whose members consist of around ten companies in the defense industry with a strong interest in cybersecurity, we are sharing information among companies in the defense industry, aggregating information, and making efforts to grasp the overall picture of cyberattacks. In addition, joint training with the defense industry is conducted once a year to enhance the cyberattack response capabilities of both the MOD/JSDF and the defense industry. b. Cooperation with the United States Japan is committed to further strengthening information sharing and enhancing efforts related to information security and cybersecurity with the United States. The Cyber Defense Policy Working Group (CDPWG) serves as a framework for policy consultations between defense authorities of the two countries. In this framework, specialized and specific considerations and exchange of views were conducted on a wide range of fields, such as the promotion of cyber policy consultations and closer information sharing. In the Guidelines for Japan-U.S. Defense Cooperation (Guidelines) and the CDPWG Joint Statement, the governments of Japan and the United States agreed to establish a prompt and appropriate information sharing structure, protect critical infrastructure essential to ensure mission assurance of the JSDF and U.S. Forces, ensure the resiliency of their respective networks and systems, and organize educational exchanges and conduct joint exercises. In addition, at the Japan-U.S. “2+2” meeting in 2019,

c. Cooperation with Like-Minded Countries, Etc. Japan will enhance its partnership and cooperation with like-minded countries and other partners through sharing views on threat awareness, exchanging views on response to cyberattacks, and participating in multilateral exercises. The MOD has participated in the Japan-NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) Cyber Dialogue, a whole-of-government framework and organized the Japan-NATO Cyber Defense Expert Staff Talks to exchange opinions on various issues related to cyberspace among defense authorities. Besides, the MOD has participated in the International Conference on Cyber Conflict (CyCon) hosted by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) established in Estonia. The MOD has been dispatching personnel to the CCDCOE since 2019. In addition, Japan has held cyber dialogues between defense authorities of Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany and France. Japan also provides capacity building support in the field of cybersecurity for ASEAN countries. With the aim of strengthening the JSDF’s cyber domain capabilities and cooperation with other countries, Japan has been participating in training and exercises. In FY2025, Japan took part in “Locked Shields 2025,” a multilateral cyber defense exercise hosted by CCDCOE in May, as a joint Japan-Australia team. Japan has been an official participant in this exercise since 2021, making this its fifth participation. The MOD has been dispatching personnel to the CCDCOE since 2019. In addition, Japan has held cyber dialogues between defense authorities of Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany and France. Japan also provides capacity building support in the field of cybersecurity for ASEAN countries. With the aim of strengthening the JSDF’s cyber domain capabilities and cooperation with other countries, Japan has been participating in training and exercises. In FY2025, Japan took part in “Locked Shields 2025,” a multilateral cyber defense exercise hosted by CCDCOE in May, as a joint Japan-Australia team. Japan has been an official participant in this exercise since 2021, making this its fifth participation. For the MOD/JSDF, incorporating innovative civilian technologies in the ICT field is an urgent priority in order to take into account these ways of warfare and achieve new ways of defense. With this pressing issue in mind, the “Next-Generation Information and Communication Strategy of the Ministry of Defense” was formulated in July 2025 to clarify the MOD/JSDF’s ICT approach and deepen public-private partnership while enhancing predictability for private-sector companies. The strategy calls for building a New Defense Information Infrastructure, with a view to developing communications networks and data infrastructure in an integrated manner for achieving decision-making superiority. Specifically, it aims to build a mesh network utilizing a variety of communication pathways, including optical technologies, thereby enabling diverse combinations of sensors and shooters. This approach will allow for flexible operations tailored to the battlespace, as well as a robust network capable of maintaining connectivity even if portions are disrupted. In addition, to build data infrastructure that leverages AI and enables appropriate and prompt processing and analysis of the enormous volumes of data transmitted through these networks, the MOD plans to move beyond the current on-premises-centric infrastructure and transition toward a hybrid cloud that integrates commercial cloud services. The realization of these initiatives will require cooperation with private-sector companies and other partners. By strengthening defense capabilities using cutting-edge civilian technologies, we also seek to contribute to technological advancement in the civilian sector, creating a virtuous cycle between defense capabilities and economic strength, where civilian technologies support defense capabilities, which will lead to the further reinforcement of defense capabilities. In recent years, defense attachés have been covering a wide range of operations, such as defense exchanges with countries of their assignment, coordination on defense equipment and technology cooperation, and arrangements for receiving Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF) aircraft for missions and activities. Their roles are expanding year by year. The security environment surrounding Japan is changing at a remarkable pace. In order to ensure the defense of Japan in this security environment, constant gathering of information is essential. Furthermore, it is necessary to make consistent effort to strengthen cooperation with countries that share our values, and with countries we should align our values with in the future. Therefore, the MOD has been enhancing its defense attachés dispatch structure. Recently, the MOD has newly dispatched/increased defense attachés to/in Africa, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, and regions along the coast of the South China Sea. Currently, a total of 83 defense attachés are dispatched to 54 embassies and 2 missions (about 1.7 times as many compared to 49 defense attachés in FY2013). When various emergencies arise in the places of assignment, international disaster relief activities or the transportation of overseas Japanese nationals may be anticipated. In such cases, timely information provided by defense attachés, such as information on local conditions or the assessments of military attachés of other countries, serves as a valuable source of information that is very difficult to obtain through other channels. IYONO Minako, Lieutenant Colonel (GSDF), Defense Attaché to Estonia Since assuming my post as Japan’s first defense attaché to Estonia, I have enjoyed heartwarming exchanges with Estonian defense officials and feel that the bonds between our two countries have steadily grown stronger with each passing day. Estonia, the northernmost of the three Baltic states and a digitally advanced nation, plays a leading role in multilateral cybersecurity cooperation. Drawing upon my experience as a cyber unit commander, I am working to advance defense cooperation between our two countries. In Estonia, which shares a direct border with Russia, airspace violations and cross-border incidents never cease, and this has created strong vigilance toward Russian aggression. I have observed firsthand the activities of the Estonian Defence League, in which defense conscious citizens conduct national defense. I have also seen the installation of the “Baltic Defence Line” that includes 600 fortified defensive positions, as well as the building of the “Drone Wall.” These experiences have renewed my resolve to fulfill my mission. The Estonian people regard the situation in Ukraine as their own matter. Their attempt to confront Russia with ingenuity and advanced technology while adapting to the rapidly changing battlefield is both highly inspiring and instructive for me, an engineering officer engaged in research and development. With gratitude for the tremendous support of my husband, a Ground Self-Defense Force personnel who is taking spouse-accompaniment leave, and for our three children’s healthy growth in this country, I remain committed to my mission, determined to apply the insights I gained at the forefront to strengthen Japan’s security. The author observing a multilateral exercise with NATO WATANABE Naoto, Captain (MSDF), Defense Attaché to Russia I was assigned to Moscow in January 2025, nearly three years after the start of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.

Estonia, the northernmost of the three Baltic states and a digitally advanced nation, plays a leading role in multilateral cybersecurity cooperation. Drawing upon my experience as a cyber unit commander, I am working to advance defense cooperation between our two countries. In Estonia, which shares a direct border with Russia, airspace violations and cross-border incidents never cease, and this has created strong vigilance toward Russian aggression. I have observed firsthand the activities of the Estonian Defence League, in which defense conscious citizens conduct national defense. I have also seen the installation of the “Baltic Defence Line” that includes 600 fortified defensive positions, as well as the building of the “Drone Wall.” These experiences have renewed my resolve to fulfill my mission. The Estonian people regard the situation in Ukraine as their own matter. Their attempt to confront Russia with ingenuity and advanced technology while adapting to the rapidly changing battlefield is both highly inspiring and instructive for me, an engineering officer engaged in research and development. With gratitude for the tremendous support of my husband, a Ground Self-Defense Force personnel who is taking spouse-accompaniment leave, and for our three children’s healthy growth in this country, I remain committed to my mission, determined to apply the insights I gained at the forefront to strengthen Japan’s security. Here in Moscow, I observe the developments in Russia, a vast nation that borders both Japan and Europe, and witness firsthand particularly the actions of Russia and the international community surrounding the aggression against Ukraine. I am reminded daily of the complex and severe realities of the international situation. Contrary to reports of extensive damage across Ukraine resulting from Russian UAV and missile strikes, the damage within Russia is concentrated in areas near the Ukrainian border. While there have been occasional instances of UAVs reaching the vicinity of Moscow, the situation in the Russian capital is generally stable. In the aggression against Ukraine, the nature of the battlefield has transformed dramatically through the evolution of unmanned assets, which has profoundly impacted military developments around the world. As Russia continues its aggression, it has pursued improvements in strategic weapons capabilities and the development of new weapons, including hypersonic missiles. Against the backdrop of melting Arctic sea ice, Russia has also been actively promoting the development of the Northern Sea Route. A defense attaché’s role extends beyond gathering and analyzing information on the military activities of the host nation. It also includes facilitating communication between the two countries to prevent unexpected circumstances. Defense attachés have a significant role to play in a challenging environment, and I will continue to carry out my mission with a strong sense of vigilance. b. Defense Intelligence Headquarters The Defense Intelligence Headquarters (DIH) is the central intelligence agency of the MOD and the largest intelligence organization in Japan. The DIH gathers various intelligence and analyzes international and military situations and other matters related to Japan’s swiftly changing security environment. In addition to information gathering and analysis, the DIH is also considered in the NDS to play a central role in responding to integrated information warfare for the defense of Japan and is to fundamentally strengthen the capabilities to gather and analyze information on international military situations and other issues. The DIH is an organization consisting of the uniformed JSDF personnel from GSDF, MSDF, and ASDF and administrative and technical officials (specialized in language, technology, administration or general office work). The JSDF personnel use the experience and knowledge gained in their own unit, etc., whereas administrative/technical officials use their expert knowledge in language, technology and other fields, to work together for their mission. Specifically, they conduct comprehensive analysis from diverse perspectives, including military, political, and economic factors, based on information received from a wide range of sources including SIGINT, IMINT, GIOINT, OSINT (newspapers, internet, etc.) and opinion exchange with relevant parties. The DIH is also strengthening information gathering and analyzing functions in space, cyberspace and electromagnetic spectrum domains. For example, it conducts the gathering and analysis of necessary information regarding trends in

24 Act on the Protection of Specially Designated Secrets threats in cyberspace through such means as gathering OSINT and exchanging information with other countries. Results of the DIH’s intelligence service are provided as analysis products to the Prime Minister, the Defense Minister, the National Security Secretariat established within the Cabinet Secretariat, the Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office, as well as GSDF, MSDF and ASDF units in a timely and appropriate manner to support policy decision and unit operation. The DIH also actively exchanges information with relevant ministries and agencies and foreign counterparts. c. Initiatives for Information Security The MOD/JSDF has been working to ensure a system necessary for information security in accordance with the Act on the Protection of Specially Designated Secrets24 and other relevant laws, in cooperation with relevant ministries, agencies and bureaus, to appropriately protect various types of classified information. However, in December 2022, the MOD announced the incident where the then Commander of the MSDF Fleet Intelligence Command intentionally disclosed specially designated secrets and other information without authorization to his then superior, who was not eligible to handle classified information. In April, July and December 2024 and December 2025, the MOD announced information security incidents including the incident where personnel who had not undergone the security clearance assessment for handling specially designated secrets were designated as personnel with eligible access and allowed to actually handle such classified information. TATSUKAWA Ryo, Colonel (ASDF), Defense Attaché to Qatar Last year, Qatar’s Al Udeid Air Base, located approximately 50 kilometers west of Doha, the capital, was attacked by Iran in June, and a Hamas office in central Doha was attacked by Israel in September. In late February of this year, Qatar once again came under attack, causing damage across a wider area than before. Qatar is facing the most unprecedented security challenge since gaining independence and statehood in 1971.

b. Initiatives of the MOD/JSDF With the increasingly severe security environment and the rapid progress of technological innovation, including information technology (IT), it is important to achieve uniquely Japanese new ways of defense based on “new ways of warfare,” including integrated information warfare with special regard to the cognitive dimension. In particular, considering Japan’s national defense in light of the situation involving Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and the conflict between Israel and Palestinian armed groups, it is urgent to enhance our response to integrated information warfare with special regard to the cognitive dimension. This includes the ability to detect and analyze disinformation, as well as to swiftly and strategically disseminate appropriate information. In line with the MOD/JSDF’s policy to develop information capabilities that can reliably respond to integrated information warfare with special regard to the cognitive dimension by 2027, the GSDF Information Operations Command and the MSDF Information Warfare Command were established in FY2025. In addition, the MOD/JSDF is taking the necessary measures at every stage of information collection, analysis, and dissemination. These measures include the promotion of the establishment of functions for automatically gathering information from social media and other sources to assess the authenticity of information provided by various countries, while policy, operational and intelligence divisions are working in close coordination with each other. Moreover, we will strive to further strengthen Japan’s capabilities in light of trends in the international community by sharing information and conducting joint training with our ally, like-minded countries, and others. In addition to the various measures mentioned above, to ensure that JSDF personnel, who are the core element of our defense capability, are not misled by disinformation and prevented from making appropriate decisions and taking precise actions, each personnel member must understand the dangers of disinformation and develop an attitude that enables them to calmly perceive and objectively analyze matters on a daily basis. To that end, efforts will be made to further strengthen the organizational structure to execute information security related duties by promoting the acquisition of necessary competencies and improving cyber and media literacy through educational opportunities and other means. Additionally, the MOD/JSDF will work to disseminate accurate information by, for example, publicly disclosing certain cases of disinformation about them originating from foreign sources. No contracts are entered into between the MOD and the relevant ministries and agencies/ national research and development agencies. In addition, the research findings are publicized (the fact that the research becomes a matching project in itself does not restrict the publication of research findings). The Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF) must be strong in order to protect Japan, but national defense cannot be achieved without a whole-of-country approach. For this reason, besides the fundamental reinforcement of its defense capabilities, Japan is developing a defense architecture for the whole country by integrating its national power, which includes its diplomatic, intelligence, economic, and technological capabilities, and systematically combining various policy means. In doing so, it is essential to strengthen such whole-of-government efforts while breaking down the stove-piping approach within the Government. From this perspective, the National Security Strategy (NSS) calls for advancing the reinforcement of Japan’s comprehensive defense architecture as a complementary initiative to the fundamental reinforcement of its defense capabilities. It sets forth promotion of efforts in four areas: (1) research and development (R&D), (2) public infrastructure development, (3) cybersecurity and (4) international cooperation to enhance the deterrence capabilities of Japan and like-minded countries. In addition to these initiatives, continuous peacetime monitoring and surveillance, initiatives related to the space domain, and responses to large-scale disasters and the rescue and transportation of Japanese nationals and others overseas are also efforts that require the full power of the nation. Thus, the Ministry of Defense (MOD)/ JSDF will reinforce the defense architecture of the whole country while responding to the aforementioned efforts in close cooperation with relevant ministries and agencies, local governments, and others.

3 Cybersecurity

1 The Whole-of-Government Approach Based on the National Security Strategy (NSS), the government of Japan as a whole intends to strengthen its response capabilities in the field of cybersecurity equal to or surpassing the level of leading Western countries, including the introduction of active cyber defense in cases where there is a possibility of serious cyberattacks that cause national security concerns even if they do not amount to an armed attack. In May 2025, the Cyber Response Capability Strengthening Act and Necessary Arrangement of Relevant Acts3 were enacted by the Diet based on recommendations from an expert panel aimed at introducing active cyber defense. These recommendations included “Enhancement of Public Private Partnership,” such as the enhancement of information sharing between Government and private companies in the event of cyberattacks and other emergencies; “Utilizing I.D.C. (Information and Data under Communications),” encompassing the analysis of I.D.C. to understand the nature of cyberattacks; and “Remote Access and Neutralization Measures,” such as accessing the source of a cyberattack to prevent damage when an attack occurs. In July 2025, following the enactment of the Cyber Response Capability Strengthening Act and other legislation, the National center of Incident readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity (NISC) was reorganized, and the National Cybersecurity Office (NCO), headed by the National Cyber Director, was established. In addition to serving as the secretariat for the Cybersecurity Strategic Headquarters, the NCO monitors and analyzes unlawful activities targeting the information systems of various government agencies, provides advice, conducts audits, and is responsible for the overall coordination of cybersecurity enforcement.

Currently, we are confronted with global security challenges that are difficult for any single country to tackle alone, including risks concerning stable use of the seas, outer space and cyberspace, acts of piracy, proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missiles, and international terrorism, and it is important for countries to work together from peacetime. The strong bonds forged between Japan and the United States are also playing an important role in the efforts implemented by Japan to effectively respond to such challenges. In particular, under the Japan-U.S. Security Arrangements, the JSDF and the U.S. Forces are working together in peacetime in a variety of areas to strengthen their cooperation. This close coordination lays the foundation for various forms of global collaboration such as counter-piracy, undertaken by the JSDF and the U.S. Forces, and leads to enhancement of the operational effectiveness of the Japan-U.S. Security Arrangements. The peace and prosperity of the international community are closely linked to those of Japan. Accordingly, by advancing initiatives for resolving global issues in cooperation with the United States, which has remarkable operational capabilities, Japan will be able to further ensure its security and prosperity.

2 Content of the Guidelines for Japan-U.S. Defense Cooperation The “Guidelines for Japan-U.S. Defense Cooperation” (the Guidelines), which show the general outline and policy direction of roles and cooperation between Japan and the United States, were formulated in 1978, and successively revised in 1997 and 2015. The current Guidelines, which were revised in 2015, update the general framework and policy direction for the roles and missions of the two countries, as well as modernizing the Alliance. The Guidelines also manifest a strategic vision for a more robust Alliance and greater shared responsibilities by enhancing its deterrence and response capabilities in all phases, from peacetime to contingencies. The Guidelines define that Japan and the United States will work on a variety of measures during peacetime, including intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) activities, air and missile defense, maritime security, training and exercises, asset protection, and logistics support, and cooperate in such activities as response to a large-scale disaster in Japan to seamlessly ensure Japan’s peace and security. For regional and global peace and security, the Guidelines also require both countries: to cooperate in international activities and promote and improve trilateral and multilateral cooperation; to cooperate on space and cyberspace; and to develop and enhance bilateral enterprise through defense equipment and technology cooperation as well as intelligence cooperation and information security for further improving the effectiveness of bilateral cooperation. 2 Recent Japan-U.S. Defense Ministerial Meetings In May 2025, then Defense Minister Nakatani held a Japan-U.S. Defense Ministerial Meeting with U.S. Secretary of War Hegseth in Singapore. Based on their exchange at the Japan-U.S. Defense Ministerial Meeting in March 2025, the Ministers discussed Japan-U.S. defense cooperation initiatives, including the following recent developments. The Ministers confirmed that they will coordinate closely together to align the strategic priorities of both countries as the U.S. Department of War formulates a new National Defense Strategy. They also concurred to further strengthen bilateral cooperation in the cyber domain. In October 2025, Defense Minister Koizumi held a Japan-U.S. Defense Ministerial Meeting with U.S. Secretary of War Hegseth at the MOD. The Ministers candidly exchanged and shared their views on the increasingly severe security situation in the Indo-Pacific, and confirmed that they will further strengthen the Alliance capabilities to deter and respond. Specifically, (1) with regard to upgrading respective command and control frameworks, the Ministers welcomed tangible progress in the upgrade of U.S. Forces Japan and on initiatives by the JSDF Joint Operations Command, and confirmed their intention to further enhance effective bilateral cooperation from peacetime to contingency; (2) the Ministers welcomed the progress and confirmed on expansion of bilateral joint presence in the southwestern region of Japan as one of the highest priorities of the Alliance, including enhancement of more advanced and realistic bilateral training across Japan, and in the southwestern region in particular; and (3) with regard to defense equipment and technology cooperation, the Ministers recognized that strengthening the defense production and technological base is a shared challenge, and reaffirmed the importance of mutually complementing the defense production and technological bases of Japan and the United States. The Ministers welcomed the progress under Defense Industrial Cooperation, Acquisition, and Sustainment (DICAS), including exploring missile co-production such as Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles (AMRAAM) and co-sustainment of vessels and aircraft of U.S. forces, and confirmed to further advance these initiatives; and (4) in addition, the Ministers concurred that they will continue to advance multilateral cooperation including information sharing and operational collaboration with regional partners, namely Australia, the Republic of Korea and the Philippines, with Japan and the U.S. at the center of such cooperation.
