2 Deterrent measures that can be flexibly selected Japan’s National Defense Strategy (NDS) and the United States’ National Defense Strategy are well aligned in prioritizing the prevention of unilateral changes to the status quo by force through integrating all approaches and means. Accordingly, from the viewpoint of reinforcing readiness and resiliency, imposing costs on opponents, and deterring invasion against Japan, Japan will further deepen discussion with the United States on their respective roles, missions, and capabilities, and further reinforce the joint deterrence capabilities of both countries in an integrated manner.1 Specifically, Japan will further deepen cooperation with the United States to smoothly implement allied cross-domain operations including space, cyber and the electromagnetic domains, as well as to improve interoperability. Regarding Japan’s counterstrike capabilities, Japan will work with the United States to establish a cooperative posture, including information gathering, in order to employ their joint capabilities more effectively. Furthermore, the bilateral collaboration will be reinforced in such areas as air-defense; anti-surface warfare; anti-submarine warfare; mine warfare; amphibious operations; airborne operations; intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting (ISRT); protection of assets and facilities; and logistics support. In order to effectively realize the division of roles and missions between Japan and the United States in light of the fundamental reinforcement of Japan’s defense capabilities, Japan will ensure close operational cooperation with the United States through Japan-U.S. bilateral planning. In addition, Japan will work to improve allied response capabilities, including readiness and interoperability of the Alliance, through more advanced and practical exercises and training. Furthermore, in order to ensure that U.S. extended deterrence with nuclear deterrence at its core remains credible and resilient, Japan will further actively engage in and deepen bilateral discussions on extended deterrence, including those at the ministerial level.

In 2015, based on the “Guidelines for Japan-U.S. Defense Cooperation” (“the Guidelines” hereafter), the Japanese and U.S. governments established the Alliance Coordination Mechanism (ACM) in order to seamlessly and effectively implement a well-aligned Japan-U.S. response to address any situation that affects Japan’s peace and security or any other situation that may require an Alliance response. Based on the framework shown in Fig. III-2-3-1, the ACM coordinates policy and operational aspects related to activities conducted by the Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF) and the U.S. Forces in all phases from peacetime to contingencies. This mechanism also contributes to timely information sharing as well as to the development and maintenance of common situational awareness. The characteristics of the mechanism include that (1) it is the standing mechanism utilizable from peacetime; (2) it can be utilized for large-scale disasters in Japan as well as for cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region and globally; and (3) it enables whole-of-government coordination while ensuring the involvement of relevant Japanese and U.S. organizations. These characteristics enable the Japanese and U.S. governments to respond appropriately and promptly when the need for coordination arises. Since the establishment of the ACM, Japan and the United States have been utilizing the ACM to coordinate closely, including in response to the 2016 Kumamoto Earthquake1 and the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake,2 the ballistic missile launches by North Korea, and Chinese activities in the waters and airspace around the Senkaku Islands. The National Defense Strategy of Japan (NDS) calls for Japan to further upgrade the overall coordination functions between Japan and the United States centered on the ACM and to promote closer operational coordination by leveraging the ACM and others to enhance collaboration with like-minded countries and others centered around the Japan-U.S. Alliance. In situations where the need for international cooperation in the security and defense fields is increasing in an unprecedented manner, the Ministry of Defense/Japan Self-Defense Forces (MOD/JSDF) is required to actively contribute to ensuring the security of Japan, the peace and stability of the region and the peace, stability and prosperity of the entire international community. The first defense objective of the National Defense Strategy of Japan (NDS) is to shape a security environment that does not tolerate unilateral changes to the status quo by force, in cooperation with Japan’s ally, like-minded countries and others. Therefore, the NDS calls for Japan to promote efforts that contribute to realizing a Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) from the perspective that it is extremely important to reinforce collaboration with not only its ally but also as many countries as possible. In addition, it is essential to deepen cooperation and coordination with its ally and like-minded countries to counter unilateral changes to the status quo by force and such attempts and to safeguard the security environment of Japan. Furthermore, Japan will also more actively advance its efforts to solve global security issues and others, including securing the freedom and safety of maritime navigation and overflight, coordination and cooperation with relevant countries in relation to the use of the space and cyber domains, international peace cooperation activities, cooperation on climate change and maritime security, arms control and disarmament and non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. For the implementation of these efforts, Japan will, while placing the Japan-U.S. Alliance as the key pillar of its security policy, proactively promote multilateral and multilayered defense cooperation and exchanges, taking into account characteristics of the region as well as situation of each country.

While multilateral frameworks such as the African Union (AU) are making positive efforts toward regional peace and stability, challenges such as serious inequality and poverty and political instability remain. Moreover, in recent years, the influences of complex crises consisting of the pandemic and Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, and those of climate change (natural disasters, food crises, etc.), continue. In the face of these global challenges, cooperation with African countries is becoming increasingly important to maintain a free and open international order. The MOD/JSDF is conducting activities to contribute to peace and stability in Africa, by such means as international peace cooperation activities in the African region and counter-piracy activities off the coast of Somalia and in the Gulf of Aden based on the JSDF facility in Djibouti, and sending JSDF personnel as instructors to PKO training centers in Africa to support African countries’ self-help efforts in peacekeeping operations. 2025 November Japan-China Field Officer Exchange Program conducted by the Sasakawa Peace Foundation Interactions between Japanese and Chinese defense authorities include the Japan-China Security Dialogue, consultations between Japanese and Chinese defense authorities, and high-level consultations on maritime affairs by Japan and China, and the two countries take advantage of such opportunities to engage in dialogues at the working level. In addition, as a way to exchange mid-level leaders, mutual visits have been conducted through the Japan-China field officer exchange program organized by the Sasakawa Peace Foundation. In addition, in January 2025, the MOD accepted the visit of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Eastern Theater Command delegation to Japan as the first resumption of unit-to-unit exchanges in about five years. In October 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi held a summit meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the occasion of the APEC Summit Meeting. The two leaders reaffirmed Japan and China’s broad direction of comprehensively promoting a “Mutually Beneficial Relationship Based on Common Strategic Interests” and building “constructive and stable Japan-China relations.” In addition, Prime Minister Takaichi expressed Japan’s serious concerns over China’s escalation and marine survey activities in the East China Sea, including around the Senkaku Islands, and the intensification of Chinese military activities near Japan, and urged the Chinese side to address these issues. The two leaders also concurred on the importance of ensuring effective crisis management and communication between defense authorities.

On the occasion of the ADMM-Plus meeting in November 2025, Defense Minister Koizumi had a meeting with Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun, and he emphasized that, in order to achieve the broad direction agreed to by the leaders of Japan and China, which is to comprehensively promote a mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests and build constructive and stable Japan-China relations, it is essential not to ignore specific challenging issues and to repeatedly engage in candid discussions and communication. In addition, the Defense Minister conveyed once again his serious concerns about China’s activities around the Senkaku Islands, an inherent part of the territory of Japan, as well as China’s increased military activities in Japan’s waters and airspace including its collaboration with Russia, and other activities. Furthermore, he pointed out the importance of ensuring the appropriate and reliable operation of the Hotline between Japanese and Chinese Defense Authorities, and the two leaders agreed on the importance of strengthening dialogues and exchanges between the two countries at all levels, including their defense authorities. As part of the Japan-China Field Officer Exchange Program conducted by the Sasakawa Peace Foundation, a delegation of 13 JSDF field officers visited China and held an exchange with the PLA. During the event, the delegation visited the Vice President of the Academy of Military Sciences, and the participants also toured the Zhanjiang Naval Base and other Army, Navy, and Air Force military facilities, where they exchanged views with military stakeholders.

(3) Maritime and Aerial Communication Mechanism between the Defense Authorities of Japan and China Utilization of the Maritime and Aerial Communication Mechanism began in June 2018. The “Maritime and Aerial Communication Mechanism between the Defense Authorities of Japan and China” has been developed (1) to promote mutual understanding and confidence between Japan and China and to enhance bilateral defense cooperation and exchanges; (2) to avoid unexpected collisions; and (3) to prevent unforeseen circumstances in the sea and air from developing into military clashes or political or diplomatic issues. The mechanism’s main components include (1) annual and expert meetings between the two countries’ defense authorities; (2) a hotline between Japanese and Chinese defense authorities; and (3) on scene communication measures between vessels and aircraft of the JSDF and the PLA. noted that while the Indo-Pacific is a region indispensable to global peace and prosperity, it is also facing a severe reality, including attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion, economic coercion, and information manipulation. The JSDF had been participating in the exercise as an observer since 2012. However, in FY2025, the JSDF dispatched MSDF vessels and other assets for the first time, and participated in a field training exercise for multilateral maritime maneuvers; subject matter expert exchanges related to integrated air and missile defense, responses to cyberattacks, etc.; humanitarian and civil assistance activities; and more.

Strategic Significance of the UK Carrier Strike Group’s Deployment to the Indo-Pacific The deployment of the UK Carrier Strike Group to the Indo-Pacific was a landmark event, symbolising the UK’s strategic intent to play a proactive role in the region. The CSG projected hard power while delivering significant diplomatic, economic, and soft power outcomes. It laid the groundwork for deeper cooperation to ensure national security and prosperity amongst like-minded partners. The deployment demonstrated the flexibility and responsiveness of maritime forces, able to react to world events on a global scale to provide choice to governments and freedom of action. Beyond the direct military benefits, the deployment also was a driver of strategic growth, with significant capability partnership and export opportunities supported throughout the region across multiple domains, including Maritime, Air, Cyber, and Complex Weapons. The breadth of opportunities under discussion underscores the UK’s role as a trusted strategic and economic partner. Building on the UK’s 2021 deployment to the region, Operation HIGHMAST marked a step-change in the UK’s strategic presence in the Indo-Pacific. By leveraging high-profile defence engagements, strengthening bilateral relationships, and fostering industry collaboration, objectives in security, diplomacy, and economic growth were realised. The deployment also highlighted the value of integrated government efforts and the unique convening power of Carrier Strike Groups.

2 Initiatives to Support UN PKO and other activities As a means to promote peace and stability in conflict regions around the world, UN PKOs have expanded their missions in recent years to include such duties as the Protection of Civilians (POC), the promotion of political processes, providing assistance in Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration (DDR) into society of former soldiers, Security Sector Reform (SSR), the rule of law, elections, human rights and other fields, in addition to such traditional missions as ceasefire monitoring. International organizations such as the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), respective governments, Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), and others conduct relief and restoration activities for the victims of conflicts and large-scale disasters from a humanitarian perspective and from the viewpoint of stabilizing affected countries. Japan has been promoting international peace cooperation assignments in various regions, including Cambodia, the Golan Heights, Timor-Leste, Nepal and South Sudan for more than 30 years and these activities have been highly praised both domestically and internationally. Currently, Japan dispatches staff officers to the United Nations Mission in the Republic of South Sudan (UNMISS) and the Multinational Force and Observers (MFO). 1 What is Women, Peace and Security (WPS)? Women, Peace and Security (WPS) is a concept that encapsulates the idea that peace is more sustainable when women take the lead and actively participate in all levels of conflict prevention, reconstruction, and peacebuilding, as well as disaster prevention, response and reconstruction, while recognizing the importance of protection and relief for women and girls, and those in need, as they are more vulnerable during conflicts and disasters. In the 1990s, large-scale sexual violence in conflict as seen in former Yugoslavia, the civil war in Rwanda, and other conflicts drew worldwide attention. In addition, the Beijing Declaration and the Platform for Action was adopted at the Fourth World Conference on Women in 1995. Increasing the participation of women in conflict resolution at decision-making levels and protecting women living in situations of armed or other conflicts or under foreign occupation was stipulated as one of the key strategic objectives in the document. Furthermore, the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court adopted in 1998 stipulated sexual violence in conflict as a war crime. Against this international backdrop, the United Nations Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 1325 on Women, Peace and Security (WPS) in 2000. This was the first Security Council Resolution focusing on the issues surrounding women in conflict. The resolution requires gender mainstreaming9 in all efforts of its four pillars: Participation, Prevention, Protection, and Relief and Recovery. Since then, nine Security Council Resolutions related to WPS have been successively adopted, complementing UNSCR 1325. The efforts described in these ten resolutions are collectively referred to as the “WPS agenda.” In recent years, given increasing uncertainty in the international situation, the concept of WPS has increased in significance. Gender Gender refers to “the socially and culturally constructed differences that society attributes to sexes.” While the term “sex” defines differences in biological and physiological characteristics acquired at birth, the term “gender” defines differences in socially and culturally constructed characteristics of the image of “a man” and of “a woman” commonly found in social norms and customs. These “socially and culturally constructed differences that society attributes to sexes” (genders) do not in themselves contain positive or negative values and are used internationally.

Section 2 Responding to Climate Change and Environmental Issues According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the average global temperature in 2025 exceeded the pre-industrial 1850-1900 baseline by 1.43°C. The period from 2015 to 2025 was the warmest 11-year period on record, with the loss of glacier ice, rising sea levels, accelerated ocean warming, and extreme weather events causing major damage to societies and economies around the world. Regarding the response to climate change and other environmental issues, countries around the world have been making efforts on this front following the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) at the UN and the Paris Agreement, an international framework on climate change, in 2015. Japan is also advancing specific climate change measures based on various plans formulated under the Basic Act on the Environment, the Climate Change Adaptation Act, and the Act on Promotion of Global Warming Countermeasures. Furthermore, it has been pointed out that climate change will also cause heavy rains, droughts, and increases in the proportion of high-intensity tropical cyclones, as well as other problems that will destroy houses and infrastructure, cause loss of properties and livelihoods, and affect food and water security, and therefore increase the likelihood of conflict. Climate change will also affect military equipment, infrastructure, and operations themselves. In July 2024, NATO released the Secretary General’s annual Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. In addition to the impact of climate change on each operational domain, the report noted that military conflict is a significant factor in climate change and environmental destruction and addressed the climate impact of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. In response to this acceleration of domestic and overseas efforts, the Ministry of Defense/Japan Self-Defense Forces (MOD/JSDF) also needs to respond to various climate change and environmental issues and contribute to their resolution while implementing measures with a greater focus on the coexistence of JSDF/USFJ facilities/areas with the surrounding areas. In addition, the issue of climate change will have an even greater impact on future MOD/JSDF operations, various plans, facilities, and equipment, as well as on the security environment surrounding Japan, including responses to future energy shifts, all of which must be addressed in an appropriate manner.

In recent years, the security environment surrounding Japan has become increasingly severe and complex, and the challenges faced by the MOD/JSDF are also changing at a pace far exceeding initial expectations. For example, learning the lessons from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, it is necessary for Japan to work to secure and maintain sustained operational capability and strongly address supply chain risks in the defense industry. Furthermore, as countries actively invest in cutting-edge science and technologies, including those in defense areas, competition intensifies, and new ways of warfare emerge and are evolving day by day, it is necessary to actively incorporate cutting-edge civilian technologies and rapidly develop and strengthen the defense technology base. • “New Ways of Warfare” and Defense Production and Technological Bases Rapid advances in science and technology in recent years have brought about fundamental changes in the nature of national security. Countries are accelerating research and development to ensure their technological superiority, especially through the acquisition of cutting-edge technologies that could become so-called “game changers” which dramatically alter the future character of warfare. New technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), quantum technology, and new forms of energy utilization are being applied to equipment,1 expanding the character of warfare not only in the conventional domains such as ground, maritime, and air, but also into space, cyber, and electromagnetic domains, including the cognitive dimension. In addition, the rapid advancements of information-related technologies and information infrastructure, such as AI and Social Networking Service (SNS), have dramatically increased the risk of hybrid warfare, in which military and non-military means are combined, and the expansion of information warfare through the spread of disinformation.

Amid the demand for fundamental reinforcement of defense capabilities, the role of the defense industry is becoming increasingly important in securing equipment for the Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF) to carry out its missions. Especially when manufacturing defense equipment,1 it is necessary to invest considerable management resources to meet the high level of functional and performance requirements and information security measures. Companies require a certain degree of predictability in order to justify such investments from an economic standpoint. Furthermore, these companies are required to produce a wide variety of products in small quantities, and in addition, due to the long operating period of equipment, it is also necessary for them to secure manufacturing and other systems over the long term. Moreover, basically their only customers are the MOD/JSDF, so production volume is extremely limited, and opportunities for companies to recoup their investments also remain limited. In addition, there are still some companies that harbor aversion to the defense business or that face reputational risks. As a result of these circumstances, Japan’s defense industry is facing various challenges, with cases of companies deciding to withdraw from defense businesses or downsize their operations emerging intermittently. Consequently, this not only interferes with the stable procurement of defense equipment essential for JSDF operations, but also causes the loss of a proper competitive environment and innovation in the long term, resulting in Japan losing its technological superiority in the field of national security. In addition to these factors, as the digital transformation (DX) of the contract performance environment for defense-related businesses has rapidly progressed in recent years, the defense industry, which holds sensitive information, is facing the growing threat of suspected state-sponsored cyberattacks against its information systems and networks. Furthermore, in 2024, it was announced that communications equipment managed by a Japanese research institution had been compromised, resulting in unauthorized access to servers and the leakage of operational information. Companies require a certain degree of predictability in order to justify such investments from an economic standpoint. Furthermore, these companies are required to produce a wide variety of products in small quantities, and in addition, due to the long operating period of equipment, it is also necessary for them to secure manufacturing and other systems over the long term. Moreover, basically their only customers are the MOD/JSDF, so production volume is extremely limited, and opportunities for companies to recoup their investments also remain limited. In addition, there are still some companies that harbor aversion to the defense business or that face reputational risks. As a result of these circumstances, Japan’s defense industry is facing various challenges, with cases of companies deciding to withdraw from defense businesses or downsize their operations emerging intermittently. Consequently, this not only interferes with the stable procurement of defense equipment essential for JSDF operations, but also causes the loss of a proper competitive environment and innovation in the long term, resulting in Japan losing its technological superiority in the field of national security. In addition to these factors, as the digital transformation (DX) of the contract performance environment for defense-related businesses has rapidly progressed in recent years, the defense industry, which holds sensitive information, is facing the growing threat of suspected state-sponsored cyberattacks against its information systems and networks. For example, in 2021, it was announced that a large-scale cyberattack had been carried out against approximately 200 companies and research institutions in Japan, including defense-related businesses, by a cyberattack group highly likely to be linked to the Chinese military. Furthermore, in 2024, it was announced that communications equipment managed by a Japanese research institution had been compromised, resulting in unauthorized access to servers and the leakage of operational information. Moreover, as the international trend of hoarding critical resources grows, the risk of being unable to import raw

materials due to export restrictions imposed by foreign governments, for example, and thus being unable to secure a stable supply of equipment, is becoming a reality. In light of this environment surrounding Japan’s defense production and technological bases, the MOD/JSDF is taking various measures to maintain and reinforce the bases. ONO Keishi, Senior Fellow, Security and Economy Division, National Institute for Defense Studies There are “structural challenges” facing Japan’s defense industry. Amid increasingly sophisticated equipment, rising tensions in the international environment, and intensifying competition for technological hegemony, conventional models of procurement and production are nearing their limits. In particular, (1) security of supply chains, (2) decline of skilled personnel, and (3) cybersecurity vulnerabilities are serious risks that could destabilize the defense industrial base itself. The first challenge is supply chain security. Defense equipment is composed of thousands of components, electronic parts, and software. A compromise in the reliability of even one of these elements directly affects the security of the equipment as a whole. In recent years, technologies with high dual-use potential, including submarine communications infrastructure and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, have become focal points of international security concern. Tightening of investment screening for acquisitions of foreign companies along with export controls on rare metals by certain countries point to the geopolitical risks facing supply chains. Given the possibility that the production of ammunition, sensors, power semiconductors, and other items could be affected, it is essential to strengthen traceability; secure alternative procurement sources, including urban mining for rare metals; and expand stockpiles of strategic materials.

The second challenge is the weakening of the human resource base. The manufacture and maintenance of defense equipment require skilled workers with advanced processing techniques and tacit knowledge. However, as large numbers of the baby-boomer generation continue to leave the workforce, the hiring of young workers has not sufficiently progressed, and the succession of skills has lagged behind. For small and medium-sized suppliers in particular, order instability and low profitability have made it difficult to secure personnel. As the defense industry is centered on high-mix, low-volume production, a loss of skills immediately leads to degradation in quality and delivery delays. In addition, the market for defense equipment is smaller than that for civilian products, and exports are also limited, creating structural constraints that make it difficult for companies to undertake capital investment and human resource development. The third challenge concerns the rise of cyberattacks centered on downstream segments of the supply chain. In recent years, methods of stealing sensitive information through subcontractors with vulnerable security systems have been increasing. Domestically, successive ransomware attacks in general industry sectors have made it clear that vulnerabilities in information management can be exploited from the outside. For defense-related companies, the leakage of design drawings or test data would not only result in the loss of technological superiority, but also constitute a serious loss from the perspective of national security. While there is a need to unify security standards across the entire supply chain, introduce an audit system, and establish a Zero Trust information management framework, the cost burden on small and medium-sized enterprises is significant, making support measures for implementation essential. These three challenges are interconnected. Going forward, it will be necessary to adopt a perspective that redefines the defense industry as foundational national security infrastructure, while rebalancing efficiency and redundancy. What is now being called into question is “industrial policy as security,” which cannot be measured in terms of economic rationality alone. 4 Establishment of the Defense Science and Technology Board The MOD/JSDF have executed their missions in a limited and restrained manner, taking into account historical circumstances and various post-war constraints. For this reason, a broader perspective encompassing the security of the entire nation and the enhancement of national strength has not been sufficiently cultivated. As a result, there has been a tendency to place importance on considerations based on internal JSDF requirements, such as the functionality and performance of equipment. Nonetheless, given the current situation that the MOD’s role and budget size within the overall government have expanded in recent years, this is insufficient and going forward it will become increasingly important to also incorporate the perspective of how the development of science and technology through the development of defense capabilities can contribute to the development of the entire nation. Given these challenges, establishment of a broad outlook that also considers the ripple effects on the entire nation is essential when considering the various challenges related to science, technology, and security that the MOD will face going forward. For that reason, there is a need to build a structure to foster cooperation not just within the MOD but also with diverse external entities and a broad community so that the enhancement of science and technology capabilities through the development of defense capabilities contributes to the enhancement of Japan’s overall national strength, and a need to build a system to support this structure. Against this backdrop, the Defense Science and Technology Board (DSTB) was established in June 2025 as a permanent body to provide necessary advice and recommendations to the Defense Minister on various challenges related to science, technology, and security. The DSTB is composed of academics, practitioners, and others with expertise in science and technology, primarily in fields such as AI, space, and cybersecurity. A total of six meetings of the DSTB had been held by March 2026.

Since 1992, Japan has implemented 29 cooperative research projects and two cooperative development projects with the United States. At present, Japan and the United States are implementing five cooperative research projects: (1) Modular Hybrid Electric Vehicle System, (2) Overwhelming Response through Collaborative Autonomy, (3) High-Power Microwave (HPM) systems, (4) Unmanned Underwater Vehicle Resilience (Underwater Obstacle Avoidance), and (5) Safety Assurance Technology for AI-Equipped Unmanned Aerial Vehicles. The two countries are also conducting mutual dispatch of scientist and engineer personnel. In addition, in order to address the challenge of intercepting hypersonic glide vehicles (HGVs) during the glide phase by leveraging the technologies of both countries together, Japan and the United States decided in August 2023 to commence the cooperative development of the Glide Phase Interceptor (GPI). Furthermore, in June 2025, the Japan MOD and U.S. Department of War signed the Project Arrangement concerning Japan-U.S. Cooperative Research on Unmanned Underwater Vehicle Resilience (Underwater Obstacle Avoidance). This research aims to enhance the situational awareness and response capabilities required to detect and avoid navigational hazards for unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) in complex real-ocean environments, in order to support increasingly long-duration missions required in underwater warfare. Moreover, in September 2025, the Japan MOD and U.S. DoW signed the Project Arrangement concerning Cooperative Research on The Strategic Advancement of Mutual Runtime Assurance Artificial Intelligence (Safety Assurance Technology for AI-equipped Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs)). This research seeks to ensure the safety of AI-equipped UAVs through cooperative joint research on Runtime Assurance (RTA)5 technology. The outcomes obtained through this research are expected to be applied to UAVs and other systems that operate in collaboration with next-generation fighter aircraft.

1 Uniformed JSDF Personnel Japan consists of around 14,000 islands. In order to defend this vast land surrounded by the sea on all sides, uniformed JSDF personnel fulfill their responsibilities 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, without regard for personal danger even under harsh conditions at home and overseas. The JSDF conducts activities to protect Japan’s territorial land, waters, and airspace under the mission of safeguarding the nation’s peace and independence. The Ground Self-Defense Force (GSDF) maintains readiness through initial response units operating 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, engaging in continuous training in preparation for disaster relief operations, contingencies, and other events to protect the lives of the people at their closest level. The Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) conducts round-the-clock, year-round activities, such as warning and surveillance, to contribute to the peace and stability of the expansive territorial waters of Japan, a maritime nation. The Air Self-Defense Force (ASDF) protects Japan’s airspace, performing scrambles day and night and ensuring the stable use of outer space. The deterrence of Japan is sustained by the presence and activities of these JSDF services and their personnel. In recent years, threats utilizing cyberspace, the maritime domain, outer space, and the electromagnetic spectrum have intensified rapidly, and the JSDF has expanded its activities into an increasingly diverse range of fields. In addition, in order to protect the lives and property of the people in the event of large-scale natural disasters, aircraft accidents, and other events, the JSDF maintains readiness to conduct swift life-saving operations, search activities, and the transportation of emergency patients from remote islands and other areas. To ensure prompt and appropriate responses to various forms of disaster, disaster relief operation plans are formulated, and regular training is conducted to enhance the effectiveness of those plans.

2 Defense Officials, Instructors, and Other Talent Administrative officials are responsible for planning and developing various policies pertaining to overall security policy, including defense administration and JSDF operations, mainly at the internal bureaus of the MOD and the Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency (ATLA). They also handle the collection, analysis, and evaluation of international affairs information at the Defense Intelligence Headquarters (DIH) and perform administrative tasks at JSDF, the Regional Defense Bureaus, and other locations nationwide. Several countries and regions surrounding Japan possess significant military capabilities, including nuclear weapons, and there has been a pronounced trend toward intensifying military activities. Against this backdrop, administrative officials specialists in defense policy who help preserve peace, protect Japan, and secure its future are expected to play an ever more active role. Effective defense policies aligned with Japan’s national interests require capable organizations and qualified personnel to develop and implement them. Furthermore, the JSDF cannot be operated without a legal framework. As the MOD/JSDF can fulfill their missions only with the trust and understanding of the Japanese people, they must also communicate clearly with the public and provide accurate information. The balance of power among nations is becoming increasingly complex and the use of new domains, such as outer space, cyberspace, and the electromagnetic spectrum, is expanding rapidly, transforming the security environment in profound ways. Even amid these rapid changes, administrative officials play a key role in addressing a wide range of security challenges in order to protect Japan’s peace and security. They also carry out administrative and logistical functions necessary to establish the foundations for unit operations at camps, bases, and other facilities throughout Japan. For example, at the General Service Units established within GSDF camps, administrative officials perform services related to the maintenance and management of camp and maneuver area facilities, as well as welfare services for assigned personnel.

I perform diverse daily duties, ranging from system maintenance and management, coordinating with highly specialized private enterprises and supervising their work, to monitoring for cyberattacks. These duties form the foundational basis of Japan’s space security. The space domain today cannot be discussed in isolation from the cyber domain. In the aggression against Ukraine, large-scale cyberattacks have been launched on satellite communication networks. As these attacks demonstrate, space and cyberspace are increasingly integrated and inseparable domains in recent years. Cyberattacks on systems significantly impact the execution of our mission and create critical gaps in the stable use of outer space. As such, cyber defense, including initial response, continues to rise in importance. At the field level, we place constant emphasis on coordination with cyber units and maintain a robust monitoring posture. In modern warfare, the sustained and stable use of the space domain is essential for advanced operations across the land, maritime, and air domains. 5 Human Resources Development Based on the DBP, the GSDF High Technical School will be jointly operated by the GSDF, MSDF, and ASDF as well as transformed into a coeducational school from FY2028. The MOD/JSDF will strengthen the joint education in each JSDF service as well as education and research including those of the cyber domain in each JSDF service and at the National Defense Academy. At the same time, the MOD/JSDF will promote standardization of the curriculum education and utilization of state-of-the-art technologies. Additionally, in order to cultivate and produce personnel possessing foreign language proficiency, networks with officer candidates from other countries, and understanding of foreign defense policies, the National Defense Academy introduced a curriculum enabling its students to undertake four-year study programs at the U.S. service academies and other institutions. Beginning in FY2025, it has sent students to the U.S. service academies. Furthermore, education requires considerable human, time, and economic commitment, including securing instructors with special skills as well as improving equipment and educational facilities. In the event that personnel need to further improve their professional knowledge and skills, or that it is difficult for them to acquire such knowledge and skills within the JSDF, the MOD/JSDF commissions education to external institutions, including those abroad, as well as domestic companies and research institutes.

6 Initiatives for Retirement and Re-employment (1) Raising of Mandatory Retirement Age To adapt to increasingly sophisticated equipment, diversified missions, and internationalization, it is important to more effectively utilize personnel who possess extensive knowledge, skills, and experience. Accordingly, between 2020 and 2024, the mandatory retirement ages for JSDF personnel holding ranks from Issa (Colonel (GSDF, ASDF)/ Captain (MSDF)) through Sanso (Sergeant (GSDF)/Staff Sergeant (ASDF)/Petty Officer 3rd Class (MSDF)) were each extended by two years. In line with the Basic Policy and with a view to effectively utilizing personnel’s accumulated knowledge, skills, and experience and establishing their lifetime career plans, it was decided to raise the mandatory retirement ages for JSDF personnel holding ranks from Sho (General/Lieutenant General (GSDF, ASDF)/Admiral/ Vice Admiral (MSDF)), to Sanso by two years each between 2028 and 2032, while balancing extended healthy longevity with the maintenance of their strength. Furthermore, the categories of personnel subject to the mandatory retirement age of 60 have been expanded to include nurses (commissioned officers), JSDF personnel assigned to space fields, and JSDF personnel engaged in cyber-related duties. It was decided to raise their mandatory retirement age incrementally by one year every two years from 2028 to age

Thus far, the scope of duties available to reappointed JSDF personnel has been expanded to include auxiliary vessel crew operations and aircraft pilotage tasks, cyberspace and flight inspection tasks, and space-domain awareness tasks. 1 Background and Objectives of the Cyber Workforce Comprehensive Strategy The Defense Buildup Program states that the establishment of posture, even under cyberattacks, to secure the JSDF’s command and control capabilities as well as its high-priority equipment systems, ensure JSDF’s mission accomplishment, and build a framework to support the cyber defense of the defense industry. Accordingly, by around FY2027, cyber units such as the JSDF Cyber Defense Command will be expanded to approximately 4,000 personnel. Besides, by providing an education to those engaged in cyber-related duties such as system procurement, maintenance, and operation, the total number of cyber workforce within the MOD/JSDF is planned to reach about 20,000. Amid this situation, the environment surrounding the recruitment and retention of MOD/JSDF personnel has grown increasingly severe every year, while at the same time the importance of cyber workforce has been rising across society. To this end, the MOD/JSDF will (1) ensure consistency within its policy for securing and developing its workforce and promote consideration of measures for workforce and cross-organizational cooperation related to human resources, and (2) clarify the ideas of the MOD/JSDF regarding cyber workforce and approaching those who aspire to join the MOD/JSDF and external cyber workforce while developing and deepening cooperative relationships with external entities. For these purposes, in July 2024, the MOD/JSDF consolidated the basic review directions into a strategy and published the “JMOD Cyber Workforce Comprehensive Strategy.” Reference 84 (The MOD Cyber Workforce Comprehensive Strategy)

3 Direction of Initiatives Related to the Cyber Workforce In order to secure an excellent cyber workforce for the MOD/ JSDF, the organizations must recruit and train a wide range of human resources, including those who are interested in MOD/JSDF cyber operations and those with extensive cyber expertise. To this end, efforts will be guided by five pillars: (1) accurate “identification” of the skills and capabilities required of a cyber workforce, (2) appropriate “recruitment” for cyber workforce, (3) appropriate “development,” (4) “retention” of a workforce, and (5) “unification” of the entire HR measures. Under these pillars, the following initiatives will advance the recruitment of human resources. (1) Initiatives for Securing the Cyber Workforce In order to further enhance the expertise of those who aspire to work in the cyber field, the MOD/JSDF will establish a career path to continuously engage in cyber-related work from the beginning of service. In addition, those who already have specialized expertise, qualifications, and work experience related to the cyber will be hired as specific fixed-term JSDF personnel, mid-career COs, or technical sergeants and will be flexibly appointed to jobs and posts where they can make use of their experience. Furthermore, the MOD/JSDF will reinforce recruitment by reaching out to an external cyber workforce while making it easier for people to imagine working at the MOD. To this end, the MOD/JSDF will establish career paths tailored to the characteristics of COs, NCOs, AOs, TOs, and others and increase the visibility of career paths of personnel engaged in cyber operations, as well as highlight attractive work experiences in the MOD. With regard to JSDF Cyber reserve personnel15 who possess cyber skills and serve in various missions together with regular JSDF personnel, they demonstrated a high level of skill and motivation during the multilateral cyber defense exercise “Locked Shields 2025” and contributed to the Japanese team in FY2025. The MOD/JSDF will also steadily advance initiatives, such as recruiting external cyber workforce with no JSDF experience as Candidates for JSDF reserve personnel and appointing them as JSDF Cyber reserve personnel. Additionally, using the JSDF Scholarship Program, which provides a fixed amount of educational funding each month, learning support will be provided to outstanding students

(2) Initiatives for Training the Cyber Workforce The MOD/JSDF possesses specialized institutions including the GSDF System and Signal/Cyber School. It is not necessary to have knowledge of JSDF operations or cyber-related knowledge in advance. Personnel can acquire cyber knowledge, depending on their level, after joining the JSDF with additional opportunities for training and studying externally. In addition, environments are currently in place for persons with advanced cyber skills field to hone their skills through a wealth of opportunities such as practical training and exchange of opinions. Leveraging these strength, the MOD/JSDF will recruit human resources interested in engaging in the MOD/JSDF cyber operations in the MOD/ JSDF and becoming part of a highly skilled cyber workforce. In order to respond to cyberattacks, which are becoming more advanced and sophisticated every day and now pose a serious threat to national security, it is vital to secure and develop an excellent cyber workforce. As the importance of the cyber workforce increases across society, it is believed that creating a virtuous cycle of the cyber workforce between the MOD and the private sector will lead to raising the level of the cyber response capabilities of Japan overall. Based on this recognition, in July 2024, the MOD formulated the MOD Cyber Workforce Comprehensive Strategy, which comprehensively presents the MOD/ JSDF’s basic approach with regard to securing and developing the cyber workforce.

In order to deepen expertise in the cyber field, it is essential to establish career paths that allow personnel to continuously engage in cyber-related duties after joining the JSDF. To achieve such career paths, an examination category covering cyber and other specialized fields was established as a recruitment category for the Employment Examination for General Officer Candidates (Ground Self-Defense Force). Recruitment under this category began in FY2025. Personnel recruited through this category are expected to cultivate further expertise primarily through assignments in cyber units, while also undergoing further education and training within and outside the organization. In the future, they will become commanders of cyber units and play a key role in Japan’s cybersecurity field. The MOD/JSDF will continue to advance the necessary initiatives to secure and develop the cyber workforce, focusing on the measures outlined in the strategy. JSDF reserve personnel participating in an international cyber exercise Commentary The MOD Cyber Workforce Comprehensive Strategy

In the future, they will become commanders of cyber units and play a key role in Japan’s cybersecurity field. The MOD/JSDF will continue to advance the necessary initiatives to secure and develop the cyber workforce, focusing on the measures outlined in the strategy. 1 Working Style Reform to Further Promote Work-Life Balance (1) Improving “Sense of Worthwhile Engagement” and Ensuring “Sense of Comfort” To enable each employee to perform their duties with a greater sense of worthwhile engagement, employees themselves will be encouraged to develop a clear understanding of and articulate their medium- to long-term career aspirations. At the same time, senior officials and others will undertake systematic and organization-wide efforts to further enhance sense of worthwhile engagement. In addition, the MOD/JSDF will promote reviews of work processes aimed at rectifying long working hours and improving productivity, while ensuring flexibility in work hours and locations, improving working environments, and developing an environment with zero tolerance for harassment of any kind. As improvements in the quality and quantity of operations are being sought after in defense administration, internal bureaus are encouraging endeavors to boost the sense of worthwhile engagement of all employees to maximize organizational performance. Boosting a sense of worthwhile engagement requires increasing both (1) a work motivation that arises from a sense of mission, feedback from others, and a keen sense of personal growth, and (2) sense of comfort derived from the workplace environment, personal relationships, and mental and physical well-being, and then TAO Issei, Captain (GSDF), Operations and Planning Officer, GSDF Cyber Protection Unit (Ichigaya) I belong to the Ground Self-Defense Force (GSDF) Cyber Protection Unit, which works around the clock to respond to various threats and protect the GSDF’s information systems from cyberattacks and other threats. I am in charge of education and training related to countering these threats. We provide trainings within and outside the JSDF, with the aim of enhancing the knowledge, skills, and operational effectiveness necessary for protecting units from cyberattacks.

Because multilateral cooperation is critical for dealing with all cyber threats, we actively participate in multilateral trainings with our ally and like-minded countries, including the U.S. and U.K. forces, for further strengthening our capabilities. The insights obtained through multilateral trainings and from persons with a wide range of experiences have contributed to our understanding of international trends required for countering cyberattacks and other threats. I will continue dedicating myself to my duty to ensure that both our workforce and units remain capable of responding to increasingly diverse and sophisticated threats. Last but not least, I am aware that a digital category (covering cyber) has been added to the FY2025 Employment Examination for JSDF General Officer Candidates. I look forward to the day when we, as personnel sharing the same aspirations, can work together to contribute to the defense of Japan by applying the knowledge and experience we have gained. 2 Reinforcement of Policy-Making Function The NDS stipulates that, for the JSDF to fully exert its capabilities and respond to the severe, complex, and fast-paced strategic environment, strategic and agile defense policy planning and making are required, including in domains such as space, cyberspace, and electromagnetic spectrum. To fundamentally strengthen these functions, the NDS calls for closely cooperating with relevant ministries and agencies, private research institutions, and private companies, particularly those in the defense industry, as well as reviewing and reinforcing the research system of the MOD/ JSDF led by the National Institute for Defense Studies (NIDS) and reinforcing its function as an intellectual base.

7 Starting with programs that commenced in FY2024, NIDS has changed what had been the Regular Course to the National Security Strategist Studies Program, and the Special Course to the National Security Senior Strategist Studies Program, to explore and develop curricula that further improve strategic characteristics. and publishes a large volume of data on military history as a facility possessing historical documents and other materials in accordance with the Act on Management of Public Records and Archives, and serves as the largest research center on military history in Japan. In FY2023, the Cyber Security Division was established at NIDS in response to research needs in the increasingly important field of cybersecurity based on the DBP, which calls for a review of the research system to support the augmentation of the functions of strategic and agile defense policy planning and formulation, and reinforcement of the system’s functions as an intellectual foundation. NIDS, an institution that plays a role in defense exchange and security dialogue, also emphasizes international exchange and conducts research exchanges with defense universities, security research institutes, etc., in other countries with the main objective of improving the quality of its research and education and contributing to national security by strengthening relations of trust with said countries. Specifically, activities include mutual dispatch of researchers for lectures, holding study groups and participating in international conferences, receiving visits from foreign government and military officials, and inviting foreign researchers and experts. Through these exchanges, the NIDS is improving the quality of its research and studies and strengthening its intellectual network. In addition, NIDS publishes major research results on its website and proactively disseminates information by issuing various publications, including the “NIDS China Security Report,” “NIDS Perspectives,” and “Security & Strategy,” which have been published annually to date. It also publishes videos of sponsored events and explanatory videos on key points of publications. Researchers at NIDS have also published many books, articles, and essays on their research findings, and include recipients of the 34th Asia-Pacific Award Grand Prize and the 43rd Ishibashi Tanzan Award.
